abstract: A simple method for training the dynamical behavior of a neu(cid:173) ral network is derived. It is applicable to any training problem in discrete-time networks with arbitrary feedback. The algorithm resembles back-propagation in that an error function is minimized using a gradient-based method, but the optimization is carried out in the hidden part of state space either instead of, or in addition to weight space. Computational results are presented for some simple dynamical training problems, one of which requires response to a signal 100 time steps in the past.

paragraphs: The paper derives a method for training how a neural network behaves over time. It applies to discrete-time networks with arbitrary feedback, allowing the training problem to involve recurrent interactions rather than only a one-way passage from input to output. The objective is to learn dynamical behavior through a gradient-based optimization procedure.

Like backpropagation, the method minimizes an error function. Its distinctive choice is where optimization occurs: the hidden portion of the network's state space can be adjusted instead of, or alongside, its weights. This makes internal states part of the training search, expanding the quantities through which the desired behavior can be pursued.

The authors present computational results on simple dynamical tasks. One requires responding to a signal encountered 100 time steps earlier, making delayed influence a concrete part of the evaluation. The paper's contribution is a training formulation centered on hidden states, together with examples that exercise temporal behavior and a dependency extending far back in the input sequence.
summary.tldr: Moving Targets trains network dynamics by optimizing hidden states, alone or alongside weights, including on a task with a 100-step delay.

title: The "Moving Targets" Training Algorithm

Our chip computes the zero-crossings associated with the difference of two ex(cid:173) ponential weighting functions. If the derivative across this zero-crossing is above a threshold, an edge is reported. Simulations indicate that this technique will extend well to two dimensions.

paragraphs: The authors built and tested an analog chip that finds changes in image intensity in real time. The device contains a one-dimensional array of 64 pixels and includes its own photoreceptors. Its purpose is to locate edges through computation performed directly by the sensing hardware and connected analog circuitry.

The design uses the filtering behavior of resistive networks. It subtracts the results of two exponential weighting functions and looks for zero-crossings, where the difference changes sign. An edge is reported only when the derivative across that crossing exceeds a threshold. This combines a candidate edge location with a requirement that the local change be sufficiently strong.

The method is motivated by the Difference of Gaussians approach to edge detection, but the implemented weighting functions are exponential. The paper’s hardware result is the tested one-dimensional chip; simulations suggest the technique can also extend to two dimensions. The contribution connects a visual filtering principle with a concrete analog implementation capable of real-time operation.
summary.tldr: A 64-pixel analog chip detects intensity edges in real time using filtered differences and thresholded zero-crossings.

title: An Analog VLSI Chip for Finding Edges from Zero-crossings

paragraphs: This paper turns a theory of psychological generalization into a connectionist model. The starting observation is that learning transfers less strongly as a test stimulus becomes more distant from a training stimulus in a space representing perceived similarity. Empirically, this decline closely follows an exponential relationship, giving the theory a specific pattern to explain.

The theory assumes that an observed consequential stimulus belongs to a broader consequential region. The learner knows that the observed stimulus lies inside this region, but initially does not know the region's position, size, or shape. Uncertainty about that region supplies a mathematical basis for predicting how strongly learning should extend to other stimuli.

Additional examples indicate which stimuli do or do not have the consequence. The theory predicts that generalization then changes toward the actual relationship between stimulus location and consequence probability. The paper implements this account in a neural model and uses simulations to explore its implications for generalization, discrimination, and classification. This makes an abstract account of similarity-based learning available for computational investigation.
summary.tldr: A connectionist implementation explores how uncertainty about consequential stimulus regions shapes generalization and changes with experience.

title: Connectionist Implementation of a Theory of Generalization

abstract: Do you want your neural net algorithm to learn sequences? Do not lim(cid:173) it yourself to conventional gradient descent (or approximations thereof). Instead, use your sequence learning algorithm (any will do) to implement the following method for history compression. No matter what your fi(cid:173) nal goals are, train a network to predict its next input from the previous ones. Since only unpredictable inputs convey new information, ignore all predictable inputs but let all unexpected inputs (plus information about the time step at which they occurred) become inputs to a higher-level network of the same kind (working on a slower, self-adjusting time scale). Go on building a hierarchy of such networks. This principle reduces the descriptions of event sequences without 1088 of information, thus easing supervised or reinforcement learning tasks. Alternatively, you may use two recurrent networks to collapse a multi-level predictor hierarchy into a single recurrent net. Experiments show that systems based on these prin(cid:173) ciples can require less computation per time step and many fewer training sequences than conventional training algorithms for recurrent nets. Final(cid:173) ly you can modify the above method such that predictability is not defined in a yes-or-no fashion but in a continuous fashion.

paragraphs: This paper proposes compressing sequence history by learning what can already be predicted. A network first learns to predict its next input from previous inputs. Predictable events need not be passed upward individually; unexpected inputs, together with their occurrence times, become the input to a higher-level predictor.

Repeating this process builds a hierarchy whose higher levels operate on slower, self-adjusting timescales. Each level focuses on events that the level below could not predict. The authors describe the resulting sequence representations as reduced without loss of information, with timing retained as part of the description. These representations are intended to make supervised or reinforcement learning easier.

The paper also describes using two recurrent networks to collapse a predictor hierarchy into a single recurrent network, and extending predictability from a binary decision to a continuous quantity. Experiments show that systems based on these principles can need less computation per step and many fewer training sequences than conventional recurrent-network training. The contribution is a way of organizing sequence information that can work with different learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of predictors compresses sequences by passing unexpected events and their timing upward, reducing learning and computational demands in experiments.

title: Learning Unambiguous Reduced Sequence Descriptions

abstract: FaceSync is an optimal linear algorithm that finds the degree of syn(cid:173) chronization between the audio and image recordings of a human speaker. Using canonical correlation, it finds the best direction to com(cid:173) bine all the audio and image data, projecting them onto a single axis. FaceSync uses Pearson's correlation to measure the degree of synchro(cid:173) nization between the audio and image data. We derive the optimal linear transform to combine the audio and visual information and describe an implementation that avoids the numerical problems caused by comput(cid:173) ing the correlation matrices. 1 Motivation In many applications, we want to know about the synchronization between an audio signal and the corresponding image data. In a teleconferencing system, we might want to know which of the several people imaged by a camera is heard by the microphones; then, we can direct the camera to the speaker. In post-production for a film, clean audio dialog is often dubbed over the video; we want to adjust the audio signal so that the lip-sync is perfect. When analyzing a film, we want to know when the person talking is in the shot, instead of off camera. When evaluating the quality of dubbed films, we can measure of how well the translated words and audio fit the actor's face. This paper describes an algorithm, FaceSync, that measures the degree of synchronization between the video image of a face and the associated audio signal. We can do this task by synthesizing the talking face, using techniques such as Video Rewrite [1], and then com(cid:173) paring the synthesized video with the test video. That process, however, is expensive. Our solution finds a linear operator that, when applied to the audio and video signals, generates an audio-video-synchronization-error signal. The linear operator gathers information from throughout the image and thus allows us to do the computation inexpensively. Hershey and Movellan [2] describe an approach based on measuring the mutual informa(cid:173) tion between the audio signal and individual pixels in the video. The correlation between the audio signal, x, and one pixel in the image y, is given by Pearson's correlation, r. The mutual information between these two variables is given by f(x,y) = -1/2 log(l-?). paragraphs: FaceSync measures how well a recording of a speaker's face is synchronized with its audio track. This can support tasks such as checking dubbed dialogue or determining which visible person is speaking. The paper treats synchronization as a relationship between audio and image measurements that can be extracted with a linear transformation.

The method uses canonical correlation to find directions that combine the audio and visual data into one-dimensional projections. Pearson correlation then measures their correspondence. By collecting information from across the image, the operator uses more than a single isolated pixel to characterize the relationship between facial activity and sound. Its stated optimality concerns the linear combination being derived.

The authors also describe an implementation that avoids numerical problems associated with computing correlation matrices. The resulting operator produces a synchronization-error signal inexpensively, without the face-synthesis process discussed as an alternative in the supplied text. The contribution combines a mathematically derived linear measure with an implementation intended to make audio-visual synchronization assessment computationally practical.
summary.tldr: FaceSync uses canonical correlation and a numerically careful linear implementation to measure synchronization between facial video and speech.

title: FaceSync: A Linear Operator for Measuring Synchronization of Video Facial Images and Audio Tracks

abstract: We consider learning to classify cognitive states of human subjects, based on their brain activity observed via functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). This problem is important because such classiﬁers con- stitute “virtual sensors” of hidden cognitive states, which may be useful in cognitive science research and clinical applications. In recent work, Mitchell, et al. [6,7,9] have demonstrated the feasibility of training such classiﬁers for individual human subjects (e.g., to distinguish whether the subject is reading an ambiguous or unambiguous sentence, or whether they are reading a noun or a verb). Here we extend that line of research, exploring how to train classiﬁers that can be applied across multiple hu- man subjects, including subjects who were not involved in training the classiﬁer. We describe the design of several machine learning approaches to training multiple-subject classiﬁers, and report experimental results demonstrating the success of these methods in learning cross-subject classiﬁers for two different fMRI data sets.

This problem is important because such classiﬁers con- stitute “virtual sensors” of hidden cognitive states, which may be useful in cognitive science research and clinical applications. In recent work, Mitchell, et al. [6,7,9] have demonstrated the feasibility of training such classiﬁers for individual human subjects (e.g., to distinguish whether the subject is reading an ambiguous or unambiguous sentence, or whether they are reading a noun or a verb). We describe the design of several machine learning approaches to training multiple-subject classiﬁers, and report experimental results demonstrating the success of these methods in learning cross-subject classiﬁers for two different fMRI data sets.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether brain activity measured with functional MRI can identify cognitive states across different people. Earlier work had shown that classifiers could be trained for individual participants, including distinctions between kinds of language-processing activity. The new question is whether a classifier can work beyond the particular person whose data helped train it.

The authors design several machine-learning approaches for training classifiers across multiple subjects. Their scope includes applying the resulting classifiers to people who did not participate in training. This makes cross-subject generalization the central requirement: the learned mapping between measured activity and cognitive state must remain useful when the person changes.

Experiments on two fMRI datasets demonstrate successful cross-subject classification. Such classifiers could serve as indirect sensors of otherwise hidden cognitive states, with possible uses in cognitive science and clinical applications. The reported contribution is evidence that this form of transfer across people can work on the studied datasets; the potential applications motivate the work rather than constitute demonstrated clinical outcomes.
summary.tldr: Several learning approaches successfully classify cognitive states from fMRI across subjects, including people absent from training.

title: Training fMRI Classifiers to Detect Cognitive States across Multiple Human Subjects

abstract: X-ray crystallography is currently the most common way protein structures are elucidated. One of the most time-consuming steps in the crystallographic process is interpretation of the electron density map, a task that involves finding patterns in a three-dimensional picture of a protein. This paper describes DEFT (DEFormable Template), an algorithm using pictorial structures to build a flexible protein model from the protein's amino-acid sequence. Matching this pictorial structure into the density map is a way of automating density-map interpretation. Also described are several extensions to the pictorial structure matching algorithm necessary for this automated interpretation. DEFT is tested on a set of density maps ranging from 2 to 4Å resolution, producing root- mean-squared errors ranging from 1.38 to 1.84Å.

paragraphs: Determining a protein structure from X-ray crystallography includes interpreting a three-dimensional electron density map. This pattern-finding step can take substantial time. The paper introduces DEFT, a deformable-template algorithm intended to automate that interpretation by matching a flexible protein model to the map.

DEFT builds its model from the protein's amino-acid sequence using pictorial structures. This representation gives the matching procedure a structured but flexible object to fit into the observed density. The paper also extends the pictorial-structure matching algorithm to support the requirements of automated density-map interpretation.

The authors test DEFT on density maps with resolutions from 2 to 4 Å and report root-mean-squared errors from 1.38 to 1.84 Å. These results provide a quantitative demonstration of the approach on the tested maps. The main significance is the connection between molecular modeling and structured visual matching: sequence information defines the protein model, while the density map supplies the spatial evidence used to position that flexible structure.
summary.tldr: DEFT fits a flexible protein model built from its amino-acid sequence into electron density maps to automate crystallographic interpretation.

title: Pictorial Structures for Molecular Modeling: Interpreting Density Maps

abstract: Long-distance language modeling is important not only in speech recognition and machine translation, but also in high-dimensional discrete sequence modeling in general. However, the problem of context length has almost been neglected so far and a nave bag-of-words history has been i employed in natural language processing. In contrast, in this paper we view topic shifts within a text as a latent stochastic process to give an explicit probabilistic generative model that has partial exchangeability. We propose an online inference algorithm using particle filters to recognize topic shifts to employ the most appropriate length of context automatically. Experiments on the BNC corpus showed consistent improvement over previous methods involving no chronological order.

However, the problem of context length has almost been neglected so far and a nave bag-of-words history has been i employed in natural language processing. In contrast, in this paper we view topic shifts within a text as a latent stochastic process to give an explicit probabilistic generative model that has partial exchangeability. We propose an online inference algorithm using particle filters to recognize topic shifts to employ the most appropriate length of context automatically. Experiments on the BNC corpus showed consistent improvement over previous methods involving no chronological order.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much earlier text a language model should use as context. A long history can contain useful information, but the subject of a passage can change. Treating that history as an unordered bag of words does not explicitly account for when those changes occurred or which portion of the history is currently relevant.

The authors model topic shifts as an unobserved stochastic process within a probabilistic generative model. The model has partial exchangeability, combining some freedom to reorder observations with structure that preserves relevant distinctions. An online particle-filtering algorithm infers topic changes as text arrives and uses that inference to select an appropriate context length automatically.

Experiments on the BNC corpus show consistent improvement over previous methods that ignore chronological order. The finding supports the value of tracking topic changes when deciding which earlier text should inform a prediction. More broadly, the paper presents context selection as an inference problem about a changing hidden process, connecting long-distance language modeling with the modeling of discrete sequences.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model of topic shifts uses online particle filtering to adapt context length and improves results over order-insensitive methods on the BNC corpus.

title: Context as Filtering

abstract: We present two new algorithms for online learning in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Our first algorithm, ILK (implicit online learning with kernels), employs a new, implicit update technique that can be applied to a wide variety of convex loss functions. We then introduce a bounded memory version, SILK (sparse ILK), that maintains a compact representation of the predictor without compromising solution quality, even in non-stationary environments. We prove loss bounds and analyze the convergence rate of both. Experimental evidence shows that our proposed algorithms outperform current methods on synthetic and real data.

We then introduce a bounded memory version, SILK (sparse ILK), that maintains a compact representation of the predictor without compromising solution quality, even in non-stationary environments. paragraphs: This paper introduces two algorithms for online learning in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In this setting, a predictor is updated as observations arrive, and kernels provide the space in which learning takes place. The first algorithm, ILK, centers on a new implicit update technique that applies to a wide variety of convex loss functions.

The second algorithm, SILK, is a sparse version of ILK designed to use bounded memory. It maintains a compact predictor representation while preserving solution quality, including in non-stationary environments where the learning setting changes over time. This addresses the representation of the predictor alongside the rule used to update it.

The authors establish loss bounds and analyze convergence rates for both methods. They also report experiments on synthetic and real data in which the proposed algorithms outperform the methods used for comparison. The contribution combines a broadly applicable update mechanism, a bounded-memory variant, and theoretical analysis, with empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of both approaches in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: ILK introduces implicit kernel-learning updates, while SILK provides a bounded-memory version with theoretical guarantees and favorable experimental results.

title: implicit Online Learning with Kernels

abstract: We consider the problem of inferring the structure of a network from cooccurrence data: observations that indicate which nodes occur in a signaling pathway but do not directly reveal node order within the pathway. This problem is motivated by network inference problems arising in computational biology and communication systems, in which it is difficult or impossible to obtain precise time ordering information. Without order information, every permutation of the activated nodes leads to a different feasible solution, resulting in combinatorial explosion of the feasible set. However, physical principles underlying most networked systems suggest that not all feasible solutions are equally likely. Intuitively, nodes that co-occur more frequently are probably more closely connected. Building on this intuition, we model path co-occurrences as randomly shuffled samples of a random walk on the network. We derive a computationally efficient network inference algorithm and, via novel concentration inequalities for importance sampling estimators, prove that a polynomial complexity Monte Carlo version of the algorithm converges with high probability.

paragraphs: Some network observations reveal which nodes participated in a pathway without recording their order. This occurs in biological and communication systems where precise timing can be difficult to obtain. Recovering connections from such observations is challenging because every ordering of the observed nodes gives another feasible explanation, creating a combinatorially large set of possibilities.

The paper introduces a probabilistic model that treats each observed co-occurrence as a randomly shuffled sample from a random walk on the network. It builds on the intuition that nodes appearing together more often are likely to be more closely connected. This model assigns structure to the missing-order problem instead of treating all feasible pathways as equally likely.

The authors derive an efficient network inference algorithm and analyze a Monte Carlo version using new concentration inequalities for importance sampling estimates. They prove high-probability convergence for a version with polynomial complexity. The result supports computationally manageable inference under the proposed model; convergence of the algorithm is the stated guarantee, rather than unconditional recovery of every network from unordered observations.
summary.tldr: Modeling unordered node co-occurrences as shuffled random walks enables efficient network inference with a high-probability convergence guarantee.

title: Inferring Network Structure from Co-Occurrences

abstract: Finite mixture model is a powerful tool in many statistical learning problems. In this paper, we propose a general, structure-preserving approach to reduce its model complexity, which can bring signiﬁcant computational beneﬁts in many applications. The basic idea is to group the original mixture components into compact clusters, and then minimize an upper bound on the approximation error between the original and simpliﬁed models. By adopting the L2 norm as the dis- tance measure between mixture models, we can derive closed-form solutions that are more robust and reliable than using the KL-based distance measure. Moreover, the complexity of our algorithm is only linear in the sample size and dimensional- ity. Experiments on density estimation and clustering-based image segmentation demonstrate its outstanding performance in terms of both speed and accuracy.

paragraphs: Finite mixture models combine multiple components to describe data, but their complexity can make them costly to use. This paper proposes a general way to simplify such models while preserving their mixture structure. The aim is to retain a useful approximation of the original model with computational benefits for downstream applications.

The method first organizes the original components into compact clusters. It then minimizes an upper bound on the difference between the original and simplified models. The authors measure that difference with an L2 norm, which allows closed-form solutions. They report that these solutions are more robust and reliable than those obtained using a KL-based distance measure.

The algorithm's complexity grows linearly with sample size and dimensionality. Experiments on density estimation and image segmentation based on clustering show strong performance in both speed and accuracy. These findings support treating simplification as a function-approximation problem: component grouping and an explicit error bound work together to reduce complexity while controlling how closely the smaller model follows the original.
summary.tldr: Grouping mixture components and minimizing an L2 approximation-error bound produces simpler models with reported speed and accuracy benefits.

title: Simplifying Mixture Models through Function Approximation

abstract: Unsupervised learning algorithms aim to discover the structure hidden in the data, and to learn representations that are more suitable as input to a supervised machine than the raw input. Many unsupervised methods are based on reconstructing the input from the representation, while constraining the representation to have certain desirable properties (e.g. low dimension, sparsity, etc). Others are based on approximating density by stochastically reconstructing the input from the representation. We describe a novel and efficient algorithm to learn sparse representations, and compare it theoretically and experimentally with a similar machines trained probabilistically, namely a Restricted Boltzmann Machine. We propose a simple criterion to compare and select different unsupervised machines based on the trade-off between the reconstruction error and the information content of the representation. We demonstrate this method by extracting features from a dataset of handwritten numerals, and from a dataset of natural image patches. We show that by stacking multiple levels of such machines and by training sequentially, high-order dependencies between the input variables can be captured.
originalAbstract: Unsupervised learning algorithms aim to discover the structure hidden in the data, and to learn representations that are more suitable as input to a supervised machine than the raw input. Many unsupervised methods are based on reconstructing the input from the representation, while constraining the representation to have certain desirable properties (e.g. low dimension, sparsity, etc). Others are based on approximating density by stochastically reconstructing the input from the representation. We describe a novel and efficient algorithm to learn sparse representations, and compare it theoretically and experimentally with a similar machines trained probabilistically, namely a Restricted Boltzmann Machine. We propose a simple criterion to compare and select different unsupervised machines based on the trade-off between the reconstruction error and the information content of the representation. We demonstrate this method by extracting features from a dataset of handwritten numerals, and from a dataset of natural image patches. We show that by stacking multiple levels of such machines and by training sequentially, high-order dependencies between the input variables can be captured.

This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for learning sparse representations. It places that algorithm in the context of methods that reconstruct their inputs while imposing desirable properties on the representation, and methods that reconstruct probabilistically.

The authors compare their approach theoretically and experimentally with a Restricted Boltzmann Machine. They also propose a criterion for comparing and selecting unsupervised learning machines based on the tradeoff between reconstruction error and the information content of the representation. This makes evaluation sensitive to both how well inputs are recovered and what the representation contains.

The method is demonstrated through feature extraction from handwritten numerals and natural image patches. The authors further show that stacking several levels of these machines and training them sequentially can capture high-order dependencies among input variables. The contribution therefore includes a sparse feature-learning algorithm, a way to judge competing representations, and evidence that layered training can represent more complex relationships in data.
summary.tldr: An efficient sparse representation learner supports layered feature extraction and a comparison criterion balancing reconstruction error against representation information.

title: Sparse Feature Learning for Deep Belief Networks

abstract: Statistical models on full and partial rankings of n items are often of limited prac- tical use for large n due to computational consideration. We explore the use of non-parametric models for partially ranked data and derive ef(cid:2)cient procedures for their use for large n. The derivations are largely possible through combinatorial and algebraic manipulations based on the lattice of partial rankings. In particular, we demonstrate for the (cid:2)rst time a non-parametric coherent and consistent model capable of ef(cid:2)ciently aggregating partially ranked data of different types.

paragraphs: Ranking data need not specify a complete ordering of every item. Different observations may provide different kinds of partial orderings, creating a challenge for combining them into one statistical model. This paper addresses that challenge when the number of items is large, a setting in which existing models of full and partial rankings can become computationally impractical.

The authors investigate nonparametric models and derive efficient procedures for working with partially ranked observations. Their derivations use combinatorial and algebraic properties of the lattice of partial rankings. This mathematical structure organizes relationships among partial rankings and supplies the basis for manipulating them without relying on computationally prohibitive conventional approaches.

The central result is a model that can efficiently aggregate different types of partial ranking data while satisfying coherence and consistency. The authors identify this combination as a first for nonparametric ranking models. Its significance lies in treating heterogeneous incomplete rankings within a common statistical framework while making computation feasible for larger collections of items.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric framework efficiently combines different kinds of partial rankings into a coherent, consistent model.

title: Non-parametric Modeling of Partially Ranked Data

abstract: In this paper we introduce the MeanNN approach for estimation of main information theoretic measures such as differential entropy, mutual information and divergence. As opposed to other nonparametric approaches the MeanNN results in smooth differentiable functions of the data samples with clear geometrical interpretation. Then we apply the proposed estimators to the ICA problem and obtain a smooth expression for the mutual information that can be analytically optimized by gradient descent methods. The improved performance on the proposed ICA algorithm is demonstrated on standard tests in comparison with state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: The paper introduces MeanNN, an approach for estimating information-theoretic quantities from data samples. These include differential entropy, mutual information, and divergence, which describe uncertainty, dependence, and differences between distributions. The distinguishing property is that its estimates are smooth, differentiable functions of the samples and have a clear geometric interpretation.

Smoothness matters when an estimate is used inside an optimization problem. If the data representation changes during learning, a differentiable estimate provides a way to calculate how the objective changes with it. The authors use this property for independent component analysis, developing a smooth expression for mutual information that can be optimized analytically with gradient-descent methods.

The resulting ICA algorithm is evaluated on standard tests, where the authors report improved performance relative to state-of-the-art techniques. The contribution thus links an estimator’s mathematical form to its practical usefulness in learning: MeanNN supplies an information measure that can also guide optimization. The stated empirical improvement concerns the proposed ICA method, while the estimation framework itself covers several information-theoretic quantities.
summary.tldr: MeanNN provides smooth information-theoretic estimates that enable gradient-based ICA and yield improved performance on reported standard tests.

title: ICA based on a Smooth Estimation of the Differential Entropy

abstract: We introduce a new type of neural network activation function based on recent physiological rate models for complex cells in visual area V1. A single-hidden-layer neural network of this kind of model achieves 1.5% error on MNIST. We also introduce an existing criterion for learning slow, decorrelated features as a pretraining strategy for image models. This pretraining strategy results in orientation-selective features, similar to the receptive fields of complex cells. With this pretraining, the same single-hidden-layer model achieves better generalization error, even though the pretraining sample distribution is very different from the fine-tuning distribution. To implement this pretraining strategy, we derive a fast algorithm for online learning of decorrelated features such that each iteration of the algorithm runs in linear time with respect to the number of features.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a neural-network activation function inspired by physiological firing-rate models of complex cells in visual area V1. A network with one hidden layer using this type of model achieves 1.5% error on MNIST. This establishes a reported classification result for the architecture before the discussion of its pretraining improvement.

This pretraining produces orientation-selective features resembling complex-cell receptive fields, connecting the learning criterion to a particular kind of visual representation.

With pretraining, the same single-hidden-layer model achieves better generalization, even though the pretraining and fine-tuning sample distributions differ substantially. This is empirical evidence that the learned representation can remain useful across that distribution difference. To make the strategy efficient, the authors also derive an online algorithm for learning decorrelated features whose per-iteration runtime is linear in the number of features. The paper thus contributes an activation model, a pretraining application, and an efficient supporting algorithm.
summary.tldr: Slow, decorrelated feature pretraining improves a complex-cell-inspired network and admits efficient online updates.

title: Slow, Decorrelated Features for Pretraining Complex Cell-like Networks

abstract: We propose a new approach to the problem of robust estimation in multiview geometry. Inspired by recent advances in the sparse recovery problem of statistics, our estimator is defined as a Bayesian maximum a posteriori with multivariate Laplace prior on the vector describing the outliers. This leads to an estimator in which the fidelity to the data is measured by the $L_\infty$-norm while the regularization is done by the $L_1$-norm. The proposed procedure is fairly fast since the outlier removal is done by solving one linear program (LP). An important difference compared to existing algorithms is that for our estimator it is not necessary to specify neither the number nor the proportion of the outliers. The theoretical results, as well as the numerical example reported in this work, confirm the efficiency of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: The paper addresses robust estimation in inverse problems arising in multiview geometry, where outlying observations can interfere with fitting a model. Its approach explicitly represents the outliers with a vector and draws on ideas from sparse recovery. This makes the treatment of outliers part of the estimation objective itself.

The estimator is derived as a Bayesian maximum a posteriori solution using a multivariate Laplace prior on the outlier vector. The resulting objective measures data fidelity with the infinity norm and uses an L1 regularization penalty. These terms combine a criterion based on the largest data discrepancy with a sparse-recovery-inspired treatment of the outliers.

Outlier removal requires solving one linear program, which the authors describe as fairly fast. A practical feature is that users need not specify either the number or the proportion of outliers beforehand. Theoretical results and a numerical example support the approach's efficiency. The contribution combines an explicit probabilistic formulation with a computationally direct outlier-removal procedure.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian estimator combines infinity-norm data fidelity with L1 regularization to remove outliers through one linear program without specifying their prevalence.

title: $L_1$-Penalized Robust Estimation for a Class of Inverse Problems Arising in Multiview Geometry

abstract: In the paper, we consider the problem of link prediction in time-evolving graphs. We assume that certain graph features, such as the node degree, follow a vector autoregressive (VAR) model and we propose to use this information to improve the accuracy of prediction. Our strategy involves a joint optimization procedure over the space of adjacency matrices and VAR matrices which takes into account both sparsity and low rank properties of the matrices. Oracle inequalities are derived and illustrate the trade-offs in the choice of smoothing parameters when modeling the joint effect of sparsity and low rank property. The estimate is computed efficiently using proximal methods through a generalized forward-backward agorithm.

paragraphs: Predicting links in a changing graph can draw on how graph-level or node-level features evolve over time. This paper assumes that selected features, such as node degree, follow a vector autoregressive model. In this formulation, past feature values inform future ones, and the authors propose using that temporal structure to improve link prediction.

The method jointly optimizes adjacency matrices, which represent connections, and the matrices governing the autoregressive feature model. It accounts for both sparsity and low rank in these matrices. Joint estimation brings the predicted network and its modeled feature dynamics into the same optimization problem, rather than handling the two as unrelated estimates.

The authors derive oracle inequalities that describe trade-offs in choosing smoothing parameters when sparsity and low rank act together. These theoretical results help characterize the effects of balancing the two structural properties. They also provide an efficient computation method using proximal optimization through a generalized forward-backward algorithm. The contribution combines a stated temporal modeling assumption, structured matrix estimation, and a practical optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Joint estimation of graph connections and autoregressive feature dynamics combines sparsity and low rank for time-evolving link prediction.

title: Link Prediction in Graphs with Autoregressive Features

abstract: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) as a canonical NP-complete decision problem is one of the most important problems in computer science. In practice, real-world SAT sentences are drawn from a distribution that may result in efficient algorithms for their solution. Such SAT instances are likely to have shared characteristics and substructures. This work approaches the exploration of a family of SAT solvers as a learning problem. In particular, we relate polynomial time solvability of a SAT subset to a notion of margin between sentences mapped by a feature function into a Hilbert space. Provided this mapping is based on polynomial time computable statistics of a sentence, we show that the existance of a margin between these data points implies the existance of a polynomial time solver for that SAT subset based on the Davis-Putnam-Logemann-Loveland algorithm. Furthermore, we show that a simple perceptron-style learning rule will find an optimal SAT solver with a bounded number of training updates. We derive a linear time computable set of features and show analytically that margins exist for important polynomial special cases of SAT. Empirical results show an order of magnitude improvement over a state-of-the-art SAT solver on a hardware verification task.

paragraphs: Boolean satisfiability asks whether a logical sentence admits an assignment that makes it true. Although SAT is NP-complete, instances arising from a particular application may share useful structure. This paper treats the search for solvers suited to such subsets as a learning problem, connecting computational tractability with geometric separation between representations of sentences.

The authors map sentences into a Hilbert space using features computed from their statistics. If those statistics are computable in polynomial time and the mapped sentences have the required margin, they show that a polynomial-time solver exists for that SAT subset within a framework based on the Davis-Putnam-Logemann-Loveland algorithm. The margin is a sufficient condition for this result.

They further show that a perceptron-style rule finds an optimal solver in the studied family with a bounded number of training updates. They construct features computable in linear time and establish margins for important tractable SAT cases. On a hardware-verification task, experiments report an order-of-magnitude improvement over a state-of-the-art solver.
summary.tldr: A margin-based learning framework identifies efficiently solvable SAT subsets and learns solvers with bounded training updates.

title: Perceptron Learning of SAT

abstract: We consider the problem of inferring direct neural network connections from Calcium imaging time series. Inverse covariance estimation has proven to be a fast and accurate method for learning macro- and micro-scale network connectivity in the brain and in a recent Kaggle Connectomics competition inverse covariance was the main component of several top ten solutions, including our own and the winning team's algorithm. However, the accuracy of inverse covariance estimation is highly sensitive to signal preprocessing of the Calcium fluorescence time series. Furthermore, brute force optimization methods such as grid search and coordinate ascent over signal processing parameters is a time intensive process, where learning may take several days and parameters that optimize one network may not generalize to networks with different size and parameters. In this paper we show how inverse covariance estimation can be dramatically improved using a simple convolution filter prior to applying sample covariance. Furthermore, these signal processing parameters can be learned quickly using a supervised optimization algorithm. In particular, we maximize a binomial log-likelihood loss function with respect to a convolution filter of the time series and the inverse covariance regularization parameter. Our proposed algorithm is relatively fast on networks the size of those in the competition (1000 neurons), producing AUC scores with similar accuracy to the winning solution in training time under 2 hours on a cpu. Prediction on new networks of the same size is carried out in less than 15 minutes, the time it takes to read in the data and write out the solution.

Searching preprocessing parameters by brute force can take days, and settings that work for one network may not transfer well to another.

The authors place a simple convolution filter before sample covariance estimation and learn its parameters through supervised optimization. summary.tldr: Jointly learning a convolution filter and inverse covariance regularization yields competitive neural connectivity estimates with substantially shorter reported training.

title: Learning convolution filters for inverse covariance estimation of neural network connectivity

abstract: Predicting depth is an essential component in understanding the 3D geometry of a scene. While for stereo images local correspondence suffices for estimation, finding depth relations from a single image is less straightforward, requiring integration of both global and local information from various cues. Moreover, the task is inherently ambiguous, with a large source of uncertainty coming from the overall scale. In this paper, we present a new method that addresses this task by employing two deep network stacks: one that makes a coarse global prediction based on the entire image, and another that refines this prediction locally. We also apply a scale-invariant error to help measure depth relations rather than scale. By leveraging the raw datasets as large sources of training data, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on both NYU Depth and KITTI, and matches detailed depth boundaries without the need for superpixelation.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from one image requires combining clues about the whole scene with details in individual regions. Unlike stereo images, a single image does not supply a second view for local correspondence. It also leaves ambiguity about overall scale, so determining how depths relate can be easier than determining their absolute size.

The paper addresses this with two deep network stacks. The first looks at the entire image and produces a coarse depth prediction. The second refines that prediction locally. This division lets the method combine a broad interpretation of scene geometry with more detailed spatial information. A scale-invariant error further emphasizes depth relationships rather than overall scale.

Using the raw datasets as large training sources, the method achieves results reported as state of the art on NYU Depth and KITTI. It also captures detailed depth boundaries without requiring superpixelation. These findings support the combination of global prediction and local refinement for single-image depth estimation, while the scale-aware formulation directly addresses a stated ambiguity of the task.
summary.tldr: Two deep networks combine global depth prediction with local refinement, achieving strong single-image depth results while accounting for scale ambiguity.

title: Depth Map Prediction from a Single Image using a Multi-Scale Deep Network

abstract: Two seemingly contradictory theories attempt to explain how humans move to intercept an airborne ball. One theory posits that humans predict the ball trajectory to optimally plan future actions; the other claims that, instead of performing such complicated computations, humans employ heuristics to reactively choose appropriate actions based on immediate visual feedback. In this paper, we show that interception strategies appearing to be heuristics can be understood as computational solutions to the optimal control problem faced by a ball-catching agent acting under uncertainty. Modeling catching as a continuous partially observable Markov decision process and employing stochastic optimal control theory, we discover that the four main heuristics described in the literature are optimal solutions if the catcher has sufficient time to continuously visually track the ball. Specifically, by varying model parameters such as noise, time to ground contact, and perceptual latency, we show that different strategies arise under different circumstances. The catcher's policy switches between generating reactive and predictive behavior based on the ratio of system to observation noise and the ratio between reaction time and task duration. Thus, we provide a rational account of human ball-catching behavior and a unifying explanation for seemingly contradictory theories of target interception on the basis of stochastic optimal control.

paragraphs: Human ball catching is often explained either as predicting a trajectory and planning ahead or as reacting to visual information through simple rules. This paper asks whether those explanations can arise from the same decision problem. It models catching as control under uncertainty, where the agent must act despite incomplete information about the ball.

The authors use a continuous partially observable Markov decision process and stochastic optimal control theory. Within this model, the four main catching heuristics described in the literature emerge as optimal solutions if the catcher has enough time to keep visually tracking the ball. That condition is central: the result does not declare these heuristics optimal under every possible catching situation.

Different strategies emerge as noise, time until ground contact, and perceptual latency change. Whether behavior is more reactive or predictive depends on the relative sizes of system and observation noise and of reaction time and task duration. The result provides a unified rational account: behavior that looks like a simple visual rule can be a solution to an optimal control problem under the appropriate circumstances.
summary.tldr: Common catching heuristics emerge as optimal control policies when the catcher has sufficient time for continuous visual tracking.

title: Catching heuristics are optimal control policies

abstract: This paper introduces the variational Rényi bound (VR) that extends traditional variational inference to Rényi's alpha-divergences. This new family of variational methods unifies a number of existing approaches, and enables a smooth interpolation from the evidence lower-bound to the log (marginal) likelihood that is controlled by the value of alpha that parametrises the divergence. The reparameterization trick, Monte Carlo approximation and stochastic optimisation methods are deployed to obtain a tractable and unified framework for optimisation. We further consider negative alpha values and propose a novel variational inference method as a new special case in the proposed framework. Experiments on Bayesian neural networks and variational auto-encoders demonstrate the wide applicability of the VR bound.

This new family of variational methods unifies a number of existing approaches, and enables a smooth interpolation from the evidence lower-bound to the log (marginal) likelihood that is controlled by the value of alpha that parametrises the divergence. The reparameterization trick, Monte Carlo approximation and stochastic optimisation methods are deployed to obtain a tractable and unified framework for optimisation. We further consider negative alpha values and propose a novel variational inference method as a new special case in the proposed framework. Experiments on Bayesian neural networks and variational auto-encoders demonstrate the wide applicability of the VR bound.

paragraphs: Variational inference makes probabilistic inference tractable through an optimization problem. This paper broadens that approach using Rényi's alpha-divergences and introduces the variational Rényi bound. Instead of committing to one variational objective, the framework provides a family whose behavior is controlled by the parameter alpha.

The family unifies several existing approaches and provides a smooth interpolation between the evidence lower bound and the log marginal likelihood. This places familiar objectives within a common mathematical construction. The authors use reparameterization, Monte Carlo approximation, and stochastic optimization to turn the construction into a tractable training framework, connecting the theoretical family to methods that can be implemented.

The paper also considers negative alpha values and derives a new variational inference method as one special case. Experiments with Bayesian neural networks and variational autoencoders demonstrate the framework's applicability across both model types. The stated empirical message is breadth of use; the abstract does not claim that one alpha setting or one member of the family is uniformly best.
summary.tldr: The variational Rényi bound unifies and extends variational inference through an alpha-controlled family of tractable objectives.

title: Rényi Divergence Variational Inference

abstract: We study probability measures induced by set functions with constraints. Such measures arise in a variety of real-world settings, where prior knowledge, resource limitations, or other pragmatic considerations impose constraints. We consider the task of rapidly sampling from such constrained measures, and develop fast Markov chain samplers for them. Our first main result is for MCMC sampling from Strongly Rayleigh (SR) measures, for which we present sharp polynomial bounds on the mixing time. As a corollary, this result yields a fast mixing sampler for Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs), yielding (to our knowledge) the first provably fast MCMC sampler for DPPs since their inception over four decades ago. Beyond SR measures, we develop MCMC samplers for probabilistic models with hard constraints and identify sufficient conditions under which their chains mix rapidly. We illustrate our claims by empirically verifying the dependence of mixing times on the key factors governing our theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: Many probabilistic models assign probabilities to sets while restricting which sets are allowed. Those restrictions can encode resource budgets, prior knowledge, or practical requirements. This paper studies how to sample rapidly from such distributions using Markov chains, where successive updates move through possible sets toward the desired probability distribution.

The first main result gives sharp polynomial bounds on mixing time for Strongly Rayleigh measures. Mixing time describes how long a chain needs to approach its target distribution. As a consequence, the result yields a rapidly mixing sampler for determinantal point processes. The authors identify this as, to their knowledge, the first provably fast MCMC sampler for that family.

The paper also develops samplers beyond Strongly Rayleigh measures for models with hard constraints. Here it identifies sufficient conditions for rapid mixing, rather than claiming that every constrained distribution is easy to sample. Experiments examine how mixing times depend on the factors appearing in the theoretical bounds, connecting the mathematical guarantees with observed sampling behavior.
summary.tldr: Polynomial mixing-time guarantees enable fast MCMC sampling for Strongly Rayleigh measures and DPPs, with sufficient conditions for additional constrained models.

title: Fast Mixing Markov Chains for Strongly Rayleigh Measures, DPPs, and Constrained Sampling

abstract: Consider samples from two different data sources $\{\mathbf{x_s^i}\} \sim P_{\rm source}$ and $\{\mathbf{x_t^i}\} \sim P_{\rm target}$. We only observe their transformed versions $h(\mathbf{x_s^i})$ and $g(\mathbf{x_t^i})$, for some known function class $h(\cdot)$ and $g(\cdot)$. Our goal is to perform a statistical test checking if $P_{\rm source}$ = $P_{\rm target}$ while removing the distortions induced by the transformations. This problem is closely related to concepts underlying numerous domain adaptation algorithms, and in our case, is motivated by the need to combine clinical and imaging based biomarkers from multiple sites and/or batches, where this problem is fairly common and an impediment in the conduct of analyses with much larger sample sizes. We develop a framework that addresses this problem using ideas from hypothesis testing on the transformed measurements, where in the distortions need to be estimated {\it in tandem} with the testing. We derive a simple algorithm and study its convergence and consistency properties in detail, and we also provide lower-bound strategies based on recent work in continuous optimization. On a dataset of individuals at risk for neurological disease, our results are competitive with alternative procedures that are twice as expensive and in some cases operationally infeasible to implement.
originalAbstract: Consider samples from two different data sources $\{\mathbf{x_s^i}\} \sim P_{\rm source}$ and $\{\mathbf{x_t^i}\} \sim P_{\rm target}$. We only observe their transformed versions $h(\mathbf{x_s^i})$ and $g(\mathbf{x_t^i})$, for some known function class $h(\cdot)$ and $g(\cdot)$. Our goal is to perform a statistical test checking if $P_{\rm source}$ = $P_{\rm target}$ while removing the distortions induced by the transformations. This problem is closely related to concepts underlying numerous domain adaptation algorithms, and in our case, is motivated by the need to combine clinical and imaging based biomarkers from multiple sites and/or batches, where this problem is fairly common and an impediment in the conduct of analyses with much larger sample sizes. We develop a framework that addresses this problem using ideas from hypothesis testing on the transformed measurements, where in the distortions need to be estimated {\it in tandem} with the testing. We derive a simple algorithm and study its convergence and consistency properties in detail, and we also provide lower-bound strategies based on recent work in continuous optimization. On a dataset of individuals at risk for neurological disease, our results are competitive with alternative procedures that are twice as expensive and in some cases operationally infeasible to implement.

paragraphs: Measurements from different sources can differ because their underlying populations differ or because the measurement processes distort them differently. This paper studies how to test whether two underlying distributions are equal when only transformed samples are observed. The transformations belong to known function classes, providing structure for separating measurement effects from distributional differences.

The authors build a hypothesis-testing framework that estimates the distortions together with the statistical test. This joint treatment addresses a problem arising when clinical and imaging biomarkers are combined across sites or batches. Such distortions can obstruct analyses that would otherwise benefit from larger pooled samples.

The paper develops a simple algorithm, examines its convergence and consistency, and supplies lower-bound strategies using ideas from continuous optimization. On data from individuals at risk for neurological disease, the reported results are competitive with alternative procedures that cost twice as much and can be operationally infeasible. The contribution concerns comparing distributions despite measurement transformations, with the biomedical application illustrating why this distinction matters.
summary.tldr: A joint testing-and-distortion-estimation framework compares underlying distributions using transformed measurements from different sources.

title: Hypothesis Testing in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation with Applications in Alzheimer's Disease

abstract: Estimating optimal phylogenetic trees or hierarchical clustering trees from metric data is an important problem in evolutionary biology and data analysis. Intuitively, the goodness-of-fit of a metric space to a tree depends on its inherent treeness, as well as other metric properties such as intrinsic dimension. Existing algorithms for embedding metric spaces into tree metrics provide distortion bounds depending on cardinality. Because cardinality is a simple property of any set, we argue that such bounds do not fully capture the rich structure endowed by the metric. We consider an embedding of a metric space into a tree proposed by Gromov. By proving a stability result, we obtain an improved additive distortion bound depending only on the hyperbolicity and doubling dimension of the metric. We observe that Gromov's method is dual to the well-known single linkage hierarchical clustering (SLHC) method. By means of this duality, we are able to transport our results to the setting of SLHC, where such additive distortion bounds were previously unknown.

Existing guarantees often depend on the number of points, but that count alone says little about the geometric structure that might make the data well suited to a tree.

summary.tldr: Tree approximation error can be bounded using hyperbolicity and doubling dimension, with corresponding new guarantees for single linkage clustering.

title: Improved Error Bounds for Tree Representations of Metric Spaces

abstract: Efficiently aggregating data from different sources is a challenging problem, particularly when samples from each source are distributed differently. These differences can be inherent to the inference task or present for other reasons: sensors in a sensor network may be placed far apart, affecting their individual measurements. Conversely, it is computationally advantageous to split Bayesian inference tasks across subsets of data, but data need not be identically distributed across subsets. One principled way to fuse probability distributions is via the lens of optimal transport: the Wasserstein barycenter is a single distribution that summarizes a collection of input measures while respecting their geometry. However, computing the barycenter scales poorly and requires discretization of all input distributions and the barycenter itself. Improving on this situation, we present a scalable, communication-efficient, parallel algorithm for computing the Wasserstein barycenter of arbitrary distributions. Our algorithm can operate directly on continuous input distributions and is optimized for streaming data. Our method is even robust to nonstationary input distributions and produces a barycenter estimate that tracks the input measures over time. The algorithm is semi-discrete, needing to discretize only the barycenter estimate. To the best of our knowledge, we also provide the first bounds on the quality of the approximate barycenter as the discretization becomes finer. Finally, we demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our method, both in tracking moving distributions on a sphere, as well as in a large-scale Bayesian inference task.

paragraphs: Combining information from different sources is difficult when their probability distributions differ. A Wasserstein barycenter summarizes several distributions while respecting their geometry through optimal transport. The paper addresses the computational cost of finding this summary, particularly when data arrive continuously or are processed across multiple sources.

It accepts continuous input distributions directly and discretizes only the barycenter estimate, making the formulation semi-discrete. Together, these contributions make geometry-aware distribution aggregation more practical while explicitly retaining an approximation in the barycenter representation.
summary.tldr: A parallel streaming algorithm estimates Wasserstein barycenters from continuous distributions and tracks changing inputs while discretizing only the barycenter.

title: Parallel Streaming Wasserstein Barycenters

abstract: We study the problem of conditional generative modeling based on designated semantics or structures. Existing models that build conditional generators either require massive labeled instances as supervision or are unable to accurately control the semantics of generated samples. We propose structured generative adversarial networks (SGANs) for semi-supervised conditional generative modeling. SGAN assumes the data x is generated conditioned on two independent latent variables: y that encodes the designated semantics, and z that contains other factors of variation. To ensure disentangled semantics in y and z, SGAN builds two collaborative games in the hidden space to minimize the reconstruction error of y and z, respectively. Training SGAN also involves solving two adversarial games that have their equilibrium concentrating at the true joint data distributions p(x, z) and p(x, y), avoiding distributing the probability mass diffusely over data space that MLE-based methods may suffer. We assess SGAN by evaluating its trained networks, and its performance on downstream tasks. We show that SGAN delivers a highly controllable generator, and disentangled representations; it also establishes start-of-the-art results across multiple datasets when applied for semi-supervised image classification (1.27%, 5.73%, 17.26% error rates on MNIST, SVHN and CIFAR-10 using 50, 1000 and 4000 labels, respectively). Benefiting from the separate modeling of y and z, SGAN can generate images with high visual quality and strictly following the designated semantic, and can be extended to a wide spectrum of applications, such as style transfer.

The goal is to control designated semantics in generated samples while separating those semantics from other variation. The model assumes two independent latent variables: y represents the designated meaning or structure, and z represents the remaining factors.

summary.tldr: SGAN separates semantic and other latent factors to support controllable image generation and strong semi-supervised classification.

title: Structured Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: We propose Random Projection Filter Bank (RPFB) as a generic and simple approach to extract features from time series data. RPFB is a set of randomly generated stable autoregressive filters that are convolved with the input time series to generate the features. These features can be used by any conventional machine learning algorithm for solving tasks such as time series prediction, classification with time series data, etc. Different filters in RPFB extract different aspects of the time series, and together they provide a reasonably good summary of the time series. RPFB is easy to implement, fast to compute, and parallelizable. We provide an error upper bound indicating that RPFB provides a reasonable approximation to a class of dynamical systems. The empirical results in a series of synthetic and real-world problems show that RPFB is an effective method to extract features from time series.

paragraphs: Time-series learning often depends on finding features that summarize useful temporal behavior. The Random Projection Filter Bank provides a generic way to construct such features before applying a conventional machine learning algorithm. The intended uses include predicting a time series and classifying examples that contain time-series data.

The filter bank consists of randomly generated stable autoregressive filters. Each filter is convolved with the input sequence, producing features that reflect different aspects of its behavior. Taken together, these outputs provide a useful summary. The method is described as easy to implement, fast to compute, and suitable for parallel execution.

The authors provide an upper bound on approximation error for a class of dynamical systems. This supplies theoretical support for the representation within that class, while experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show effective feature extraction. The contribution is a simple, reusable front end for time-series learning: a collection of random temporal filters can provide informative inputs without tying the representation to a single downstream prediction algorithm.
summary.tldr: Random Projection Filter Banks turn time series into reusable features using randomly generated stable autoregressive filters.

title: Random Projection Filter Bank for Time Series Data

abstract: Uplift modeling is aimed at estimating the incremental impact of an action on an individual's behavior, which is useful in various application domains such as targeted marketing (advertisement campaigns) and personalized medicine (medical treatments). Conventional methods of uplift modeling require every instance to be jointly equipped with two types of labels: the taken action and its outcome. However, obtaining two labels for each instance at the same time is difficult or expensive in many real-world problems. In this paper, we propose a novel method of uplift modeling that is applicable to a more practical setting where only one type of labels is available for each instance. We show a mean squared error bound for the proposed estimator and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments.

paragraphs: Uplift modeling estimates how much an action changes an individual’s behavior. This makes it relevant to decisions such as whom to target with a campaign or how to personalize a treatment. The paper addresses a data-collection obstacle: conventional methods require each instance to include both the action taken and its observed outcome.

Obtaining those two labels together can be costly or difficult. The proposed method instead works in a setting where an instance has only one of the two label types. Its contribution is therefore a change in the supervision available for learning: action information and outcome information need not be jointly attached to every instance.

The authors provide a mean squared error bound for their estimator and demonstrate its effectiveness experimentally. The bound supplies a theoretical assessment of estimation error, while the experiments support the usefulness of the proposed approach. Together, these findings extend uplift modeling to the separate-label setting studied, making incomplete label pairing a problem the estimator explicitly accommodates rather than a reason to require fully paired data.
summary.tldr: An uplift estimator learns from separately available action and outcome labels, with a mean squared error bound and experimental support.

title: Uplift Modeling from Separate Labels

abstract: We propose a novel Wasserstein method with a distillation mechanism, yielding joint learning of word embeddings and topics. The proposed method is based on the fact that the Euclidean distance between word embeddings may be employed as the underlying distance in the Wasserstein topic model. The word distributions of topics, their optimal transport to the word distributions of documents, and the embeddings of words are learned in a unified framework. When learning the topic model, we leverage a distilled ground-distance matrix to update the topic distributions and smoothly calculate the corresponding optimal transports. Such a strategy provides the updating of word embeddings with robust guidance, improving algorithm convergence. As an application, we focus on patient admission records, in which the proposed method embeds the codes of diseases and procedures and learns the topics of admissions, obtaining superior performance on clinically-meaningful disease network construction, mortality prediction as a function of admission codes, and procedure recommendation.

paragraphs: Word embeddings describe words as vectors, while topic models describe topics through distributions over words. This paper joins the two by using distances between word vectors as the underlying distances in a Wasserstein topic model. The geometry of the embeddings thereby becomes part of how topic and document distributions are compared.

The framework jointly learns word embeddings, topic distributions, and optimal transports connecting topics to documents. Its distillation mechanism supplies a ground-distance matrix for updating topics and smoothly computing the associated transports. These calculations then guide the embedding updates. The authors describe this guidance as more robust and report that it improves algorithm convergence.

The application uses patient admission records, treating disease and procedure codes as the elements to embed and learning topics of admissions. The paper reports superior performance on constructing clinically meaningful disease networks, predicting mortality from admission codes, and recommending procedures. These findings support the joint learning approach in the evaluated setting: the learned relationships between codes and the learned admission topics inform one another.
summary.tldr: A distilled Wasserstein framework jointly learns embeddings and topics, with reported improvements on several tasks using patient admission records.

title: Distilled Wasserstein Learning for Word Embedding and Topic Modeling

abstract: Navigation guided by natural language instructions presents a challenging reasoning problem for instruction followers. Natural language instructions typically identify only a few high-level decisions and landmarks rather than complete low-level motor behaviors; much of the missing information must be inferred based on perceptual context. In machine learning settings, this is doubly challenging: it is difficult to collect enough annotated data to enable learning of this reasoning process from scratch, and also difficult to implement the reasoning process using generic sequence models. Here we describe an approach to vision-and-language navigation that addresses both these issues with an embedded speaker model. We use this speaker model to (1) synthesize new instructions for data augmentation and to (2) implement pragmatic reasoning, which evaluates how well candidate action sequences explain an instruction. Both steps are supported by a panoramic action space that reflects the granularity of human-generated instructions. Experiments show that all three components of this approach---speaker-driven data augmentation, pragmatic reasoning and panoramic action space---dramatically improve the performance of a baseline instruction follower, more than doubling the success rate over the best existing approach on a standard benchmark.

This paper addresses both the shortage of annotated navigation data and the difficulty of learning that reasoning with generic sequence models.

The approach adds a speaker model with two jobs. It generates additional instructions for training, and it evaluates how well candidate action sequences explain a given instruction. The second use supplies pragmatic reasoning: possible routes are assessed through the language they would account for. A panoramic action space supports both uses by matching the level of detail in human instructions.

Experiments show that speaker-generated training data, pragmatic reasoning, and the panoramic action space each substantially improve the baseline follower. The complete approach more than doubles the success rate of the best existing method on the reported standard benchmark. The results support combining instruction generation with instruction following, so language modeling helps both expand training data and evaluate possible navigation behavior.
summary.tldr: A speaker model supplies synthetic instructions and evaluates candidate routes, helping more than double navigation success on the reported benchmark.

title: Speaker-Follower Models for Vision-and-Language Navigation

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are well-suited to recommender systems where the goal is to generate collections of diverse, high-quality items. In the existing literature this is usually formulated as finding the mode of the DPP (the so-called MAP set). However, the MAP objective inherently assumes that the DPP models "optimal" recommendation sets, and yet obtaining such a DPP is nontrivial when there is no ready source of example optimal sets. In this paper we advocate an alternative framework for applying DPPs to recommender systems. Our approach assumes that the DPP simply models user engagements with recommended items, which is more consistent with how DPPs for recommender systems are typically trained. With this assumption, we are able to formulate a metric that measures the expected number of items that a user will engage with. We formalize this optimization of this metric as the Maximum Induced Cardinality (MIC) problem. Although the MIC objective is not submodular, we show that it can be approximated by a submodular function, and that empirically it is well-optimized by a greedy algorithm.
