paragraphs: Determinantal point processes can describe collections that balance item quality and diversity. Recommendation methods often choose the most probable collection under such a model. This paper points out that this objective treats the model as a distribution over optimal recommendation sets, although examples of those optimal sets may be unavailable.

The proposed alternative assumes that the DPP describes which recommended items users engage with. That interpretation better matches the training data commonly used for these systems. Under this assumption, the authors define an objective measuring the expected number of items a user will engage with, and call its optimization Maximum Induced Cardinality.

This changes the recommendation target from finding a probable set to maximizing modeled engagement count. The objective is not submodular, so it does not directly possess that useful optimization structure. Nevertheless, the authors show that a submodular function can approximate it and report that a greedy algorithm optimizes it well empirically. The contribution aligns the decision objective with the stated meaning of the learned engagement model.
summary.tldr: Maximum Induced Cardinality uses a DPP engagement model to select recommendations that maximize expected engagement count.

title: Maximizing Induced Cardinality Under a Determinantal Point Process

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of linear regression with heavy-tailed distributions. Different from previous studies that use the squared loss to measure the performance, we choose the absolute loss, which is capable of estimating the conditional median. To address the challenge that both the input and output could be heavy-tailed, we propose a truncated minimization problem, and demonstrate that it enjoys an $O(\sqrt{d/n})$ excess risk, where $d$ is the dimensionality and $n$ is the number of samples. Compared with traditional work on $\ell_1$-regression, the main advantage of our result is that we achieve a high-probability risk bound without exponential moment conditions on the input and output. Furthermore, if the input is bounded, we show that the classical empirical risk minimization is competent for $\ell_1$-regression even when the output is heavy-tailed.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when unusually large observations can occur in both the inputs and outputs. It evaluates predictions with absolute error rather than squared error. That choice makes the regression objective suitable for estimating a conditional median, shifting the target of prediction as well as the way errors are measured.

To handle heavy tails on both sides of the problem, the authors propose a truncated minimization objective. They establish an excess-risk bound of order square root of d divided by n, where d is the input dimension and n is the sample count. The guarantee holds with high probability without requiring exponential moment conditions on either inputs or outputs.

A second result distinguishes the case of bounded inputs. There, ordinary empirical risk minimization with absolute loss remains adequate even if the outputs are heavy-tailed. The findings therefore clarify when a modified objective is useful and when the classical procedure can suffice. Their main theoretical advance is obtaining strong probability guarantees while relaxing tail requirements that would exclude the distributions under consideration.
summary.tldr: A truncated absolute-loss regression objective provides high-probability risk guarantees without exponential moment assumptions on inputs or outputs.

title: $\ell_1$-regression with Heavy-tailed Distributions

abstract: Building systems that autonomously create temporal abstractions from data is a key challenge in scaling learning and planning in reinforcement learning. One popular approach for addressing this challenge is the options framework (Sutton et al., 1999). However, only recently in (Bacon et al., 2017) was a policy gradient theorem derived for online learning of general purpose options in an end to end fashion. In this work, we extend previous work on this topic that only focuses on learning a two-level hierarchy including options and primitive actions to enable learning simultaneously at multiple resolutions in time. We achieve this by considering an arbitrarily deep hierarchy of options where high level temporally extended options are composed of lower level options with finer resolutions in time. We extend results from (Bacon et al., 2017) and derive policy gradient theorems for a deep hierarchy of options. Our proposed hierarchical option-critic architecture is capable of learning internal policies, termination conditions, and hierarchical compositions over options without the need for any intrinsic rewards or subgoals. Our empirical results in both discrete and continuous environments demonstrate the efficiency of our framework.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems can plan and learn at different time scales by using options: behaviors that extend over multiple steps. This paper addresses how to learn several levels of such temporal abstraction together. It extends earlier option learning that focused on a hierarchy containing options and primitive actions.

The proposed framework allows an arbitrarily deep hierarchy. Higher-level options are composed of lower-level options that operate at finer time scales. The authors derive policy gradient theorems for this structure, supplying a foundation for learning the hierarchy through the reinforcement learning objective.

The contribution is a way to learn coordinated behaviors at multiple temporal resolutions within one architecture, including the decisions that determine where those behaviors begin to give way to others.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical option-critic learns behaviors, stopping rules, and compositions across multiple time scales without supplied subgoals or intrinsic rewards.

title: Learning Abstract Options

abstract: Estimating the structure of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs, also known as Bayesian networks) is a challenging problem since the search space of DAGs is combinatorial and scales superexponentially with the number of nodes. Existing approaches rely on various local heuristics for enforcing the acyclicity constraint. In this paper, we introduce a fundamentally different strategy: we formulate the structure learning problem as a purely continuous optimization problem over real matrices that avoids this combinatorial constraint entirely. This is achieved by a novel characterization of acyclicity that is not only smooth but also exact. The resulting problem can be efficiently solved by standard numerical algorithms, which also makes implementation effortless. The proposed method outperforms existing ones, without imposing any structural assumptions on the graph such as bounded treewidth or in-degree.

This is achieved by a novel characterization of acyclicity that is not only smooth but also exact. The proposed method outperforms existing ones, without imposing any structural assumptions on the graph such as bounded treewidth or in-degree.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph means identifying directed relationships while ensuring that no path loops back to its starting point. Searching over possible graphs is difficult because the number of candidates grows superexponentially with the number of nodes. Traditional approaches use local heuristics to keep the search within the set of graphs without cycles.

This paper replaces that discrete search formulation with continuous optimization over real-valued matrices. Its central contribution is a characterization of acyclicity that is both smooth and exact. Smoothness allows numerical optimization methods to work with the condition, while exactness means the condition captures the absence of cycles rather than merely approximating it.

The resulting problem can be handled efficiently by standard numerical algorithms, simplifying implementation. The authors report that their method outperforms existing approaches without requiring graph restrictions such as bounded treewidth or a bound on incoming edges. The broader significance is that a difficult structural requirement can be expressed in a form compatible with continuous optimization, opening a different route to learning graph structure.
summary.tldr: An exact, smooth characterization of acyclicity turns directed graph structure learning into continuous optimization over matrices.

title: DAGs with NO TEARS: Continuous Optimization for Structure Learning

abstract: Continuous word representation (aka word embedding) is a basic building block in many neural network-based models used in natural language processing tasks. Although it is widely accepted that words with similar semantics should be close to each other in the embedding space, we find that word embeddings learned in several tasks are biased towards word frequency: the embeddings of high-frequency and low-frequency words lie in different subregions of the embedding space, and the embedding of a rare word and a popular word can be far from each other even if they are semantically similar. This makes learned word embeddings ineffective, especially for rare words, and consequently limits the performance of these neural network models. In order to mitigate the issue, in this paper, we propose a neat, simple yet effective adversarial training method to blur the boundary between the embeddings of high-frequency words and low-frequency words. We conducted comprehensive studies on ten datasets across four natural language processing tasks, including word similarity, language modeling, machine translation and text classification. Results show that we achieve higher performance than the baselines in all tasks.

The authors find that embeddings learned in several tasks also separate words according to how frequently they occur. A rare word can therefore sit far from a common word with a similar meaning, weakening the usefulness of the representation.

FRAGE addresses this frequency bias with adversarial training that blurs the boundary between embeddings of common and rare words. The purpose is to reduce the separation associated with frequency, which the paper identifies as particularly harmful for rare words. The approach targets a basic representation used inside many language models, so the same issue can affect several downstream tasks.

The study evaluates the method on ten datasets across word similarity, language modeling, machine translation, and text classification. It reports higher performance than the baselines in all four tasks. These results support reducing frequency-related structure in embeddings as a useful intervention across the evaluated applications, rather than treating frequency separation as harmless organization of the representation space.
summary.tldr: FRAGE uses adversarial training to reduce frequency-based separation in word embeddings and improves results across four evaluated language tasks.

title: FRAGE: Frequency-Agnostic Word Representation

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel controllable text-to-image generative adversarial network (ControlGAN), which can effectively synthesise high-quality images and also control parts of the image generation according to natural language descriptions. To achieve this, we introduce a word-level spatial and channel-wise attention-driven generator that can disentangle different visual attributes, and allow the model to focus on generating and manipulating subregions corresponding to the most relevant words. Also, a word-level discriminator is proposed to provide fine-grained supervisory feedback by correlating words with image regions, facilitating training an effective generator which is able to manipulate specific visual attributes without affecting the generation of other content. Furthermore, perceptual loss is adopted to reduce the randomness involved in the image generation, and to encourage the generator to manipulate specific attributes required in the modified text. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state of the art, and is able to effectively manipulate synthetic images using natural language descriptions.

paragraphs: Generating an image from text becomes more useful when changing a description can selectively change the relevant visual content. This paper introduces ControlGAN, a generative adversarial network designed to produce high-quality images and manipulate particular parts through natural language. Its goal is to connect individual textual changes with specific visual attributes.

The generator uses attention at the word level across spatial locations and channels. This helps separate visual attributes and focus generation on regions associated with relevant words. A word-level discriminator supplies detailed feedback by relating words to image regions, supporting the generator’s ability to change selected attributes while preserving other content.

The method also uses perceptual loss to reduce randomness in generation and encourage changes corresponding to the modified text. Experiments on benchmark datasets report performance beyond existing state-of-the-art approaches and demonstrate effective manipulation of synthetic images through descriptions. Together, these components address the connection between text and image at a finer level than treating the whole description as one undifferentiated instruction.
summary.tldr: ControlGAN links words to visual regions and attributes so text changes can selectively modify generated images.

title: Controllable Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Eigendecomposition (ED) is widely used in deep networks. However, the backpropagation of its results tends to be numerically unstable, whether using ED directly or approximating it with the Power Iteration method, particularly when dealing with large matrices. While this can be mitigated by partitioning the data in small and arbitrary groups, doing so has no theoretical basis and makes its impossible to exploit the power of ED to the full. In this paper, we introduce a numerically stable and differentiable approach to leveraging eigenvectors in deep networks. It can handle large matrices without requiring to split them. We demonstrate the better robustness of our approach over standard ED and PI for ZCA whitening, an alternative to batch normalization, and for PCA denoising, which we introduce as a new normalization strategy for deep networks, aiming to further denoise the network's features.

paragraphs: Eigendecomposition supplies eigenvectors that deep networks can use to transform their features, but passing learning signals backward through this operation can be numerically unstable. The paper identifies this problem in both direct eigendecomposition and Power Iteration approximations, particularly for large matrices. This makes the backward computation a practical obstacle to using the operation inside trainable networks.

A workaround is to divide data into small groups before applying eigendecomposition. The authors argue that these arbitrary divisions lack a theoretical basis and prevent the operation from being used to its full extent. They introduce a differentiable, numerically stable approach that can use eigenvectors from large matrices without requiring such a split.

The paper demonstrates improved robustness over standard eigendecomposition and Power Iteration in two settings. One is ZCA whitening, used as an alternative to batch normalization. The other is PCA denoising, introduced here as a normalization strategy intended to further remove noise from network features. These results support the method's usefulness for incorporating eigenvector-based feature processing into deep-network training.
summary.tldr: A stable differentiable approach lets deep networks use eigenvectors from large matrices without splitting the data into small groups.

title: Backpropagation-Friendly Eigendecomposition

abstract: We might hope that when faced with unexpected inputs, well-designed software systems would fire off warnings. Machine learning (ML) systems, however, which depend strongly on properties of their inputs (e.g. the i.i.d. assumption), tend to fail silently. This paper explores the problem of building ML systems that fail loudly, investigating methods for detecting dataset shift, identifying exemplars that most typify the shift, and quantifying shift malignancy. We focus on several datasets and various perturbations to both covariates and label distributions with varying magnitudes and fractions of data affected. Interestingly, we show that across the dataset shifts that we explore, a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best. Moreover, we demonstrate that domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts qualitatively and determining if they are harmful.

paragraphs: Machine learning systems can encounter inputs that differ from their training data without issuing any warning. This paper studies how to detect those distribution changes, show examples that characterize them, and assess whether they are harmful. These are related but distinct needs: noticing a shift does not by itself explain its nature or its consequences.

The authors compare methods across several datasets, changing both input-variable distributions and label distributions. They vary the strength of the changes and the fraction of examples affected. Across the shifts studied, the strongest detection approach combines dimensionality reduction through pretrained classifiers with a two-sample test, which compares whether two data collections follow the same distribution.

Methods trained to distinguish the source domains of examples serve another useful role. The study finds that they tend to help characterize shifts qualitatively and determine their harmfulness. The results therefore distinguish effective shift detection from useful shift diagnosis, providing empirical guidance for systems intended to make changing data conditions visible.
summary.tldr: An empirical study identifies effective approaches for detecting dataset shift, describing its characteristic examples, and assessing whether it is harmful.

title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are effective models for many dynamical systems consisting of entities and relations. Although most GNN applications assume a single type of entity and relation, many situations involve multiple types of interactions. Relational inference is the problem of inferring these interactions and learning the dynamics from observational data. We frame relational inference as a modular meta-learning problem, where neural modules are trained to be composed in different ways to solve many tasks. This meta-learning framework allows us to implicitly encode time invariance and infer relations in context of one another rather than independently, which increases inference capacity. Framing inference as the inner-loop optimization of meta-learning leads to a model-based approach that is more data-efficient and capable of estimating the state of entities that we do not observe directly, but whose existence can be inferred from their effect on observed entities. To address the large search space of graph neural network compositions, we meta-learn a proposal function that speeds up the inner-loop simulated annealing search within the modular meta-learning algorithm, providing two orders of magnitude increase in the size of problems that can be addressed.

paragraphs: Relational inference seeks to discover how entities interact while learning the dynamics those interactions produce. This paper addresses systems with multiple interaction types by treating inference as modular meta-learning. Neural modules are learned across tasks and then composed in different ways to explain particular observed systems.

Choosing a composition becomes the inner optimization problem of the meta-learning procedure. This formulation implicitly encodes time invariance and evaluates relations in the context of other relations, increasing inference capacity. The authors describe the resulting model-based approach as more data-efficient and capable of estimating states of unobserved entities whose presence can be inferred through their effects on observed ones.

Searching possible graph neural network compositions is computationally demanding. To accelerate that search, the authors also meta-learn a proposal function for the inner-loop simulated annealing procedure. They report that this increases the size of addressable problems by two orders of magnitude. The contribution combines reusable interaction modules with a learned search mechanism, addressing both the expressiveness of relational inference and the cost of finding suitable compositions.
summary.tldr: Modular meta-learning infers interacting systems through reusable neural components, while learned search proposals enable much larger problems.

title: Neural Relational Inference with Fast Modular Meta-learning

abstract: We present a deep imitation learning framework for robotic bimanual manipulation in a continuous state-action space. A core challenge is to generalize the manipulation skills to objects in different locations. We hypothesize that modeling the relational information in the environment can significantly improve generalization. To achieve this, we propose to (i) decompose the multi-modal dynamics into elemental movement primitives, (ii) parameterize each primitive using a recurrent graph neural network to capture interactions, and (iii) integrate a high-level planner that composes primitives sequentially and a low-level controller to combine primitive dynamics and inverse kinematics control. Our model is a deep, hierarchical, modular architecture. Compared to baselines, our model generalizes better and achieves higher success rates on several simulated bimanual robotic manipulation tasks. We open source the code for simulation, data, and models at: https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/HDR-IL.

paragraphs: A robot learning to manipulate objects with two arms must coordinate continuous movements and adapt when objects move to different locations. This paper proposes an imitation learning framework built around the hypothesis that representing relationships in the environment can improve this generalization. The goal is to learn manipulation skills whose usefulness extends across object placements.

The architecture divides complex movement dynamics into elemental primitives. Each primitive uses a recurrent graph neural network to represent interactions over time. A high-level planner arranges these primitives into a sequence, while a low-level controller combines their movement dynamics with inverse kinematics control. This creates a hierarchical, modular system connecting task organization to physical movement.

On several simulated two-arm manipulation tasks, the method generalizes better and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated baselines. These findings support the proposed use of relational information within a hierarchy of movement skills. The evidence described concerns simulated manipulation, and the authors make the simulation code, data, and models available to support further use of the framework.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of graph-based movement primitives improves simulated two-arm robot manipulation across different object locations.

title: Deep Imitation Learning for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation

abstract: We challenge the longstanding assumption that the mean-field approximation for variational inference in Bayesian neural networks is severely restrictive, and show this is not the case in deep networks. We prove several results indicating that deep mean-field variational weight posteriors can induce similar distributions in function-space to those induced by shallower networks with complex weight posteriors. We validate our theoretical contributions empirically, both through examination of the weight posterior using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in small models and by comparing diagonal- to structured-covariance in large settings. Since complex variational posteriors are often expensive and cumbersome to implement, our results suggest that using mean-field variational inference in a deeper model is both a practical and theoretically justified alternative to structured approximations.

We validate our theoretical contributions empirically, both through examination of the weight posterior using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in small models and by comparing diagonal- to structured-covariance in large settings. paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through distributions over network weights. Mean-field variational inference simplifies those distributions by treating weights independently, which can appear restrictive compared with approximations that represent correlations. This paper examines whether that restriction necessarily translates into limited uncertainty over the functions a network can express.

The theoretical results show that deeper networks with mean-field weight posteriors can induce function distributions similar to those produced by shallower networks with more complex posteriors. The key distinction is between simplicity in the weight distribution and simplicity in the resulting function distribution. Network depth can help bridge that gap.

The authors investigate weight posteriors using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in small models and compare diagonal and structured covariance approximations in larger settings. These experiments support the theoretical findings. Since structured posterior approximations can be costly and cumbersome, the results suggest a practical alternative: use a deeper model with mean-field inference. The claim supports this design option rather than establishing that posterior structure is unnecessary for every Bayesian network.
summary.tldr: Greater network depth can let simple mean-field weight posteriors express function uncertainty similar to shallower networks with complex posteriors.

title: Liberty or Depth: Deep Bayesian Neural Nets Do Not Need Complex Weight Posterior Approximations

abstract: Understanding the nature of representation in neural networks is a goal shared by neuroscience and machine learning. It is therefore exciting that both fields converge not only on shared questions but also on similar approaches. A pressing question in these areas is understanding how the structure of the representation used by neural networks affects both their generalization, and robustness to perturbations. In this work, we investigate the latter by juxtaposing experimental results regarding the covariance spectrum of neural representations in the mouse V1 (Stringer et al) with artificial neural networks. We use adversarial robustness to probe Stringer et al’s theory regarding the causal role of a 1/n covariance spectrum. We empirically investigate the benefits such a neural code confers in neural networks, and illuminate its role in multi-layer architectures. Our results show that imposing the experimentally observed structure on artificial neural networks makes them more robust to adversarial attacks. Moreover, our findings complement the existing theory relating wide neural networks to kernel methods, by showing the role of intermediate representations.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the internal structure of a neural representation affects resistance to perturbations. It connects observations from mouse visual cortex with artificial neural networks, focusing on a covariance spectrum that follows a 1/n pattern. The spectrum describes how variation is distributed across the representation, making it a structural property of the neural code.

The authors use adversarial robustness to investigate a theory about the causal role of that spectral pattern. They impose the experimentally observed structure on artificial networks and examine the resulting benefits empirically. They also study its role in multilayer architectures, bringing attention to the representations formed inside the network as computation passes through successive layers.

The reported results show increased resistance to adversarial attacks when this structure is imposed. These findings provide empirical support for a connection between representation structure and robustness in the tested artificial networks. They also complement theory linking wide neural networks with kernel methods by highlighting the role of intermediate representations, rather than considering only the network’s overall input-output relationship.
summary.tldr: Imposing a covariance-spectrum pattern observed in mouse visual cortex improves adversarial robustness in the artificial networks studied.

title: On 1/n neural representation and robustness

abstract: This work proposes a novel smoothing method, called Bend, Mix and Release (BMR), that extends two well-known smooth approximations of the convex optimization literature: randomized smoothing and the Moreau envelope. The BMR smoothing method allows to trade-off between the computational simplicity of randomized smoothing (RS) and the approximation efficiency of the Moreau envelope (ME). More specifically, we show that BMR achieves up to a $\sqrt{d}$ multiplicative improvement compared to the approximation error of RS, where $d$ is the dimension of the search space, while being less computation intensive than the ME. For non-convex objectives, BMR also has the desirable property to widen local minima, allowing optimization methods to reach small cracks and crevices of extremely irregular and non-convex functions, while being well-suited to a distributed setting. This novel smoothing method is then used to improve first-order non-smooth optimization (both convex and non-convex) by allowing for a local exploration of the search space. More specifically, our analysis sheds light on the similarities between evolution strategies and BMR, creating a link between exploration strategies of zeroth-order methods and the regularity of first-order optimization problems. Finally, we evidence the impact of BMR through synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes difficult when an objective has sharp changes or a highly irregular landscape. This paper introduces Bend, Mix and Release, or BMR, a smoothing method that connects randomized smoothing with the Moreau envelope. Its purpose is to balance the computational simplicity of the former with the approximation quality of the latter.

The authors show that BMR can improve approximation error over randomized smoothing by a multiplicative factor of up to the square root of the search-space dimension, while requiring less computation than the Moreau envelope. For nonconvex objectives, it also widens local minima. This makes narrow regions of the landscape more accessible to optimization methods and supports local exploration.

The paper applies BMR to first-order optimization of nonsmooth convex and nonconvex objectives, and describes it as suitable for distributed computation. Its analysis connects the exploration used by evolution strategies with the regularity of first-order optimization problems. Synthetic experiments illustrate the method's impact, complementing the theoretical account of its computational and approximation tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: BMR smooths difficult optimization landscapes while balancing computational cost, approximation accuracy, and local exploration.

title: A Simple and Efficient Smoothing Method for Faster Optimization and Local Exploration

abstract: We study the problem of improving the performance of online algorithms by incorporating machine-learned predictions. The goal is to design algorithms that are both consistent and robust, meaning that the algorithm performs well when predictions are accurate and maintains worst-case guarantees. Such algorithms have been studied in a recent line of works due to Lykouris and Vassilvitskii (ICML '18) and Purohit et al (NeurIPS '18). They provide robustness-consistency trade-offs for a variety of online problems. However, they leave open the question of whether these trade-offs are tight, i.e., to what extent to such trade-offs are necessary. In this paper, we provide the first set of non-trivial lower bounds for competitive analysis using machine-learned predictions. We focus on the classic problems of ski-rental and non-clairvoyant scheduling and provide optimal trade-offs in various settings.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions as information arrives, and machine-learned predictions can help them anticipate what comes next. Two goals arise: consistency, meaning strong performance when predictions are accurate, and robustness, meaning a worst-case guarantee even when advice is poor. Earlier work established algorithms that trade between these goals.

This paper asks whether those trade-offs are unavoidable or merely consequences of particular algorithm designs. The authors provide the first nontrivial lower bounds for competitive analysis with machine-learned predictions. A lower bound limits what algorithms can achieve, so it can establish that a desired combination of consistency and robustness is impossible within a given setting.

The analysis focuses on ski rental and non-clairvoyant scheduling, establishing optimal trade-offs in various settings. Optimality here concerns the balance between benefiting from accurate predictions and retaining worst-case protection. The contribution therefore clarifies the limits of prediction-assisted online decision making: for the settings covered, improving one guarantee has a provably necessary cost in the other.
summary.tldr: The paper proves lower bounds and optimal trade-offs between accurate-prediction performance and worst-case protection for online rental and scheduling problems.

title: Optimal Robustness-Consistency Trade-offs for Learning-Augmented Online Algorithms

abstract: Normalization layers and activation functions are fundamental components in deep networks and typically co-locate with each other. Here we propose to design them using an automated approach. Instead of designing them separately, we unify them into a single tensor-to-tensor computation graph, and evolve its structure starting from basic mathematical functions. Examples of such mathematical functions are addition, multiplication and statistical moments. The use of low-level mathematical functions, in contrast to the use of high-level modules in mainstream NAS, leads to a highly sparse and large search space which can be challenging for search methods. To address the challenge, we develop efficient rejection protocols to quickly filter out candidate layers that do not work well. We also use multi-objective evolution to optimize each layer's performance across many architectures to prevent overfitting. Our method leads to the discovery of EvoNorms, a set of new normalization-activation layers with novel, and sometimes surprising structures that go beyond existing design patterns. For example, some EvoNorms do not assume that normalization and activation functions must be applied sequentially, nor need to center the feature maps, nor require explicit activation functions. Our experiments show that EvoNorms work well on image classification models including ResNets, MobileNets and EfficientNets but also transfer well to Mask R-CNN with FPN/SpineNet for instance segmentation and to BigGAN for image synthesis, outperforming BatchNorm and GroupNorm based layers in many cases.

paragraphs: Normalization and activation usually appear together in deep networks, yet they are commonly designed as separate components. This paper searches for them jointly. It represents a combined layer as a computation graph built from elementary operations such as addition, multiplication, and statistical moments, allowing the search to explore arrangements beyond established layer designs.

Searching at this low level creates a large space with relatively few useful candidates. The authors develop rejection procedures that quickly discard poor layers and use multi-objective evolution to assess performance across several architectures. Evaluating candidates across architectures is intended to prevent the search from producing a layer suited too narrowly to one network.

The resulting EvoNorm layers sometimes depart from familiar patterns: some do not center feature maps, require an explicit activation function, or separate normalization and activation into successive steps. Experiments show successful use in image classification and transfer to instance segmentation and image synthesis. EvoNorms outperform BatchNorm- and GroupNorm-based layers in many tested cases, supporting joint automated design as a productive alternative.
summary.tldr: An evolutionary search jointly designs normalization and activation layers that perform well across several architectures and visual tasks.

title: Evolving Normalization-Activation Layers

abstract: In this paper, we consider an online optimization problem in which the reward functions are DR-submodular, and in addition to maximizing the total reward, the sequence of decisions must satisfy some convex constraints on average. Specifically, at each round $t\in\{1,\dots,T\}$, upon committing to an action $x_t$, a DR-submodular utility function $f_t(\cdot)$ and a convex constraint function $g_t(\cdot)$ are revealed, and the goal is to maximize the overall utility while ensuring the average of the constraint functions $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(x_t)$ is non-positive. Such cumulative constraints arise naturally in applications where the average resource consumption is required to remain below a prespecified threshold. We study this problem under an adversarial model and a stochastic model for the convex constraints, where the functions $g_t$ can vary arbitrarily or according to an i.i.d. process over time slots $t\in\{1,\dots,T\}$, respectively. We propose a single algorithm which achieves sub-linear (with respect to $T$) regret as well as sub-linear constraint violation bounds in both settings, without prior knowledge of the regime. Prior works have studied this problem in the special case of linear constraint functions. Our results not only improve upon the existing bounds under linear cumulative constraints, but also give the first sub-linear bounds for general convex long-term constraints.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions made over time when their rewards and resource costs become known only after each decision. Rewards have a diminishing-returns structure called DR-submodularity. The decisions must also meet convex constraints on average, making the setting relevant to resource budgets that apply across many rounds rather than separately at every round.

The authors consider two ways constraints can change: arbitrarily, as in an adversarial setting, or through independent draws from a fixed distribution. They propose one algorithm that works in both settings without needing advance knowledge of which regime applies. This removes the need to select a different method based on how constraints arrive.

The analysis establishes regret and cumulative constraint-violation bounds that grow sublinearly with the number of rounds. Consequently, the corresponding bounds per round decrease as the horizon grows; this is not a promise of satisfying every individual constraint immediately. The results improve earlier bounds for linear constraints and extend sublinear guarantees to general convex long-term constraints.
summary.tldr: One online optimization algorithm achieves sublinear regret and constraint violation under both adversarial and stochastic convex constraints.

title: A Single Recipe for Online Submodular Maximization with Adversarial or Stochastic Constraints

abstract: Many objects in the real world undergo dramatic variations in visual appearance. For example, a tomato may be red or green, sliced or chopped, fresh or fried, liquid or solid. Training a single detector to accurately recognize tomatoes in all these different states is challenging. On the other hand, contextual cues (e.g., the presence of a knife, a cutting board, a strainer or a pan) are often strongly indicative of how the object appears in the scene. Recognizing such contextual cues is useful not only to improve the accuracy of object detection or to determine the state of the object, but also to understand its functional properties and to infer ongoing or upcoming human-object interactions. A fully-supervised approach to recognizing object states and their contexts in the real-world is unfortunately marred by the long-tailed, open-ended distribution of the data, which would effectively require massive amounts of annotations to capture the appearance of objects in all their different forms. Instead of relying on manually-labeled data for this task, we propose a new framework for learning Contextualized OBject Embeddings (COBE) from automatically-transcribed narrations of instructional videos. We leverage the semantic and compositional structure of language by training a visual detector to predict a contextualized word embedding of the object and its associated narration. This enables the learning of an object representation where concepts relate according to a semantic language metric. Our experiments show that our detector learns to predict a rich variety of contextual object information, and that it is highly effective in the settings of few-shot and zero-shot learning.

The central contribution is connecting visual detection to language-derived context, so that an object's representation can reflect how it appears and is being used.
summary.tldr: COBE uses automatically transcribed instructional videos to learn object representations that capture visual states and context.

title: COBE: Contextualized Object Embeddings from Narrated Instructional Video

abstract: AI systems often rely on two key components: a specified goal or reward function and an optimization algorithm to compute the optimal behavior for that goal. This approach is intended to provide value for a principal: the user on whose behalf the agent acts. The objectives given to these agents often refer to a partial specification of the principal's goals. We consider the cost of this incompleteness by analyzing a model of a principal and an agent in a resource constrained world where the L features of the state correspond to different sources of utility for the principal. We assume that the reward function given to the agent only has support on J < L features. The contributions of our paper are as follows: 1) we propose a novel model of an incomplete principal—agent problem from artificial intelligence; 2) we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which indefinitely optimizing for any incomplete proxy objective leads to arbitrarily low overall utility; and 3) we show how modifying the setup to allow reward functions that reference the full state or allowing the principal to update the proxy objective over time can lead to higher utility solutions. The results in this paper argue that we should view the design of reward functions as an interactive and dynamic process and identifies a theoretical scenario where some degree of interactivity is desirable.

paragraphs: An AI agent often optimizes a reward function intended to represent what its user wants. That representation can omit parts of the user's preferences. This paper studies the consequences through a mathematical model of a principal and an agent operating with constrained resources, where multiple features of the world contribute to the principal's overall utility.

The model explicitly assumes that the agent's reward depends on only J of the L relevant features, with J smaller than L. Within this setup, the authors give necessary and sufficient conditions under which indefinitely optimizing any incomplete proxy drives overall utility arbitrarily low. The result is conditional on those conditions; it does not establish that every incomplete reward inevitably produces that outcome.

The paper also examines changes that can produce higher-utility solutions. These include allowing rewards to reference the full state and letting the principal revise the proxy over time. The analysis therefore gives a theoretical reason to treat reward design as an ongoing interaction: updating an objective can matter when its initial specification leaves out things the user values.
summary.tldr: A resource-constrained principal–agent model identifies when optimizing incomplete rewards can drive utility arbitrarily low and how interactive reward updates can help.

title: Consequences of Misaligned AI

abstract: In images of complex scenes, objects are often occluding each other which makes perception tasks such as object detection and tracking, or robotic control tasks such as planning, challenging. To facilitate downstream tasks, it is thus important to reason about the full extent of objects, i.e., seeing behind occlusion, typically referred to as amodal instance completion. In this paper, we propose a variational generative framework for amodal completion, referred to as AMODAL-VAE, which does not require any amodal labels at training time, as it is able to utilize widely available object instance masks. We showcase our approach on the downstream task of scene editing where the user is presented with interactive tools to complete and erase objects in photographs. Experiments on complex street scenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in amodal mask completion and showcase high-quality scene editing results. Interestingly, a user study shows that humans prefer object completions inferred by our model to the human-labeled ones.

paragraphs: When objects overlap in a photograph, only part of an object's extent is visible. Amodal completion estimates the whole object, including the region hidden behind another object. This paper introduces AMODAL-VAE, a variational generative framework for that task, motivated by applications such as detection, tracking, planning, and scene editing.

The method trains without amodal labels that explicitly mark the hidden extent of objects. Instead, it uses widely available object instance masks. That training setup matters because it allows the model to learn completion without requiring the specialized annotations that directly describe the desired completed shape.

The authors demonstrate interactive tools for completing and erasing objects in photographs. Experiments on complex street scenes achieve leading amodal-mask completion performance and produce high-quality scene edits. In a user study, participants prefer the model's inferred completions to human-labeled ones. That preference is evidence about perceived completion quality in the study, complementing the reported mask-completion results and the editing demonstration.
summary.tldr: AMODAL-VAE learns to complete occluded object masks without amodal training labels and supports interactive scene editing.

title: Variational Amodal Object Completion

abstract: We study the regularisation induced in neural networks by Gaussian noise injections (GNIs). Though such injections have been extensively studied when applied to data, there have been few studies on understanding the regularising effect they induce when applied to network activations. Here we derive the explicit regulariser of GNIs, obtained by marginalising out the injected noise, and show that it penalises functions with high-frequency components in the Fourier domain; particularly in layers closer to a neural network's output. We show analytically and empirically that such regularisation produces calibrated classifiers with large classification margins.

paragraphs: Adding Gaussian noise during neural network training can change which functions the network learns. This paper examines that regularizing effect when noise is injected into network activations. Its focus is on explaining the mathematical preference introduced by this practice, an aspect less studied than adding noise directly to training data.

The authors derive an explicit regularizer by averaging over the injected noise. This makes the effect of random perturbations expressible as a penalty on the learned function. In the Fourier domain, the penalty discourages high-frequency components, which describe rapidly varying aspects of a function. The effect is particularly pronounced in layers closer to the network’s output.

The paper connects this regularization to classification behavior through both analysis and experiments. It reports calibrated classifiers with large classification margins. Calibration concerns how well predictive confidence reflects correctness, while margins describe separation in classification decisions. These findings give a concrete interpretation to activation noise: its influence includes a preference against rapid functional variation, with demonstrated consequences for confidence and decision separation.
summary.tldr: Gaussian activation noise induces a penalty on high-frequency functions and is linked analytically and empirically to calibrated, large-margin classifiers.

title: Explicit Regularisation in Gaussian Noise Injections

abstract: We introduce a framework for designing primal methods under the decentralized optimization setting where local functions are smooth and strongly convex. Our approach consists of approximately solving a sequence of sub-problems induced by the accelerated augmented Lagrangian method, thereby providing a systematic way for deriving several well-known decentralized algorithms including EXTRA and SSDA. When coupled with accelerated gradient descent, our framework yields a novel primal algorithm whose convergence rate is optimal and matched by recently derived lower bounds. We provide experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm on highly ill-conditioned problems.

paragraphs: Decentralized optimization distributes an optimization problem across participants with local objective functions. This paper develops a framework for designing primal methods in that setting, assuming the local functions are smooth and strongly convex. Those assumptions define the mathematical regime in which the framework and its convergence results apply.

The approach approximately solves a sequence of subproblems generated by an accelerated augmented Lagrangian method. Allowing approximate solutions is central to the construction: the framework organizes the larger optimization process around these inexact intermediate computations. It also provides a systematic derivation of established decentralized algorithms, including EXTRA and SSDA, connecting them through a common design approach.

Combining the framework with accelerated gradient descent yields a new primal algorithm with an optimal convergence rate matched by lower bounds. Experiments further demonstrate effectiveness on highly ill-conditioned problems, where optimization can be difficult. The contribution therefore combines a unifying way to derive decentralized algorithms with a new method whose theoretical rate reaches the stated benchmark for the setting.
summary.tldr: IDEAL unifies decentralized optimization methods and yields an algorithm with an optimal convergence rate for smooth, strongly convex local objectives.

title: IDEAL: Inexact DEcentralized Accelerated Augmented Lagrangian Method

abstract: Backpropagation (BP) has been the most successful algorithm used to train artificial neural networks. However, there are several gaps between BP and learning in biologically plausible neuronal networks of the brain (learning in the brain, or simply BL, for short), in particular, (1) it has been unclear to date, if BP can be implemented exactly via BL, (2) there is a lack of local plasticity in BP, i.e., weight updates require information that is not locally available, while BL utilizes only locally available information, and (3)~there is a lack of autonomy in BP, i.e., some external control over the neural network is required (e.g., switching between prediction and learning stages requires changes to dynamics and synaptic plasticity rules), while BL works fully autonomously. Bridging such gaps, i.e., understanding how BP can be approximated by BL, has been of major interest in both neuroscience and machine learning. Despite tremendous efforts, however, no previous model has bridged the gaps at a degree of demonstrating an equivalence to BP, instead, only approximations to BP have been shown. Here, we present for the first time a framework within BL that bridges the above crucial gaps. We propose a BL model that (1) produces \emph{exactly the same} updates of the neural weights as~BP, while (2)~employing local plasticity, i.e., all neurons perform only local computations, done simultaneously. We then modify it to an alternative BL model that (3) also works fully autonomously. Overall, our work provides important evidence for the debate on the long-disputed question whether the brain can perform~BP.

paragraphs: Backpropagation trains neural networks effectively, but its usual formulation differs from biologically plausible learning in several ways. Weight updates can depend on information unavailable locally, and external control may be needed to switch between prediction and learning. This paper asks whether a model of brain-like learning can reproduce backpropagation exactly while addressing those differences.

The authors propose a framework in which neurons perform simultaneous local computations, yet the resulting neural weight updates are exactly the same as those produced by backpropagation. This is a stronger correspondence than merely approximating the updates. They then modify the construction into an alternative model that also operates autonomously, addressing the need for external switching of dynamics or plasticity rules.

The contribution is a demonstration that exact backpropagation updates can be compatible with the local learning computations of the proposed framework. The autonomous variant extends that argument to another important aspect of biological plausibility. These constructions provide evidence relevant to whether the brain could perform backpropagation; they are not presented as observations establishing that biological brains actually use the proposed mechanism.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs a biologically plausible learning framework with exact backpropagation weight updates and local computations, then develops an autonomous variant.

title: Can the Brain Do Backpropagation? --- Exact Implementation of Backpropagation in Predictive Coding Networks

abstract: Keyword search is a fundamental task to retrieve information that is the most relevant to the query keywords. Keyword search over graphs aims to find subtrees or subgraphs containing all query keywords ranked according to some criteria. Existing studies all assume that the graphs have complete information. However, real-world graphs may contain some missing information (such as edges or keywords), thus making the problem much more challenging. To solve the problem of keyword search over incomplete graphs, we propose a novel model named KS-GNN based on the graph neural network and the auto-encoder. By considering the latent relationships and the frequency of different keywords, the proposed KS-GNN aims to alleviate the effect of missing information and is able to learn low-dimensional representative node embeddings that preserve both graph structure and keyword features. Our model can effectively answer keyword search queries with linear time complexity over incomplete graphs. The experiments on four real-world datasets show that our model consistently achieves better performance than state-of-the-art baseline methods in graphs having missing information.

paragraphs: Keyword search on a graph seeks a subtree or subgraph containing the requested keywords, with results ordered by a chosen criterion. The paper focuses on graphs where some edges or keywords are missing. In that setting, relevant information can be obscured by incomplete connections or descriptions, undermining methods that assume the graph is complete.

KS-GNN combines a graph neural network with an autoencoder to learn compact representations of nodes. These representations preserve information about both graph structure and keyword features. The model also considers latent relationships and how frequently different keywords occur, aiming to reduce the damage caused by missing information when representing and searching the graph.

The authors report that their model answers keyword queries over incomplete graphs with linear time complexity. Experiments on four real-world datasets show consistently better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods when information is missing. The contribution is therefore both representational and computational: it learns node descriptions suited to incomplete data while supporting efficient query answering, with empirical gains demonstrated in the tested graphs.
summary.tldr: KS-GNN learns structural and keyword representations that improve keyword search on incomplete graphs while supporting linear-time query answering.

title: KS-GNN: Keywords Search over Incomplete Graphs via Graphs Neural Network

abstract: Feature importance (FI) estimates are a popular form of explanation, and they are commonly created and evaluated by computing the change in model confidence caused by removing certain input features at test time. For example, in the standard Sufficiency metric, only the top-k most important tokens are kept. In this paper, we study several under-explored dimensions of FI explanations, providing conceptual and empirical improvements for this form of explanation. First, we advance a new argument for why it can be problematic to remove features from an input when creating or evaluating explanations: the fact that these counterfactual inputs are out-of-distribution (OOD) to models implies that the resulting explanations are socially misaligned. The crux of the problem is that the model prior and random weight initialization influence the explanations (and explanation metrics) in unintended ways. To resolve this issue, we propose a simple alteration to the model training process, which results in more socially aligned explanations and metrics. Second, we compare among five approaches for removing features from model inputs. We find that some methods produce more OOD counterfactuals than others, and we make recommendations for selecting a feature-replacement function. Finally, we introduce four search-based methods for identifying FI explanations and compare them to strong baselines, including LIME, Anchors, and Integrated Gradients. Through experiments with six diverse text classification datasets, we find that the only method that consistently outperforms random search is a Parallel Local Search (PLS) that we introduce. Improvements over the second best method are as large as 5.4 points for Sufficiency and 17 points for Comprehensiveness.

summary.tldr: The paper addresses distribution shift caused by feature removal and introduces a search method that consistently outperforms random search in its text-classification experiments.

title: The Out-of-Distribution Problem in Explainability and Search Methods for Feature Importance Explanations

abstract: To achieve human-like common sense about everyday life, machine learning systems must understand and reason about the goals, preferences, and actions of other agents in the environment. By the end of their first year of life, human infants intuitively achieve such common sense, and these cognitive achievements lay the foundation for humans' rich and complex understanding of the mental states of others. Can machines achieve generalizable, commonsense reasoning about other agents like human infants? The Baby Intuitions Benchmark (BIB) challenges machines to predict the plausibility of an agent's behavior based on the underlying causes of its actions. Because BIB's content and paradigm are adopted from developmental cognitive science, BIB allows for direct comparison between human and machine performance. Nevertheless, recently proposed, deep-learning-based agency reasoning models fail to show infant-like reasoning, leaving BIB an open challenge.

paragraphs: Understanding another agent involves reasoning about why it acts: what it wants, what it prefers, and how its actions relate to those motivations. This paper introduces the Baby Intuitions Benchmark, or BIB, to test whether machine learning systems can make such judgments in a generalizable way. Its reference point is the intuitive understanding that human infants develop by the end of their first year.

BIB asks models to judge how plausible an agent's behavior is in light of the underlying causes of its actions. Its content and testing approach come from developmental cognitive science. That connection matters because it allows human and machine performance to be compared within a shared framework for studying reasoning about agents.

The authors report that the recently proposed deep learning models they examine do not demonstrate infant-like reasoning on the benchmark. BIB thus supplies both an evaluation framework and an unresolved challenge. The finding concerns the evaluated models' ability to reason about agency, while the benchmark's broader purpose is to make that ability directly testable.
summary.tldr: BIB tests reasoning about other agents using developmental-science tasks, on which the evaluated deep learning models fail to show infant-like understanding.

title: Baby Intuitions Benchmark (BIB): Discerning the goals, preferences, and actions of others

abstract: Humans and animals explore their environment and acquire useful skills even in the absence of clear goals, exhibiting intrinsic motivation. The study of intrinsic motivation in artificial agents is concerned with the following question: what is a good general-purpose objective for an agent? We study this question in dynamic partially-observed environments, and argue that a compact and general learning objective is to minimize the entropy of the agent's state visitation estimated using a latent state-space model. This objective induces an agent to both gather information about its environment, corresponding to reducing uncertainty, and to gain control over its environment, corresponding to reducing the unpredictability of future world states. We instantiate this approach as a deep reinforcement learning agent equipped with a deep variational Bayes filter. We find that our agent learns to discover, represent, and exercise control of dynamic objects in a variety of partially-observed environments sensed with visual observations without extrinsic reward.

paragraphs: An agent without an externally assigned reward still needs a reason to explore and acquire useful abilities. This paper studies that question in environments that change over time and are only partially observable. The proposed objective is to minimize the entropy of the agent's state visitation, estimated through a latent state-space model.

The objective connects two behaviors through uncertainty. Gathering information can reduce uncertainty about the current environment, while exercising control can reduce the unpredictability of future world states. The authors argue that these motivations can emerge from one compact objective. The latent model matters because visual observations provide incomplete access to the underlying state.

The implementation combines deep reinforcement learning with a deep variational Bayes filter. In a variety of visually observed, partially observable environments, the agent learns to discover dynamic objects, represent them, and exercise control over them without extrinsic reward. These results support the proposed connection between acquiring information and acquiring control as a basis for intrinsically motivated behavior in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: Minimizing model-estimated state-visitation entropy enables an agent to gather information and learn object control without external rewards.

title: Information is Power: Intrinsic Control via Information Capture

abstract: Inferring the parameters of a stochastic model based on experimental observations is central to the scientific method. A particularly challenging setting is when the model is strongly indeterminate, i.e. when distinct sets of parameters yield identical observations. This arises in many practical situations, such as when inferring the distance and power of a radio source (is the source close and weak or far and strong?) or when estimating the amplifier gain and underlying brain activity of an electrophysiological experiment. In this work, we present hierarchical neural posterior estimation (HNPE), a novel method for cracking such indeterminacy by exploiting additional information conveyed by an auxiliary set of observations sharing global parameters. Our method extends recent developments in simulation-based inference (SBI) based on normalizing flows to Bayesian hierarchical models. We validate quantitatively our proposal on a motivating example amenable to analytical solutions and then apply it to invert a well known non-linear model from computational neuroscience, using both simulated and real EEG data.

paragraphs: Different parameter settings in a stochastic model can produce identical observations, making inference ambiguous. A radio signal, for example, might come from a nearby weak source or a distant strong one. HNPE addresses this kind of indeterminacy by using additional observations that share some global parameters with the observation of interest.

The method places neural posterior estimation within a Bayesian hierarchical model. It extends simulation-based inference using normalizing flows so that information from the auxiliary observations can help constrain shared parameters. This changes the available evidence: relationships across observations can help distinguish explanations that are indistinguishable from a single observation alone.

They then apply it to infer parameters of a nonlinear computational-neuroscience model using simulated and real EEG recordings. The contribution is a way to incorporate shared structure into neural inference. Its mechanism depends on the auxiliary observations conveying information through common global parameters, allowing the hierarchy to help resolve ambiguity in the underlying scientific model.
summary.tldr: HNPE uses observations with shared global parameters to help resolve ambiguity in simulation-based parameter inference.

title: HNPE: Leveraging Global Parameters for Neural Posterior Estimation

abstract: Prediction of a molecule’s 3D conformer ensemble from the molecular graph holds a key role in areas of cheminformatics and drug discovery. Existing generative models have several drawbacks including lack of modeling important molecular geometry elements (e.g., torsion angles), separate optimization stages prone to error accumulation, and the need for structure fine-tuning based on approximate classical force-fields or computationally expensive methods. We propose GEOMOL --- an end-to-end, non-autoregressive, and SE(3)-invariant machine learning approach to generate distributions of low-energy molecular 3D conformers. Leveraging the power of message passing neural networks (MPNNs) to capture local and global graph information, we predict local atomic 3D structures and torsion angles, avoid- ing unnecessary over-parameterization of the geometric degrees of freedom (e.g., one angle per non-terminal bond). Such local predictions suffice both for both the training loss computation and for the full deterministic conformer assembly (at test time). We devise a non-adversarial optimal transport based loss function to promote diverse conformer generation. GEOMOL predominantly outperforms popular open-source, commercial, or state-of-the-art machine learning (ML) models, while achieving significant speed-ups. We expect such differentiable 3D structure generators to significantly impact molecular modeling and related applications.

paragraphs: A molecular graph can correspond to multiple three-dimensional conformations. Predicting this collection matters for molecular modeling and drug discovery. GeoMol tackles the problem by generating distributions of low-energy structures while explicitly modeling local atomic geometry and torsion angles, which describe twisting around bonds.

The authors report that GeoMol outperforms most of the compared open-source, commercial, and machine learning approaches while delivering substantial speed improvements. The findings support generating molecular ensembles through carefully chosen geometric components, with diversity addressed explicitly during training.
summary.tldr: GeoMol generates diverse molecular conformers from local geometry and torsion predictions, predominantly outperforming compared methods with substantial speedups.

title: GeoMol: Torsional Geometric Generation of Molecular 3D Conformer Ensembles

abstract: The continuous-time model of Nesterov's momentum provides a thought-provoking perspective for understanding the nature of the acceleration phenomenon in convex optimization. One of the main ideas in this line of research comes from the field of classical mechanics and proposes to link Nesterov's trajectory to the solution of a set of Euler-Lagrange equations relative to the so-called Bregman Lagrangian. In the last years, this approach led to the discovery of many new (stochastic) accelerated algorithms and provided a solid theoretical foundation for the design of structure-preserving accelerated methods. In this work, we revisit this idea and provide an in-depth analysis of the action relative to the Bregman Lagrangian from the point of view of calculus of variations. Our main finding is that, while Nesterov's method is a stationary point for the action, it is often not a minimizer but instead a saddle point for this functional in the space of differentiable curves. This finding challenges the main intuition behind the variational interpretation of Nesterov's method and provides additional insights into the intriguing geometry of accelerated paths.

paragraphs: One way to understand accelerated optimization is to view the algorithm's path as a continuous-time trajectory. For Nesterov's momentum, an influential interpretation connects that trajectory to Euler-Lagrange equations derived from a Bregman Lagrangian. This connection to classical mechanics has supported the design of accelerated algorithms and structure-preserving methods.

The paper reexamines the corresponding action using calculus of variations. An action assigns a value to an entire differentiable path, so the question is about optimization over trajectories. Satisfying its Euler-Lagrange equations establishes stationarity, but stationarity alone does not establish that a trajectory minimizes the action.

The main finding is that Nesterov's path is often a saddle point of this action rather than a minimum. Thus, the equation-based connection remains, while the interpretation of the path as action-minimizing needs qualification. The work sharpens the geometric understanding of acceleration by separating the valid stationary-path characterization from a stronger minimizing-path intuition that does not always hold.
summary.tldr: Nesterov's continuous-time trajectory is stationary for the Bregman action but is often a saddle point, challenging its interpretation as an action minimizer.

title: Rethinking the Variational Interpretation of Accelerated Optimization Methods

abstract: Understanding generalization in deep learning has been one of the major challenges in statistical learning theory over the last decade. While recent work has illustrated that the dataset and the training algorithm must be taken into account in order to obtain meaningful generalization bounds, it is still theoretically not clear which properties of the data and the algorithm determine the generalization performance. In this study, we approach this problem from a dynamical systems theory perspective and represent stochastic optimization algorithms as \emph{random iterated function systems} (IFS). Well studied in the dynamical systems literature, under mild assumptions, such IFSs can be shown to be ergodic with an invariant measure that is often supported on sets with a \emph{fractal structure}. As our main contribution, we prove that the generalization error of a stochastic optimization algorithm can be bounded based on the `complexity' of the fractal structure that underlies its invariant measure. Then, by leveraging results from dynamical systems theory, we show that the generalization error can be explicitly linked to the choice of the algorithm (e.g., stochastic gradient descent -- SGD), algorithm hyperparameters (e.g., step-size, batch-size), and the geometry of the problem (e.g., Hessian of the loss). We further specialize our results to specific problems (e.g., linear/logistic regression, one hidden-layered neural networks) and algorithms (e.g., SGD and preconditioned variants), and obtain analytical estimates for our bound. For modern neural networks, we develop an efficient algorithm to compute the developed bound and support our theory with various experiments on neural networks.

For modern neural networks, they develop an efficient procedure to compute the proposed bound and provide supporting experiments. The contribution is a bound-based explanation of generalization that explicitly incorporates properties of the training dynamics.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds generalization through the fractal complexity of stochastic training dynamics, linking it to algorithm choices and problem geometry.

title: Fractal Structure and Generalization Properties of Stochastic Optimization Algorithms

abstract: We study the Solid Isotropic Material Penalization (SIMP) method with a density field generated by a fully-connected neural network, taking the coordinates as inputs. In the large width limit, we show that the use of DNNs leads to a filtering effect similar to traditional filtering techniques for SIMP, with a filter described by the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). This filter is however not invariant under translation, leading to visual artifacts and non-optimal shapes. We propose two embeddings of the input coordinates, which lead to (approximate) spatial invariance of the NTK and of the filter. We empirically confirm our theoretical observations and study how the filter size is affected by the architecture of the network. Our solution can easily be applied to any other coordinates-based generation method.

paragraphs: Topology optimization seeks a material layout, represented here through a density field. The paper studies the SIMP method when a fully connected neural network generates that field from spatial coordinates. This representation changes how optimization behaves, so the authors investigate the filtering effect introduced by the network itself.

In the limit of large network width, they show that this effect resembles traditional SIMP filtering and is described by the neural tangent kernel. However, the resulting filter is not translation invariant: its behavior depends on spatial position. The paper connects this lack of invariance to visual artifacts and shapes that are not optimal.

The proposed remedy is to transform the input coordinates using two embeddings that make the kernel and its filter approximately spatially invariant. Experiments confirm the theoretical observations and examine how network architecture affects filter size. The work explains a source of unwanted behavior in neural density representations and offers coordinate transformations that the authors identify as readily applicable to other coordinate-based generation methods.
summary.tldr: Neural tangent kernel analysis reveals position-dependent filtering in neural topology optimization, motivating coordinate embeddings that restore approximate spatial invariance.

title: DNN-based Topology Optimisation: Spatial Invariance and Neural Tangent Kernel

abstract: We consider a price-based network revenue management problem with multiple products and multiple reusable resources. Each randomly arriving customer requests a product (service) that needs to occupy a sequence of reusable resources (servers). We adopt an incomplete information setting where the firm does not know the price-demand function for each product and the goal is to dynamically set prices of all products to maximize the total expected revenue of serving customers. We propose novel batched bandit learning algorithms for finding near-optimal pricing policies, and show that they admit a near-optimal cumulative regret bound of $\tilde{O}(J\sqrt{XT})$, where $J$, $X$, and $T$ are the numbers of products, candidate prices, and service periods, respectively. As part of our regret analysis, we develop the first finite-time mixing time analysis of an open network queueing system (i.e., the celebrated Jackson Network), which could be of independent interest. Our numerical studies show that the proposed approaches perform consistently well.
