paragraphs: Some software concerns matter greatly during execution but occupy little source code, making them difficult for topic models to discover. The paper distinguishes these subtle topics from topics that are prominent in only a few documents. Existing focused topic models address the latter form of rarity but fail to capture topics with low presence within individual documents.

The proposed subtle topic model uses a generalized stick-breaking process as a prior over multiple topic distributions. This creates a hierarchical topic structure intended to capture rare patterns beyond the capabilities of focused topic models. Its nonstandard inference procedure exploits a relationship between the stick-breaking process and the generalized Dirichlet distribution.

Experiments show discovery of subtle cross-cutting concerns in two benchmark codebases that existing topic models do not recover. The authors also report better subtle-topic discovery on general text collections. These results support treating weak document-level presence as a distinct modeling challenge, especially when a topic’s practical importance is not reflected by how much text or code it occupies.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical topic model discovers weakly expressed software concerns and subtle text topics that existing models struggle to identify.

title: Subtle Topic Models and Discovering Subtly Manifested Software Concerns Automatically

abstract: We propose a framework for collaborative filtering based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM), which extends previous RBM-based approaches in several important directions. First, while previous RBM research has focused on modeling the correlation between item ratings, we model both user-user and item-item correlations in a unified hybrid non-IID framework. We further use real values in the visible layer as opposed to multinomial variables, thus taking advantage of the natural order between user-item ratings. Finally, we explore the potential of combining the original training data with data generated by the RBM-based model itself in a bootstrapping fashion. The evaluation on two MovieLens datasets (with 100K and 1M user-item ratings, respectively), shows that our RBM model rivals the best previously-proposed approaches.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering uses patterns in user ratings to make recommendations. This paper develops a framework based on restricted Boltzmann machines that accounts for relationships among both users and items. Earlier RBM approaches emphasized correlations between item ratings; the proposed hybrid framework brings user-user correlations into the same model. Its non-IID framing treats these dependencies as information to model.

The framework also changes how ratings are represented. It uses real-valued visible variables instead of multinomial variables, allowing the model to take advantage of ratings having a natural order. The authors additionally explore a bootstrapping strategy that combines observed training data with data generated by the model itself.

Evaluation on the MovieLens datasets containing 100,000 and one million ratings shows performance competitive with the best previously proposed approaches. This supports the combined framework as a promising recommendation method. The abstract presents bootstrapping as an explored possibility, however, and does not attribute the overall result to any single modification.
summary.tldr: A hybrid RBM recommendation framework models relationships among both users and items and achieves competitive results on two MovieLens datasets.

title: A non-IID Framework for Collaborative Filtering with Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: Many semi-supervised clustering algorithms have been proposed to improve the clustering accuracy by effectively exploring the available side information that is usually in the form of pairwise constraints. Despite the progress, there are two main shortcomings of the existing semi-supervised clustering algorithms. First, they have to deal with non-convex optimization problems, leading to clustering results that are sensitive to the initialization. Second, none of these algorithms is equipped with theoretical guarantee regarding the clustering performance. We address these limitations by developing a framework for semi-supervised clustering based on \it input pattern assisted matrix completion. The key idea is to cast clustering into a matrix completion problem, and solve it efficiently by exploiting the correlation between input patterns and cluster assignments. Our analysis shows that under appropriate conditions, only O(\log n) pairwise constraints are needed to accurately recover the true cluster partition. We verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm by comparing it to the state-of-the-art semi-supervised clustering algorithms on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised clustering uses limited side information, often pairwise constraints, to help identify groups. The paper highlights two shortcomings of existing approaches: nonconvex optimization can make results sensitive to initialization, and clustering-performance guarantees are lacking. It proposes a framework based on completing a pairwise similarity matrix.

The key idea is to use the relationship between observed input patterns and cluster assignments when filling in the matrix. Pairwise supervision is therefore combined with information already present in the observations. This provides an efficient route to estimating the grouping structure from partially specified relationships.

Under appropriate conditions, the authors show that O(log n) pairwise constraints are sufficient to recover the true cluster partition accurately. The condition is essential to interpreting this small supervision requirement. Comparisons with state-of-the-art semi-supervised clustering algorithms on several benchmark datasets support the method's effectiveness. The contribution joins a data-assisted matrix-completion formulation with a conditional recovery guarantee and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Input-assisted matrix completion enables semi-supervised clustering with accurate recovery from O(log n) pairwise constraints under appropriate conditions.

title: Semi-supervised Clustering by Input Pattern Assisted Pairwise Similarity Matrix Completion

abstract: This paper studies dimensionality reduction in a weakly supervised setting, in which the preference relationship between examples is indicated by weak cues. A novel framework is proposed that integrates two aspects of the large margin principle (angle and distance), which simultaneously encourage angle consistency between preference pairs and maximize the distance between examples in preference pairs. Two specific algorithms are developed: an alternating direction method to learn a linear transformation matrix and a gradient boosting technique to optimize a non-linear transformation directly in the function space. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed large margin optimization criteria can strengthen and improve the robustness and generalization performance of preference learning algorithms on the obtained low-dimensional subspace. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the significance of studying dimensionality reduction in the weakly supervised setting and the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: This paper studies dimensionality reduction when supervision consists of weak cues about preferences between examples. The aim is to construct a lower-dimensional representation useful for learning those preferences. The framework uses the preference relationships to shape the geometry of the resulting space.

Its large-margin objective combines two geometric requirements. One encourages consistency of angles between preference pairs; the other increases distances between examples within those pairs. The authors develop two implementations: an alternating direction method for learning a linear transformation matrix, and a gradient boosting method that directly optimizes a nonlinear transformation in function space.

The theoretical analysis shows that these optimization criteria can improve robustness and generalization for preference learning in the learned subspace. Experiments on real-world datasets support the framework's effectiveness and the value of studying dimensionality reduction with weak supervision. Together, the results connect how a representation is shaped to how well subsequent preference learning can behave, while providing both linear and nonlinear approaches.
summary.tldr: A dimensionality-reduction framework combines angular and distance margins to learn representations from weak preference cues.

title: Large-margin Weakly Supervised Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: In this paper, we study randomized reduction methods, which reduce high-dimensional features into low-dimensional space by randomized methods (e.g., random projection, random hashing), for large-scale high-dimensional classification. Previous theoretical results on randomized reduction methods hinge on strong assumptions about the data, e.g., low rank of the data matrix or a large separable margin of classification, which hinder their in broad domains. To address these limitations, we propose dual-sparse regularized randomized reduction methods that introduce a sparse regularizer into the reduced dual problem. Under a mild condition that the original dual solution is a (nearly) sparse vector, we show that the resulting dual solution is close to the original dual solution and concentrates on its support set. In numerical experiments, we present an empirical study to support the analysis and we also present a novel application of the dual-sparse randomized reduction methods to reducing the communication cost of distributed learning from large-scale high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Randomized reduction compresses high-dimensional features into a smaller space using techniques such as random projection or random hashing. This can make large classification problems easier to handle, but earlier theoretical guarantees relied on conditions such as a low-rank data matrix or a large separable classification margin. Those conditions restrict where the guarantees apply.

The paper proposes adding a sparsity-promoting regularizer to the reduced problem's dual formulation. Its main assumption concerns the original dual solution: that vector must be sparse or nearly sparse. Under this condition, the authors show that the reduced dual solution remains close to the original and concentrates on the original solution's support, the locations of its nonzero entries.

The contribution shifts the basis of the reduction guarantee toward structure in the dual solution. Numerical experiments support the analysis, and the authors also present an application to reducing communication costs in distributed learning from high-dimensional data. The result offers a conditional route to useful compression without relying on the particular low-rank or large-margin assumptions highlighted in earlier work.
summary.tldr: Sparse regularization in a reduced dual problem preserves the original dual solution approximately when that solution is sparse or nearly sparse.

title: Theory of Dual-sparse Regularized Randomized Reduction

abstract: A commonly used learning rule is to approximately minimize the \emphaverage loss over the training set. Other learning algorithms, such as AdaBoost and hard-SVM, aim at minimizing the \emphmaximal loss over the training set. The average loss is more popular, particularly in deep learning, due to three main reasons. First, it can be conveniently minimized using online algorithms, that process few examples at each iteration. Second, it is often argued that there is no sense to minimize the loss on the training set too much, as it will not be reflected in the generalization loss. Last, the maximal loss is not robust to outliers. In this paper we describe and analyze an algorithm that can convert any online algorithm to a minimizer of the maximal loss. We show, theoretically and empirically, that in some situations better accuracy on the training set is crucial to obtain good performance on unseen examples. Last, we propose robust versions of the approach that can handle outliers.

paragraphs: Average training loss summarizes performance across examples, whereas maximal loss focuses on the example with the largest loss. The paper examines why and how to optimize this latter objective. It addresses three concerns: compatibility with online learning, whether improving training accuracy helps on unseen examples, and sensitivity to outliers.

The authors describe and analyze a procedure that converts any online algorithm into a maximal-loss minimizer. This connects a worst-example objective with algorithms that process only a few examples per iteration. The construction addresses the computational appeal commonly associated with average-loss training by making online algorithms available for the maximal-loss objective as well.

The paper also provides theoretical and empirical evidence that, in some situations, better training accuracy is crucial for good performance on unseen data. It proposes robust variants to handle outliers, addressing a stated weakness of maximal-loss training. These results support considering the objective when the situation warrants it, while preserving the paper's qualified claim about when improved training performance benefits generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper converts online algorithms into maximal-loss minimizers and shows why this objective can improve generalization in some situations.

title: Minimizing the Maximal Loss: How and Why

abstract: We propose a novel Riemannian manifold preconditioning approach for the tensor completion problem with rank constraint. A novel Riemannian metric or inner product is proposed that exploits the least-squares structure of the cost function and takes into account the structured symmetry that exists in Tucker decomposition. The specific metric allows to use the versatile framework of Riemannian optimization on quotient manifolds to develop preconditioned nonlinear conjugate gradient and stochastic gradient descent algorithms in batch and online setups, respectively. Concrete matrix representations of various optimization-related ingredients are listed. Numerical comparisons suggest that our proposed algorithms robustly outperform state-of-the-art algorithms across different synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Tensor completion estimates missing entries in a multidimensional array while imposing a rank constraint. This paper develops a preconditioning approach that uses the geometry of the tensor representation to guide optimization. Its central contribution is a new Riemannian metric: an inner product adapted to the particular completion problem.

The metric incorporates both the least-squares structure of the objective and the structured symmetry of the Tucker decomposition. The authors use this construction within optimization on quotient manifolds, which accounts for that symmetry. From this framework, they develop a preconditioned nonlinear conjugate-gradient algorithm for batch processing and a stochastic-gradient algorithm for online processing.

The paper also provides concrete matrix expressions for the ingredients needed to implement the optimization methods. Numerical comparisons across synthetic and real datasets suggest that the resulting algorithms robustly outperform the leading alternatives tested. The significance is the connection between a problem-specific geometric design and practical algorithms for two processing settings, supported by numerical evidence rather than a universal claim of superiority.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware preconditioner yields batch and online algorithms for rank-constrained tensor completion with favorable numerical results.

title: Low-rank tensor completion: a Riemannian manifold preconditioning approach

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to texture synthesis based on generative adversarial networks (GAN) (Goodfellow et al., 2014), and call this technique Periodic Spatial GAN (PSGAN). The PSGAN has several novel abilities which surpass the current state of the art in texture synthesis. First, we can learn multiple textures, periodic or non-periodic, from datasets of one or more complex large images. Second, we show that the image generation with PSGANs has properties of a texture manifold: we can smoothly interpolate between samples in the structured noise space and generate novel samples, which lie perceptually between the textures of the original dataset. We make multiple experiments which show that PSGANs can flexibly handle diverse texture and image data sources, and the method is highly scalable and can generate output images of arbitrary large size.

The method can learn multiple textures from datasets containing one or more complex large images. It handles both periodic textures, which repeat, and non-periodic textures, giving the same approach scope across different visual patterns.

A central result concerns the organization of the generator’s structured noise space. Moving smoothly between samples in that space produces new images that appear perceptually between textures in the training data. The authors describe this behavior as having the properties of a texture manifold. It means the learned representation supports transitions among textures as well as the generation of individual samples.

Multiple experiments demonstrate flexibility across diverse texture and image sources. The authors also report that the method scales well and can generate images of arbitrarily large size. Together, these capabilities support learning a collection of textures, exploring visual mixtures between them, and producing outputs whose size is not fixed to a single image dimension.
summary.tldr: PSGAN learns diverse textures, smoothly interpolates between them, and supports generating arbitrarily large texture images.

title: Learning Texture Manifolds with the Periodic Spatial GAN

abstract: We propose an algorithm for meta-learning that is model-agnostic, in the sense that it is compatible with any model trained with gradient descent and applicable to a variety of different learning problems, including classification, regression, and reinforcement learning. The goal of meta-learning is to train a model on a variety of learning tasks, such that it can solve new learning tasks using only a small number of training samples. In our approach, the parameters of the model are explicitly trained such that a small number of gradient steps with a small amount of training data from a new task will produce good generalization performance on that task. In effect, our method trains the model to be easy to fine-tune. We demonstrate that this approach leads to state-of-the-art performance on two few-shot image classification benchmarks, produces good results on few-shot regression, and accelerates fine-tuning for policy gradient reinforcement learning with neural network policies.

paragraphs: The paper asks how training across multiple tasks can prepare a model to learn a new task from very little data. Its algorithm, model-agnostic meta-learning, explicitly trains model parameters for rapid adaptation. The desired outcome is a starting point from which a small number of gradient updates can produce good performance on a new task.

This changes what training is trying to achieve: the parameters are optimized for how effectively they can be fine-tuned. The method is model-agnostic in the stated sense that it is compatible with any model trained by gradient descent. That makes the approach applicable across different learning problems, including classification, regression, and reinforcement learning.

The authors demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on two few-shot image classification benchmarks, good results on few-shot regression, and faster fine-tuning for policy-gradient reinforcement learning with neural-network policies. These findings support training models to be easy to adapt across the evaluated settings. The central contribution is an adaptation-oriented training objective whose usefulness extends beyond a single architecture or task type.
summary.tldr: MAML trains model parameters so that a few gradient updates on limited new-task data can produce good generalization.

title: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning for Fast Adaptation of Deep Networks

abstract: There exist many problem domains where the interpretability of neural network models is essential for deployment. Here we introduce a recurrent architecture composed of input-switched affine transformations – in other words an RNN without any explicit nonlinearities, but with input-dependent recurrent weights. This simple form allows the RNN to be analyzed via straightforward linear methods: we can exactly characterize the linear contribution of each input to the model predictions; we can use a change-of-basis to disentangle input, output, and computational hidden unit subspaces; we can fully reverse-engineer the architecture’s solution to a simple task. Despite this ease of interpretation, the input switched affine network achieves reasonable performance on a text modeling tasks, and allows greater computational efficiency than networks with standard nonlinearities.

This simple form allows the RNN to be analyzed via straightforward linear methods: we can exactly characterize the linear contribution of each input to the model predictions; we can use a change-of-basis to disentangle input, output, and computational hidden unit subspaces; we can fully reverse-engineer the architecture’s solution to a simple task. paragraphs: The paper introduces a recurrent neural network designed so that its internal computations can be analyzed directly. It uses affine transformations whose recurrent weights depend on the input, without explicit nonlinearities. This architectural choice gives the model a simple mathematical form while allowing its state updates to change according to the incoming sequence.

That form makes several kinds of interpretation possible using linear methods. The authors can exactly characterize each input's linear contribution to a prediction. They can also change the coordinate system of the hidden state to separate subspaces associated with inputs, outputs, and computation. On a simple task, they fully reverse-engineer the solution learned by the architecture.

The model achieves reasonable performance on text modeling tasks and offers greater computational efficiency than networks with standard nonlinearities. The result is a concrete example of designing interpretability into a recurrent architecture. Its strongest interpretive claims concern exact contributions and structural analysis, while the full reconstruction of a learned solution is demonstrated for a simple task.
summary.tldr: Input-dependent affine recurrent updates make a sequence model directly analyzable while retaining reasonable text-modeling performance.

title: Input Switched Affine Networks: An RNN Architecture Designed for Interpretability

abstract: Standard clustering methods such as K-means, Gaussian mixture models, and hierarchical clustering are beset by local minima, which are sometimes drastically suboptimal. Moreover the number of clusters K must be known in advance. The recently introduced the sum-of-norms (SON) or Clusterpath convex relaxation of k-means and hierarchical clustering shrinks cluster centroids toward one another and ensure a unique global minimizer. We give a scalable stochastic incremental algorithm based on proximal iterations to solve the SON problem with convergence guarantees. We also show that the algorithm recovers clusters under quite general conditions which have a similar form to the unifying proximity condition introduced in the approximation algorithms community (that covers paradigm cases such as Gaussian mixtures and planted partition models). We give experimental results to confirm that our algorithm scales much better than previous methods while producing clusters of comparable quality.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational challenge of sum-of-norms clustering, a convex formulation that draws cluster centers toward one another. This formulation has a unique global minimizer, addressing the risk of poor local solutions highlighted for standard clustering methods. The authors focus on making this approach scalable while retaining mathematical guarantees.

Their algorithm uses stochastic incremental updates built from proximal iterations. Rather than contributing only a faster implementation, the paper establishes convergence guarantees for solving the clustering objective. It also analyzes when the resulting solution recovers the underlying clusters, connecting efficient optimization to the quality of the grouping it produces.

The recovery conditions have a form similar to a general proximity condition used in approximation algorithms, which covers examples such as Gaussian mixtures and planted partition models. Recovery is therefore conditional on the stated structure of the data. Experiments show substantially better scaling than previous methods with comparable clustering quality, supporting the algorithm's practical value as well as its theoretical motivation.
summary.tldr: A stochastic proximal algorithm makes convex sum-of-norms clustering more scalable, with convergence guarantees and conditional cluster-recovery results.

title: Clustering by Sum of Norms: Stochastic Incremental Algorithm, Convergence and Cluster Recovery

abstract: Motivated by Supervised Opinion Analysis, we propose a novel framework devoted to Structured Output Learning with Abstention (SOLA). The structure prediction model is able to abstain from predicting some labels in the structured output at a cost chosen by the user in a flexible way. For that purpose, we decompose the problem into the learning of a pair of predictors, one devoted to structured abstention and the other, to structured output prediction. To compare fully labeled training data with predictions potentially containing abstentions, we define a wide class of asymmetric abstention-aware losses. Learning is achieved by surrogate regression in an appropriate feature space while prediction with abstention is performed by solving a new pre-image problem. Thus, SOLA extends recent ideas about Structured Output Prediction via surrogate problems and calibration theory and enjoys statistical guarantees on the resulting excess risk. Instantiated on a hierarchical abstention-aware loss, SOLA is shown to be relevant for fine-grained opinion mining and gives state-of-the-art results on this task. Moreover, the abstention-aware representations can be used to competitively predict user-review ratings based on a sentence-level opinion predictor.

paragraphs: Structured predictions contain multiple related labels, and a model may benefit from leaving some labels unanswered. This paper introduces Structured Output Learning with Abstention, or SOLA, to make that choice part of prediction. Users can flexibly specify the cost of abstaining, allowing the prediction objective to reflect how unanswered labels should be treated.

The framework learns two predictors: one for structured abstention and another for structured outputs. Asymmetric, abstention-aware losses compare fully labeled training examples with predictions that may omit some labels. Learning uses surrogate regression in a feature space, and a new pre-image problem converts the result into a structured prediction with abstentions.

SOLA provides statistical guarantees on excess risk and is instantiated with a hierarchical abstention-aware loss for fine-grained opinion mining. The authors report state-of-the-art results on that task. They also show that the representations support competitive user-review rating prediction using a sentence-level opinion predictor. The work connects selective structured prediction with both theoretical support and practical opinion-analysis applications.
summary.tldr: SOLA learns structured predictions with selective abstention, user-defined abstention costs, and statistical excess-risk guarantees.

title: Structured Output Learning with Abstention: Application to Accurate Opinion Prediction

abstract: The problem of splitting attributes is one of the main steps in the construction of decision trees. In order to decide the best split, impurity measures such as Entropy and Gini are widely used. In practice, decision-tree inducers use heuristics for finding splits with small impurity when they consider nominal attributes with a large number of distinct values. However, there are no known guarantees for the quality of the splits obtained by these heuristics. To fill this gap, we propose two new splitting procedures that provably achieve near-optimal impurity. We also report experiments that provide evidence that the proposed methods are interesting candidates to be employed in splitting nominal attributes with many values during decision tree/random forest induction.

In practice, decision-tree inducers use heuristics for finding splits with small impurity when they consider nominal attributes with a large number of distinct values. However, there are no known guarantees for the quality of the splits obtained by these heuristics. To fill this gap, we propose two new splitting procedures that provably achieve near-optimal impurity. paragraphs: Building a decision tree requires choosing how to split examples at each step. Measures such as entropy and Gini impurity assess how mixed the resulting groups are. For a categorical attribute with many possible values, deciding which values belong on each side of a binary split creates a difficult search problem.

Practical tree-building methods commonly use heuristics to find low-impurity splits in this setting. The paper identifies a gap in that approach: the quality of those heuristic choices lacks known guarantees. It introduces two splitting procedures with proofs that their impurity is near optimal, giving a principled quality guarantee for this individual decision within tree construction.

The authors also report experiments supporting the procedures as promising choices for categorical attributes with many values in decision trees and random forests. The theoretical result concerns the quality of the splits themselves. The experimental evidence motivates using those procedures during induction without claiming that every resulting tree or forest must achieve superior predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Two decision-tree splitting procedures provide near-optimal impurity guarantees for categorical attributes with many values.

title: Binary Partitions with Approximate Minimum Impurity

abstract: Lossy compression algorithms are typically designed and analyzed through the lens of Shannon’s rate-distortion theory, where the goal is to achieve the lowest possible distortion (e.g., low MSE or high SSIM) at any given bit rate. However, in recent years, it has become increasingly accepted that "low distortion" is not a synonym for "high perceptual quality", and in fact optimization of one often comes at the expense of the other. In light of this understanding, it is natural to seek for a generalization of rate-distortion theory which takes perceptual quality into account. In this paper, we adopt the mathematical definition of perceptual quality recently proposed by Blau & Michaeli (2018), and use it to study the three-way tradeoff between rate, distortion, and perception. We show that restricting the perceptual quality to be high, generally leads to an elevation of the rate-distortion curve, thus necessitating a sacrifice in either rate or distortion. We prove several fundamental properties of this triple-tradeoff, calculate it in closed form for a Bernoulli source, and illustrate it visually on a toy MNIST example.

paragraphs: Lossy compression traditionally balances the number of bits used against distortion in the reconstructed data. Yet a reconstruction with low numerical distortion need not have high perceptual quality, and improving one can worsen the other. This paper extends the analysis to treat rate, distortion, and perception as three distinct quantities that must be considered together.

The authors adopt an existing mathematical definition of perceptual quality and study the resulting three-way tradeoff. They show that requiring high perceptual quality generally raises the rate-distortion curve. In practical terms, imposing that additional requirement typically demands either more bits or greater distortion, even when a compression method is judged favorably by the traditional two-way analysis.

The paper proves fundamental properties of the tradeoff, derives a closed-form expression for a Bernoulli source, and provides a visual illustration using a toy MNIST example. These contributions explain why perceptually appealing compression can carry a measurable cost elsewhere. The result is a framework for reasoning about competing objectives, rather than assuming that improving a distortion measure also improves perceived quality.
summary.tldr: Adding perceptual quality to compression theory reveals a three-way tradeoff in which better perception generally requires sacrificing bit rate or distortion.

title: Rethinking Lossy Compression: The Rate-Distortion-Perception Tradeoff

abstract: The use of target networks has been a popular and key component of recent deep Q-learning algorithms for reinforcement learning, yet little is known from the theory side. In this work, we introduce a new family of target-based temporal difference (TD) learning algorithms that maintain two separate learning parameters {–} the target variable and online variable. We propose three members in the family, the averaging TD, double TD, and periodic TD, where the target variable is updated through an averaging, symmetric, or periodic fashion, respectively, mirroring those techniques used in deep Q-learning practice. We establish asymptotic convergence analyses for both averaging TD and double TD and a finite sample analysis for periodic TD. In addition, we provide some simulation results showing potentially superior convergence of these target-based TD algorithms compared to the standard TD-learning. While this work focuses on linear function approximation and policy evaluation setting, we consider this as a meaningful step towards the theoretical understanding of deep Q-learning variants with target networks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the theoretical role of target variables in temporal-difference learning, motivated by target networks used in deep Q-learning. The proposed family maintains separate online and target learning parameters. Separating these quantities allows the target to evolve according to its own update rule rather than always matching the online parameters.

The authors introduce three variants: averaging TD, double TD, and periodic TD. Their target updates use averaging, symmetric updates, and periodic updates, respectively, reflecting techniques used in deep Q-learning practice. They establish asymptotic convergence results for averaging and double TD, while periodic TD receives a finite-sample analysis.

Simulations suggest potentially better convergence than standard TD learning. The theoretical setting is specifically policy evaluation with linear function approximation, which defines the scope of the analysis. Within that setting, the work supplies mathematical results for several ways of maintaining targets. The authors present it as a step toward understanding target networks in deep Q-learning, whose motivating use extends beyond the setting analyzed here.
summary.tldr: Three target-based TD methods receive convergence analyses for linear policy evaluation, helping explain techniques used in deep Q-learning.

title: Target-Based Temporal-Difference Learning

abstract: Advanced methods of applying deep learning to structured data such as graphs have been proposed in recent years. In particular, studies have focused on generalizing convolutional neural networks to graph data, which includes redefining the convolution and the downsampling (pooling) operations for graphs. The method of generalizing the convolution operation to graphs has been proven to improve performance and is widely used. However, the method of applying downsampling to graphs is still difficult to perform and has room for improvement. In this paper, we propose a graph pooling method based on self-attention. Self-attention using graph convolution allows our pooling method to consider both node features and graph topology. To ensure a fair comparison, the same training procedures and model architectures were used for the existing pooling methods and our method. The experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior graph classification performance on the benchmark datasets using a reasonable number of parameters.

paragraphs: This paper tackles pooling for graph neural networks: reducing a graph representation while retaining information useful for prediction. Although graph convolution is already an established way to process graph data, the abstract identifies downsampling as a harder operation with room for improvement. The proposed method uses self-attention to guide this reduction.

Its attention mechanism is computed using graph convolution, allowing pooling to consider both node features and graph topology. In other words, the information attached to a node and the pattern of connections around it can both influence the pooling process. This links the reduction of the graph to the structure that makes graph data distinctive.

The authors compare pooling methods using the same model architectures and training procedures, helping make the pooling operation the focus of the comparison. On the benchmark datasets evaluated, their method achieves superior graph classification performance with a reasonable parameter count. The findings support using structure-aware attention to improve graph downsampling within the tested classification systems.
summary.tldr: Graph-convolution-based self-attention uses node features and connectivity to improve pooling and benchmark graph classification.

title: Self-Attention Graph Pooling

abstract: Random Fourier features is a widely used, simple, and effective technique for scaling up kernel methods. The existing theoretical analysis of the approach, however, remains focused on specific learning tasks and typically gives pessimistic bounds which are at odds with the empirical results. We tackle these problems and provide the first unified risk analysis of learning with random Fourier features using the squared error and Lipschitz continuous loss functions. In our bounds, the trade-off between the computational cost and the expected risk convergence rate is problem specific and expressed in terms of the regularization parameter and the number of effective degrees of freedom . We study both the standard random Fourier features method for which we improve the existing bounds on the number of features required to guarantee the corresponding minimax risk convergence rate of kernel ridge regression, as well as a data-dependent modification which samples features proportional to ridge leverage scores and further reduces the required number of features. As ridge leverage scores are expensive to compute, we devise a simple approximation scheme which provably reduces the computational cost without loss of statistical efficiency.

paragraphs: Random Fourier features help scale kernel methods, but earlier theory often focused on individual tasks and predicted more demanding requirements than experiments suggested. This paper develops a unified risk analysis covering squared-error and Lipschitz-continuous losses. It makes the trade-off between computation and expected risk depend on the problem’s regularization and effective degrees of freedom.

For standard random Fourier features, the authors improve bounds on how many features are needed to retain the corresponding minimax risk convergence rate of kernel ridge regression. They also analyze a data-dependent alternative that samples features according to ridge leverage scores. This choice further reduces the required number of features.

Computing the leverage scores is itself expensive, so the paper introduces a simple approximation scheme. The authors prove that it reduces computational cost without sacrificing statistical efficiency. The overall contribution connects feature counts, sampling choices, and approximation cost within one analysis, helping explain how computational savings can coexist with strong statistical convergence guarantees.
summary.tldr: A unified risk analysis sharpens random-feature requirements and supports cheaper leverage-based sampling without loss of statistical efficiency.

title: Towards a Unified Analysis of Random Fourier Features

abstract: The Bayesian learning rule is a natural-gradient variational inference method, which not only contains many existing learning algorithms as special cases but also enables the design of new algorithms. Unfortunately, when variational parameters lie in an open constraint set, the rule may not satisfy the constraint and requires line-searches which could slow down the algorithm. In this work, we address this issue for positive-definite constraints by proposing an improved rule that naturally handles the constraints. Our modification is obtained by using Riemannian gradient methods, and is valid when the approximation attains a block-coordinate natural parameterization (e.g., Gaussian distributions and their mixtures). Our method outperforms existing methods without any significant increase in computation. Our work makes it easier to apply the rule in the presence of positive-definite constraints in parameter spaces.

paragraphs: The Bayesian learning rule is a variational inference method based on natural gradients, and it encompasses many existing learning algorithms. A difficulty arises when its parameters must remain inside an open constraint set: an update can leave the permitted region. Correcting that through line searches can slow learning. This paper focuses on positive-definite matrix constraints.

The authors modify the rule using Riemannian gradient methods so that it naturally respects positive definiteness. The modification applies when the approximation admits a block-coordinate natural parameterization, with Gaussian distributions and Gaussian mixtures given as examples. This is a stated structural requirement on where the method applies, rather than a claim that the same update handles every constrained approximation.

The paper reports better performance than existing methods without a significant increase in computation. Its practical contribution is to incorporate the required matrix constraint into the learning update itself. For suitable variational approximations, this makes the Bayesian learning rule easier to use while addressing the constraint violations that otherwise motivate additional line-search work.
summary.tldr: A Riemannian modification of the Bayesian learning rule preserves positive-definite constraints for approximations with a suitable parameterization.

title: Handling the Positive-Definite Constraint in the Bayesian Learning Rule

abstract: In this paper, we investigate a Lyapunov-like differential inequality that allows us to establish finite-time stability of a continuous-time state-space dynamical system represented via a multivariate ordinary differential equation or differential inclusion. Equipped with this condition, we successfully synthesize first and second-order dynamical systems that achieve finite-time convergence to the minima of a given sufficiently regular cost function. As a byproduct, we show that the p-rescaled gradient flow (p-RGF) proposed by Wibisono et al. (2016) is indeed finite-time convergent, provided the cost function is gradient dominated of order q in (1,p). Thus, we effectively bridge a gap between the p-RGF and the normalized gradient flow (NGF) (p=\infty) proposed by Cortes (2006) in his seminal paper in the context of multi-agent systems. We discuss strategies to discretize our proposed flows and conclude by conducting some numerical experiments to illustrate our results.

paragraphs: Continuous-time optimization describes a changing state through differential equations or differential inclusions. This paper asks when such a system reaches a minimum in finite time. The distinction matters mathematically: approaching a minimum indefinitely is different from reaching it after a finite amount of continuous evolution.

The authors study a Lyapunov-like differential inequality that establishes finite-time stability. Using this condition, they construct first- and second-order dynamical systems that converge in finite time to minima of sufficiently regular cost functions. The inequality acts as a tool for designing optimization dynamics as well as analyzing their behavior.

They also prove finite-time convergence for p-rescaled gradient flow when the cost function is gradient dominated of order q, with q strictly between 1 and p. This conditional result connects that flow with normalized gradient flow, corresponding to the infinite-p case. Finally, the paper discusses discretization strategies and supplies numerical illustrations. Its principal guarantees concern continuous-time systems under the stated regularity and gradient-domination conditions; the discussion of discretization addresses how those flows might inform computational methods.
summary.tldr: A differential inequality enables continuous-time optimization systems with finite-time convergence under stated regularity conditions.

title: Finite-Time Convergence in Continuous-Time Optimization

abstract: Attention based neural networks are state of the art in a large range of applications. However, their performance tends to degrade when the number of layers increases. In this work, we show that enforcing Lipschitz continuity by normalizing the attention scores can significantly improve the performance of deep attention models. First, we show that, for deep graph attention networks (GAT), gradient explosion appears during training, leading to poor performance of gradient-based training algorithms. To address this issue, we derive a theoretical analysis of the Lipschitz continuity of attention modules and introduce LipschitzNorm, a simple and parameter-free normalization for self-attention mechanisms that enforces the model to be Lipschitz continuous. We then apply LipschitzNorm to GAT and Graph Transformers and show that their performance is substantially improved in the deep setting (10 to 30 layers). More specifically, we show that a deep GAT model with LipschitzNorm achieves state of the art results for node label prediction tasks that exhibit long-range dependencies, while showing consistent improvements over their unnormalized counterparts in benchmark node classification tasks.

paragraphs: Adding layers to attention networks can worsen performance even though greater depth expands their computation. This paper identifies exploding gradients during training in deep graph attention networks as a source of difficulty. When gradients grow excessively, gradient-based training becomes less effective, motivating a direct way to control attention’s sensitivity.

The authors analyze the Lipschitz continuity of attention modules, a property that bounds how much outputs can change relative to inputs. From that analysis they introduce LipschitzNorm, a parameter-free normalization of attention scores that enforces Lipschitz continuity. The method changes the attention computation without introducing additional learned parameters.

Applied to graph attention networks and Graph Transformers with 10 to 30 layers, LipschitzNorm substantially improves performance in the reported experiments. A deep normalized graph attention model achieves state-of-the-art results on node-label prediction tasks with long-range dependencies. Benchmark node-classification tasks also show consistent gains over unnormalized counterparts. These findings connect theoretical control of attention sensitivity with practical benefits for deeper graph models.
summary.tldr: Parameter-free normalization of attention scores controls sensitivity and improves deep graph attention models, including tasks with long-range dependencies.

title: Lipschitz normalization for self-attention layers with application to graph neural networks

abstract: Gradient staleness is a major side effect in decoupled learning when training convolutional neural networks asynchronously. Existing methods that ignore this effect might result in reduced generalization and even divergence. In this paper, we propose an accumulated decoupled learning (ADL), which includes a module-wise gradient accumulation in order to mitigate the gradient staleness. Unlike prior arts ignoring the gradient staleness, we quantify the staleness in such a way that its mitigation can be quantitatively visualized. As a new learning scheme, the proposed ADL is theoretically shown to converge to critical points in spite of its asynchronism. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets are conducted, demonstrating that ADL gives promising generalization results while the state-of-the-art methods experience reduced generalization and divergence. In addition, our ADL is shown to have the fastest training speed among the compared methods.

Unlike prior arts ignoring the gradient staleness, we quantify the staleness in such a way that its mitigation can be quantitatively visualized. paragraphs: Asynchronous training lets parts of a convolutional neural network learn without waiting for every other part. This creates a problem called gradient staleness: an update can reflect an earlier state of the network. The paper identifies this as a major source of trouble in decoupled learning, where ignoring stale gradients can weaken generalization or even cause training to diverge.

The proposed accumulated decoupled learning method collects gradients within individual modules to mitigate this staleness. The authors also define a quantitative measure of staleness, making its reduction something that can be tracked and visualized. Their theoretical analysis establishes convergence to critical points despite the asynchronous learning process; this is a convergence result, rather than a guarantee of finding the best possible solution.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show promising generalization while compared methods suffer reduced generalization or divergence. ADL also trains fastest among the methods compared. Together, these results support gradient accumulation as a way to retain asynchronous training speed while addressing a specific source of instability.
summary.tldr: Accumulating gradients within network modules mitigates stale updates and supports fast, convergent asynchronous training.

title: Accumulated Decoupled Learning with Gradient Staleness Mitigation for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: This paper discusses a new approach to the fundamental problem of learning optimal Q-functions. In this approach, optimal Q-functions are formulated as saddle points of a nonlinear Lagrangian function derived from the classic Bellman optimality equation. The paper shows that the Lagrangian enjoys strong duality, in spite of its nonlinearity, which paves the way to a general Lagrangian method to Q-function learning. As a demonstration, the paper develops an imitation learning algorithm based on the duality theory, and applies the algorithm to a state-of-the-art machine translation benchmark. The paper then turns to demonstrate a symmetry breaking phenomenon regarding the optimality of the Lagrangian saddle points, which justifies a largely overlooked direction in developing the Lagrangian method.

paragraphs: Learning an optimal Q-function is a central task in reinforcement learning: it concerns the value of taking actions when future decisions are also accounted for. This paper develops an approach based on a nonlinear Lagrangian derived from the Bellman optimality equation. It formulates optimal Q-functions through saddle points of that Lagrangian.

The main theoretical result establishes strong duality despite the Lagrangian’s nonlinearity. This provides a foundation for developing Q-function learning methods through the associated optimization formulation. The contribution therefore includes a justification for the formulation, beyond proposing a new procedure for updating value estimates.

As a demonstration, the authors derive an imitation learning algorithm from the duality theory and apply it to a machine translation benchmark. They also establish a symmetry breaking phenomenon concerning the optimality of Lagrangian saddle points. That finding motivates a direction in Lagrangian method development that the authors describe as overlooked. The abstract presents translation as an application of the theory, without claiming a particular performance improvement.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear Lagrangian formulation with strong duality provides a foundation for Q-function learning and an imitation learning application to translation.

title: Lagrangian Method for Q-Function Learning (with Applications to Machine Translation)

abstract: In this paper we provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first comprehensive approach for incorporating various masking mechanisms into Transformers architectures in a scalable way. We show that recent results on linear causal attention (Choromanski et al., 2021) and log-linear RPE-attention (Luo et al., 2021) are special cases of this general mechanism. However by casting the problem as a topological (graph-based) modulation of unmasked attention, we obtain several results unknown before, including efficient d-dimensional RPE-masking and graph-kernel masking. We leverage many mathematical techniques ranging from spectral analysis through dynamic programming and random walks to new algorithms for solving Markov processes on graphs. We provide a corresponding empirical evaluation.

We show that recent results on linear causal attention (Choromanski et al., 2021) and log-linear RPE-attention (Luo et al., 2021) are special cases of this general mechanism. However by casting the problem as a topological (graph-based) modulation of unmasked attention, we obtain several results unknown before, including efficient d-dimensional RPE-masking and graph-kernel masking. We leverage many mathematical techniques ranging from spectral analysis through dynamic programming and random walks to new algorithms for solving Markov processes on graphs. We provide a corresponding empirical evaluation.

paragraphs: Transformers use attention masks to structure interactions among positions, but incorporating different masking rules efficiently can require different methods. This paper proposes a common approach for scalable masked attention. Its organizing idea is to treat masking as a graph-based modulation of attention that would otherwise be unmasked.

Within this formulation, existing results for linear causal attention and log-linear attention with relative positional encoding become special cases. The framework also yields efficient masking methods for relative positional encoding in multiple dimensions and for graph kernels. This gives the approach value both as a unification of earlier techniques and as a route to additional masking mechanisms.

The authors draw on spectral analysis, dynamic programming, random walks, and new algorithms for Markov processes on graphs. These mathematical tools connect the structure of a mask with ways to compute attention efficiently. The paper includes an empirical evaluation alongside the theoretical development. Its stated contribution is a broad framework for scalable masking, with several concrete mechanisms obtained from the same graph-based perspective.
summary.tldr: A graph-based formulation unifies scalable Transformer masking methods and enables efficient multidimensional positional and graph-kernel masks.

title: From block-Toeplitz matrices to differential equations on graphs: towards a general theory for scalable masked Transformers

abstract: Quantized neural networks typically require smaller memory footprints and lower computation complexity, which is crucial for efficient deployment. However, quantization inevitably leads to a distribution divergence from the original network, which generally degrades the performance. To tackle this issue, massive efforts have been made, but most existing approaches lack statistical considerations and depend on several manual configurations. In this paper, we present an adaptive-mapping quantization method to learn an optimal latent sub-distribution that is inherent within models and smoothly approximated with a concrete Gaussian Mixture (GM). In particular, the network weights are projected in compliance with the GM-approximated sub-distribution. This sub-distribution evolves along with the weight update in a co-tuning schema guided by the direct task-objective optimization. Sufficient experiments on image classification and object detection over various modern architectures demonstrate the effectiveness, generalization property, and transferability of the proposed method. Besides, an efficient deployment flow for the mobile CPU is developed, achieving up to 7.46$\times$ inference acceleration on an octa-core ARM CPU. Our codes have been publicly released at https://github.com/RunpeiDong/DGMS.

paragraphs: Quantization represents neural-network weights with fewer bits, reducing memory and computational demands. It also changes the distribution of weights relative to the original network, which can harm performance. This paper approaches that mismatch statistically, learning a low-bit representation that is guided by the task rather than relying on several manually chosen configurations.

The method learns a latent sub-distribution within the model and smoothly approximates it using a Gaussian mixture. Network weights are projected according to that approximation. As training updates the weights, the sub-distribution changes alongside them, with both driven by the task objective. The mapping used for quantization is therefore part of the learning process.

Experiments on image classification and object detection across multiple architectures support the method’s effectiveness, generalization, and transferability. The authors also develop a mobile-CPU deployment flow and report up to 7.46× inference acceleration on an octa-core ARM processor. That deployment result connects the learned low-bit representation to measured execution speed, with the reported maximum tied to the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Gaussian-mixture quantization jointly learns low-bit weight mappings and network weights, with reported mobile-CPU speedups up to 7.46×.

title: Finding the Task-Optimal Low-Bit Sub-Distribution in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: To study the resilience of distributed learning, the “Byzantine" literature considers a strong threat model where workers can report arbitrary gradients to the parameter server. Whereas this model helped obtain several fundamental results, it has sometimes been considered unrealistic, when the workers are mostly trustworthy machines. In this paper, we show a surprising equivalence between this model and data poisoning, a threat considered much more realistic. More specifically, we prove that every gradient attack can be reduced to data poisoning, in any personalized federated learning system with PAC guarantees (which we show are both desirable and realistic). This equivalence makes it possible to obtain new impossibility results on the resilience of any “robust” learning algorithm to data poisoning in highly heterogeneous applications, as corollaries of existing impossibility theorems on Byzantine machine learning. Moreover, using our equivalence, we derive a practical attack that we show (theoretically and empirically) can be very effective against classical personalized federated learning models.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can be attacked by corrupting training data or by sending deliberately misleading gradient updates to the server. These threats can appear quite different: arbitrary gradient manipulation assumes substantial control over a worker, while poisoned data can affect a machine that otherwise follows its training procedure correctly. This paper establishes a connection between the two.

The central result is conditional on a particular setting: personalized federated learning systems with probably approximately correct, or PAC, guarantees. Within that setting, the authors prove that every gradient attack can be reduced to data poisoning. This gives a way to transfer conclusions about the stronger-looking attack model into conclusions about malicious training data.

The authors use the reduction to derive impossibility results for resistance to data poisoning in highly heterogeneous applications. They also construct a practical attack against classical personalized federated learning models and support its effectiveness theoretically and empirically. The result makes Byzantine attack theory relevant even when the participating machines themselves are largely trusted.
summary.tldr: Under PAC guarantees for personalized federated learning, arbitrary gradient attacks can be reduced to data poisoning, transferring attack results between the two settings.

title: An Equivalence Between Data Poisoning and Byzantine Gradient Attacks

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has proven to be successful in overcoming labeling difficulties by leveraging unlabeled data. Previous SSL algorithms typically assume a balanced class distribution. However, real-world datasets are usually class-imbalanced, causing the performance of existing SSL algorithms to be seriously decreased. One essential reason is that pseudo-labels for unlabeled data are selected based on a fixed confidence threshold, resulting in low performance on minority classes. In this paper, we develop a simple yet effective framework, which only involves adaptive thresholding for different classes in SSL algorithms, and achieves remarkable performance improvement on more than twenty imbalance ratios. Specifically, we explicitly optimize the number of pseudo-labels for each class in the SSL objective, so as to simultaneously obtain adaptive thresholds and minimize empirical risk. Moreover, the determination of the adaptive threshold can be efficiently obtained by a closed-form solution. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples to supplement labeled training data. A common step assigns provisional labels to examples whose predictions exceed a confidence threshold. This paper identifies a problem when classes are imbalanced: using the same fixed threshold across classes contributes to poor performance on classes with fewer examples.

The proposed framework gives different classes adaptive thresholds. It does this by explicitly optimizing how many pseudo-labels each class contributes within the learning objective, jointly determining those quantities while minimizing empirical risk. Threshold selection becomes part of the optimization process, allowing the treatment of unlabeled examples to respond to class differences.

The thresholds have a closed-form solution, making their determination efficient. Experiments across more than twenty imbalance ratios report substantial performance improvements and support the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution is a relatively simple change to the pseudo-label selection mechanism, addressing a specific source of difficulty when semi-supervised learning is applied to uneven class distributions.
summary.tldr: Optimizing class-specific pseudo-label counts yields efficient adaptive confidence thresholds that improve semi-supervised learning under class imbalance.

title: Class-Imbalanced Semi-Supervised Learning with Adaptive Thresholding

abstract: We propose efficient Langevin Monte Carlo algorithms for sampling distributions with nonsmooth convex composite potentials, which is the sum of a continuously differentiable function and a possibly nonsmooth function. We devise such algorithms leveraging recent advances in convex analysis and optimization methods involving Bregman divergences, namely the Bregman–Moreau envelopes and the Bregman proximity operators, and in the Langevin Monte Carlo algorithms reminiscent of mirror descent. The proposed algorithms extend existing Langevin Monte Carlo algorithms in two aspects—the ability to sample nonsmooth distributions with mirror descent-like algorithms, and the use of the more general Bregman–Moreau envelope in place of the Moreau envelope as a smooth approximation of the nonsmooth part of the potential. A particular case of the proposed scheme is reminiscent of the Bregman proximal gradient algorithm. The efficiency of the proposed methodology is illustrated with various sampling tasks at which existing Langevin Monte Carlo methods are known to perform poorly.

paragraphs: This paper develops sampling algorithms for distributions whose convex potential combines a continuously differentiable term with a term that may be nonsmooth. The nonsmooth component complicates methods that rely on ordinary gradients. The authors address this setting through Langevin Monte Carlo algorithms built from tools in convex analysis and optimization.

Their approach uses Bregman–Moreau envelopes to smoothly approximate the nonsmooth component and Bregman proximity operators to handle its structure. These tools are paired with Langevin methods resembling mirror descent. The resulting framework extends existing methods both by allowing mirror-descent-like sampling of nonsmooth distributions and by replacing the usual Moreau smoothing with its more general Bregman counterpart.

A particular instance of the proposed scheme resembles a Bregman proximal gradient algorithm, connecting the sampling procedure to an optimization method. The authors illustrate efficiency on several sampling tasks where existing Langevin Monte Carlo methods are known to struggle. The contribution is a broader algorithmic toolkit for this class of convex sampling problems, supported by demonstrations on challenging tasks.
summary.tldr: Bregman smoothing and proximity operators extend Langevin sampling to nonsmooth convex distributions using mirror-descent-like algorithms.

title: Bregman Proximal Langevin Monte Carlo via Bregman-Moreau Envelopes

abstract: This paper proposes a self-supervised objective for learning representations that localize objects under occlusion - a property known as object permanence. A central question is the choice of learning signal in cases of total occlusion. Rather than directly supervising the locations of invisible objects, we propose a self-supervised objective that requires neither human annotation, nor assumptions about object dynamics. This leads to a memory representation that stores occluded objects and predicts their motion, to better localize them. The resulting model outperforms existing approaches on several datasets of increasing complexity and realism, despite requiring minimal supervision, and hence being broadly applicable.

paragraphs: Tracking an object becomes especially difficult when it disappears completely behind something else. The visible image no longer directly tells a model where the object is. Optimizing this objective produces a memory representation that retains occluded objects and predicts their motion to improve localization. summary.tldr: A self-supervised memory-coherence objective learns to localize occluded objects without annotations of hidden locations or assumptions about their dynamics.

title: Object Permanence Emerges in a Random Walk along Memory

abstract: Recent progress has been made towards learning invariant or equivariant representations with self-supervised learning. While invariant methods are evaluated on large scale datasets, equivariant ones are evaluated in smaller, more controlled, settings. We aim at bridging the gap between the two in order to learn more diverse representations that are suitable for a wide range of tasks. We start by introducing a dataset called 3DIEBench, consisting of renderings from 3D models over 55 classes and more than 2.5 million images where we have full control on the transformations applied to the objects. We further introduce a predictor architecture based on hypernetworks to learn equivariant representations with no possible collapse to invariance. We introduce SIE (Split Invariant-Equivariant) which combines the hypernetwork-based predictor with representations split in two parts, one invariant, the other equivariant, to learn richer representations. We demonstrate significant performance gains over existing methods on equivariance related tasks from both a qualitative and quantitative point of view. We further analyze our introduced predictor and show how it steers the learned latent space. We hope that both our introduced dataset and approach will enable learning richer representations without supervision in more complex scenarios. Code and data are available at https://github.com/garridoq/SIE.

paragraphs: A useful representation may need to ignore some transformations while retaining information about others. Invariant representations stay unchanged under transformations, whereas equivariant representations change in a corresponding way. This paper seeks to combine these properties and bring equivariant self-supervised learning into larger, more varied evaluation settings.

The authors introduce 3DIEBench, containing more than 2.5 million rendered images across 55 classes, with control over transformations applied to the objects. They also develop a hypernetwork-based predictor designed to learn equivariant representations without collapsing into invariance. Their SIE method splits each representation into invariant and equivariant parts and combines that split with the predictor.

The paper reports significant qualitative and quantitative gains over existing methods on tasks related to equivariance. It also analyzes how the predictor shapes the learned latent space. The split gives the model separate places to represent information that should remain stable and information that should track transformations. The results support richer self-supervised representations for these tasks, while the dataset provides controlled transformations for studying that behavior.
summary.tldr: SIE separates invariant and equivariant features and uses a hypernetwork predictor to improve performance on transformation-sensitive tasks.

title: Self-supervised learning of Split Invariant Equivariant representations

abstract: The concentration of measure inequalities serves an essential role in statistics and machine learning. This paper gives unbounded analogues of the McDiarmid-type exponential inequalities for three popular classes of distributions, namely sub-Gaussian, sub-exponential and heavy-tailed distributions. The inequalities in the sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential cases are distribution-dependent compared with the recent results, and the inequalities in the heavy-tailed case are not available in the previous works. The usefulness of the inequalities is illustrated through applications to the sample mean, U-statistics and V-statistics.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how strongly random quantities cluster around their typical behavior. They provide tools for analyzing statistical estimates and learning procedures. This paper develops McDiarmid-type exponential inequalities for functions with unbounded interactions, extending the available analysis to settings where the relevant effects cannot simply be treated as bounded.

The results cover three distribution classes: sub-Gaussian, sub-exponential, and heavy-tailed. For the first two classes, the proposed inequalities depend on the distribution, distinguishing them from the recent results discussed by the authors. For heavy-tailed distributions, the paper supplies inequalities that the authors identify as unavailable in previous work. These are separate contributions within the same concentration framework.

The paper illustrates the inequalities through applications to the sample mean, U-statistics, and V-statistics. These examples connect the mathematical bounds to concrete statistical quantities rather than leaving them as abstract statements about random functions. The significance is a broader set of tools for studying concentration under different distributional behaviors, including heavy tails, with the relevant distribution class remaining part of the result.
summary.tldr: The paper extends McDiarmid-type concentration bounds to unbounded interactions across sub-Gaussian, sub-exponential, and heavy-tailed distributions.

title: Distribution-dependent McDiarmid-type Inequalities for Functions of Unbounded Interaction

abstract: We develop an analytical framework to characterize the set of optimal ReLU neural networks by reformulating the non-convex training problem as a convex program. We show that the global optima of the convex parameterization are given by a polyhedral set and then extend this characterization to the optimal set of the non-convex training objective. Since all stationary points of the ReLU training problem can be represented as optima of sub-sampled convex programs, our work provide a general expression for all critical points of the non-convex objective. We then leverage our results to provide an optimal pruning algorithm for computing minimal networks, establish conditions for the regularization path of ReLU networks to be continuous, and develop sensitivity results for minimal ReLU networks.

paragraphs: A neural-network training problem can have many optimal parameter settings, making the structure of the full solution set important. This paper develops an analytical framework for studying optimal ReLU networks by reformulating the nonconvex training problem as a convex program.

The authors show that global optima in the convex parameterization form a polyhedral set, a geometric object described by linear constraints. They then transfer this characterization to the original nonconvex objective. Stationary points of the ReLU problem can also be represented as optima of subsampled convex programs, providing a general expression for its critical points.

It yields an optimal pruning algorithm for computing minimal networks and conditions under which the regularization path is continuous as regularization changes. These applications connect the geometry of training solutions to network size and to how solutions respond to changes in the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: A convex reformulation characterizes optimal ReLU networks and supports results on pruning, regularization paths, and sensitivity.

title: Optimal Sets and Solution Paths of ReLU Networks

abstract: Decentralized bilevel optimization based machine learning techniques are achieving remarkable success in a wide variety of domains. However, the intensive exchange of information (involving nested-loops of consensus or communication iterations) in existing decentralized bilevel optimization algorithms leads to a great challenge to ensure rigorous differential privacy, which, however, is necessary to bring the benefits of machine learning to domains where involved data are sensitive. By proposing a new decentralized stochastic bilevel-optimization algorithm which avoids nested-loops of information-exchange iterations, we achieve, for the first time, both differential privacy and accurate convergence in decentralized bilevel optimization. This is significant since even for single-level decentralized optimization and learning, existing differential-privacy solutions have to sacrifice convergence accuracy for privacy. Besides characterizing the convergence rate under nonconvex/convex/strongly convex conditions, we also rigorously quantify the price of differential privacy in the convergence rate. Experimental results on machine learning models confirm the efficacy of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves two linked optimization problems, and decentralized versions distribute the work across participants. Existing algorithms can require nested rounds of communication to coordinate their computations. The paper identifies this intensive information exchange as a major obstacle to providing rigorous differential privacy when the underlying data are sensitive.

The proposed stochastic algorithm avoids nested loops of information exchange. The authors establish both differential privacy and accurate convergence, presenting this combination as a first for decentralized bilevel optimization. Their motivation is especially notable because existing privacy methods for even single-level decentralized learning can require sacrificing convergence accuracy.

The theoretical analysis covers nonconvex, convex, and strongly convex settings and characterizes convergence rates in each. It also quantifies how privacy affects the rate, separating the ability to converge accurately from the speed of doing so. Experiments on machine learning models support the algorithm’s effectiveness. The central contribution is a communication design that makes privacy compatible with accurate convergence while explicitly accounting for its cost in convergence rate.
summary.tldr: A decentralized bilevel algorithm avoids nested communication loops and provides privacy with accurate convergence while quantifying the effect on convergence speed.

title: Locally Differentially Private Decentralized Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Guaranteed Convergence Accuracy

abstract: Fine-tuning language models (LMs) has demonstrated success in a wide array of downstream tasks. However, as LMs are scaled up, the memory requirements for backpropagation become prohibitively high. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization methods can leverage memory-efficient forward passes to estimate gradients. More recently, MeZO, an adaptation of ZO-SGD, has been shown to consistently outperform zero-shot and in-context learning when combined with suitable task prompts. In this work, we couple ZO methods with variance reduction techniques to enhance stability and convergence for inference-based LM fine-tuning. We introduce Memory-Efficient Zeroth-Order Stochastic Variance-Reduced Gradient (MeZO-SVRG) and demonstrate its efficacy across multiple LM fine-tuning tasks, eliminating the reliance on task-specific prompts. Evaluated across a range of both masked and autoregressive LMs on benchmark GLUE tasks, MeZO-SVRG outperforms MeZO with up to 20% increase in test accuracies in both full- and partial-parameter fine-tuning settings. MeZO-SVRG benefits from reduced computation time as it often surpasses MeZO’s peak test accuracy with a $2\times$ reduction in GPU-hours. MeZO-SVRG significantly reduces the required memory footprint compared to first-order SGD, i.e. by $2\times$ for autoregressive models. Our experiments highlight that MeZO-SVRG’s memory savings progressively improve compared to SGD with larger batch sizes.
