paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks aim to produce diverse samples, but stochastic environments and sparse rewards can make their training unstable. High variance can obscure useful learning signals and hinder convergence. Spectral Time-Dependent GFlowNets reformulates the training objective in the frequency domain, using Fourier analysis to promote smoothness and stability in the learned policies.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the proposed spectral loss is equivalent to regularized value iteration. In that formulation, it acts as a low-pass filter that separates signal from noise. To address exploration when useful rewards are scarce, the framework also introduces an autocorrelated intrinsic reward derived from the Wiener-Khinchin theorem. This supplies a separate mechanism for encouraging exploration in sparse landscapes.

Experiments cover adversarial games, noisy sequence generation, and high-dimensional modeling of single-cell perturbations. The authors report significant improvements over existing baselines in robustness, sample efficiency, and discovery of modes. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support frequency-domain regularization as a principled way to stabilize learning while retaining the diverse-sampling purpose of GFlowNets.
summary.tldr: Spectral Time-Dependent GFlowNets use frequency-domain regularization and intrinsic rewards to improve stability, sample efficiency, and mode discovery.

title: Spectral Flow Matching: Stabilizing Stochastic GFlowNets via Frequency-Domain Regularization

abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a prominent algorithm within the Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) framework, has achieved strong results in improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, GRPO is prone to advantage collapse, a failure mode where homogeneous rewards within a group (e.g., all correct or all incorrect answers) yield near-zero advantages and vanishing gradients. To address this, we introduce the Advantage Collapse Rate (ACR), the first diagnostic metric quantifying the proportion of training batches with ineffective gradients. Across models from 0.5B to 14B parameters on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, we show that ACR strongly predicts training stagnation and final performance. We then propose Adaptive Virtual Sample Policy Optimization (AVSPO), a lightweight extension of GRPO that injects virtual reward samples, guided by real-time ACR monitoring, to enable learning from homogeneous groups without additional model rollouts. AVSPO reduces advantage collapse by 58–63% relative to GRPO and yields consistent accuracy gains of 4–6 percentage points across all model scales, while maintaining generalization on the evaluated out-of-domain task. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/hexixiang/Advantage-Collapse-Rate.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization trains language models by comparing rewards among answers generated in the same group. This comparison becomes uninformative when every answer receives the same reward, whether all answers are correct or all are incorrect. The resulting advantages approach zero, leaving little gradient signal for learning. The paper calls this failure mode advantage collapse.

The authors introduce Advantage Collapse Rate, which measures the proportion of training batches with ineffective gradients. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks with models ranging from 0.5 billion to 14 billion parameters, this rate strongly predicts training stagnation and final performance. It therefore provides a diagnostic connection between an apparently routine batch of answers and stalled optimization.

Their mitigation, Adaptive Virtual Sample Policy Optimization, uses live collapse measurements to decide when to inject virtual reward samples. These samples let homogeneous groups contribute to learning without generating additional model rollouts. In the reported evaluations, the method reduces collapse by 58–63% relative to GRPO and improves accuracy by 4–6 percentage points across tested model sizes, while maintaining generalization on the evaluated out-of-domain task.
summary.tldr: Monitoring uninformative reward groups and adding virtual reward samples reduces GRPO training collapse and improves mathematical reasoning accuracy.

title: Advantage Collapse in Group Relative Policy Optimization: Diagnosis and Mitigation

abstract: Federated Graph Learning (FGL) facilitates privacy-preserving collaborative training of graph neural networks, yet homophily heterogeneity across subgraphs can induce optimization conflicts that degrade model generalization. Many existing solutions rely on multi-channel architectures to mitigate such conflicts, which increase the burden on edge devices and lack theoretical convergence analysis. To overcome these limitations, we propose FedGCM, a novel FGL framework with Group-oriented Conflict Mitigation, which aligns inconsistent optimization objectives via a tailored gradient surgery. Specifically, FedGCM first divides clients into distinct groups based on their homophily levels, thereby avoiding exhaustive client-to-client conflict assessments. To resolve inter-group interference, we develop RPGrad, a gradient surgery mechanism based on residual projection, which integrates synergistic knowledge while filtering inter-group conflicts. The refined updates are then transmitted in a group-wise fashion, effectively alleviating optimization conflicts induced by homophily heterogeneity without augmenting the client-side burden. Furthermore, we provide a formal theoretical analysis establishing the convergence. Extensive experiments on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs demonstrate that FedGCM consistently achieves superior performance.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning allows clients to collaborate on a graph neural network while keeping their data distributed. A complication arises when clients’ subgraphs differ in homophily, or how strongly connected nodes resemble one another. Those differences can produce conflicting training objectives and weaken the resulting model’s generalization.

FedGCM addresses the conflict by grouping clients according to their homophily levels. This avoids checking every client against every other client. Its RPGrad mechanism then uses residual projection to modify group updates, retaining compatible knowledge while filtering interference between groups. The refined updates are transmitted by group, targeting the source of disagreement without adding client-side architectural burden.

The paper provides a theoretical convergence analysis and reports superior performance across experiments involving both homophilous and heterophilous graphs. Its contribution is therefore both an optimization mechanism and supporting analysis. By organizing conflict management around graph similarity patterns, FedGCM provides an alternative to multi-channel solutions that increase work on edge devices, while preserving useful information shared across groups.
summary.tldr: FedGCM groups graph-learning clients by homophily and modifies conflicting group gradients to improve collaborative training without increasing client-side burden.

title: Homophily-Heterogeneity Gradient Surgery for Federated Graph Learning

abstract: Where do learning signals come from when there is no ground truth in post-training? We show that inference compute itself can serve as supervision. By generating parallel rollouts and converting them into reference estimates, models can learn without human labels—critically, even in non-verifiable domains like healthcare guidance where no programmatic checker exists. We call this framework Compute as Teacher (CaT) and it turns inference-time compute from parallel rollouts into supervision for RL training. The framework has two components: (1) reference estimation which aggregates rollouts into a pseudo-reference answer, and (2) reward derivation which converts that pseudo-reference into RL rewards. For (1), we explore a simple method we call synthesis, but the framework admits any aggregator. For (2), we introduce self-proposed rubrics for non-verifiable domains. These are binary, auditable criteria generated from the pseudo-reference and scored by an LLM judge. On HealthBench, models trained with CaT match or exceed inference-time aggregation quality while using 9$\times$ less test-time compute. Here, CaT also competes with learning from expert physician annotations, yielding up to +30% relative improvement over the initial policy. The framework extends naturally to verifiable rewards, matching the best existing baselines on MATH-500 in test-time RL and demonstrating ’drop-in’ versatility across both types of domains.

paragraphs: Compute as Teacher asks how a model can improve when post-training has no ground-truth answers. Its answer is to turn multiple generated responses into a training signal. Parallel rollouts are aggregated into an estimated reference, which then supports reinforcement learning, including in domains where a program cannot directly check whether an answer is correct.

The framework separates reference estimation from reward construction. The authors explore an aggregation method called synthesis, while allowing other aggregators. For non-verifiable tasks, the estimated reference generates binary evaluation criteria called self-proposed rubrics. A language-model judge scores these auditable criteria to produce rewards, giving training a structured target derived from the model’s own inference compute.

On HealthBench, trained models match or exceed inference-time aggregation quality with nine times less test-time compute. They also compete with training from physician annotations, with improvements of up to 30% relative to the initial policy. In a verifiable setting, the framework matches leading baselines on MATH-500 in test-time reinforcement learning, supporting its applicability across both reward settings.
summary.tldr: Compute as Teacher converts aggregated model responses into reinforcement learning supervision, reducing the inference compute needed for strong answers.

title: Compute as Teacher: Turning Inference Compute Into Reference-Free Supervision

abstract: Domain generalized object detection (DGOD) aims to train an object detector on a single source domain and generalize it to unseen target domains. Recent advances in DGOD have increasingly exploited vision foundation models (VFMs) via parameter-efficient finetuning strategies. However, existing approaches typically adapt VFMs with fixed, style-agnostic parameters, overlooking that different visual styles may induce distinct task discrepancies. To address this challenge, we propose SCoA, a novel Style Conditioned Adaptation framework for dynamic, style-aware task compensation. Specifically, we introduce a Spectral Style Modeling (SSM) module that preserves local style cues via a memory-based mechanism, enabling diverse style characterization from a single source domain. Conditioned on the extracted style signals, we design a Mixture-of-Tokens Adaptation (MTA) mechanism, which maintains multiple adaptation tokens and dynamically routes each sample to an optimal combination of tokens, thereby explicitly modeling style-dependent task mismatches. In addition, we propose a Style-Conditioned Query Refinement (SCQR) module that injects style information into object queries, enabling a style-aware detection head. By jointly integrating these components, SCoA allows the model to follow style-specific adaptation trajectories, achieving effective and flexible task compensation for VFM-based DGOD. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SCoA achieves state-of-the-art performance across two challenging scenarios.

paragraphs: SCoA tackles object detection when training data come from one source domain but deployment involves unseen domains. The paper argues that adapting a vision foundation model with one fixed set of style-independent parameters overlooks an important difference: distinct visual styles can create distinct mismatches for the detection task.

Its Spectral Style Modeling component uses memory to preserve local style cues and characterize varied styles within the source domain. Those signals guide a Mixture-of-Tokens Adaptation mechanism, which maintains multiple adaptation tokens and routes each sample to an appropriate combination. A third component refines object queries with style information, extending the adaptation into the detection head.

Together, these components let the detector adjust its adaptation according to the style of each sample. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across two challenging scenarios. The results support using style as an explicit conditioning signal throughout detection, from the adaptation tokens to the object queries, when learning from a single source domain and seeking generalization to domains absent from training.
summary.tldr: SCoA conditions detector adaptation and object queries on visual style to improve generalization from one training domain to unseen domains.

title: SCoA: Revisiting Domain Generalized Object Detection with Style-Conditioned Adaptation

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in robot manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, their representations arguably remain suboptimal, lacking sensitivity to robotic signals such as control actions and proprioceptive information. To address the issue, we introduce Robot State-aware Contrastive Loss (RS-CL), a simple and effective representation regularization for VLA models, designed to bridge the gap between VLM representations and robotic signals. In particular, RS-CL aligns the representations more closely with the robot’s proprioceptive states by using relative distances between the states as soft supervision. Complementing the original action prediction objective, RS-CL enhances control-relevant representation learning, while being lightweight and fully compatible with standard VLA training pipelines. Our empirical results demonstrate that RS-CL substantially improves the performance of state-of-the-art VLA models; it pushes the prior art to 69.7% achieving the state-of-the-art performance on the RoboCasa-Kitchen benchmark, and boosts success rates from 45.0% to 58.3% on challenging real-robot manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models adapt rich visual and language representations for robot control. Those representations may nevertheless be insufficiently sensitive to signals that matter for manipulation, including actions and the robot’s own physical state. This paper introduces an additional training objective intended to make the learned representations more responsive to those control-relevant distinctions.

Robot State-aware Contrastive Loss uses relative distances between proprioceptive states as soft supervision. In effect, relationships among the robot’s states provide guidance about how its internal representations should relate to one another. The loss supplements the original action-prediction objective and is designed as a lightweight addition compatible with standard vision-language-action training pipelines.

The authors report substantial improvements for the evaluated models, reaching 69.7% on RoboCasa-Kitchen and increasing success on challenging real-robot manipulation tasks from 45.0% to 58.3%. These findings suggest that explicitly organizing representations around robot-state information can improve control. The contribution is a relatively simple training regularizer that helps connect pretrained visual-language features to the physical distinctions required for successful action.
summary.tldr: A robot-state-aware contrastive loss improves vision-language-action representations and manipulation success.

title: Contrastive Representation Regularization for Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Relational Foundation Models (RFMs) facilitate data-driven decision-making by learning from complex multi-table databases. However, the diverse relational databases needed to train such models are rarely public due to privacy constraints. While there are methods to generate synthetic tabular data of arbitrary size, incorporating schema structure and primary–foreign key connectivity for multi-table generation remains challenging. Here we introduce PluRel, a framework to synthesize multi-tabular relational databases from scratch. In a step-by-step fashion, PluRel models (1) schemas with directed graphs, (2) inter-table primary-foreign key connectivity with bipartite graphs, and, (3) feature distributions in tables via conditional causal mechanisms. The design space across these stages supports the synthesis of a wide range of diverse databases, while being computationally lightweight. Using PluRel, we observe for the first time that (1) RFM pretraining loss exhibits power-law scaling with the number of synthetic databases and total pretraining tokens, (2) scaling the number of synthetic databases improves generalization to real databases, and (3) synthetic pretraining yields strong base models for continued pretraining on real databases. Overall, our framework and results position synthetic data scaling as a promising paradigm for RFMs. Webpage: https://star-project.stanford.edu/plurel
originalAbstract: Relational Foundation Models (RFMs) facilitate data-driven decision-making by learning from complex multi-table databases. However, the diverse relational databases needed to train such models are rarely public due to privacy constraints. While there are methods to generate synthetic tabular data of arbitrary size, incorporating schema structure and primary–foreign key connectivity for multi-table generation remains challenging. Here we introduce PluRel, a framework to synthesize multi-tabular relational databases from scratch. In a step-by-step fashion, PluRel models (1) schemas with directed graphs, (2) inter-table primary-foreign key connectivity with bipartite graphs, and, (3) feature distributions in tables via conditional causal mechanisms. The design space across these stages supports the synthesis of a wide range of diverse databases, while being computationally lightweight. Using PluRel, we observe for the first time that (1) RFM pretraining loss exhibits power-law scaling with the number of synthetic databases and total pretraining tokens, (2) scaling the number of synthetic databases improves generalization to real databases, and (3) synthetic pretraining yields strong base models for continued pretraining on real databases. Overall, our framework and results position synthetic data scaling as a promising paradigm for RFMs. Webpage: https://star-project.stanford.edu/plurel

paragraphs: Relational foundation models learn from databases containing multiple connected tables, but privacy restrictions make diverse training databases difficult to obtain. The framework builds databases in three stages. Directed graphs describe the schema, bipartite graphs specify primary-key and foreign-key connections between tables, and conditional causal mechanisms generate table features. Separating these stages provides a broad design space for varying both database structure and contents while keeping generation computationally lightweight.

Using these synthetic databases, the authors observe power-law relationships between pretraining loss and both database count and total pretraining tokens. Increasing the number of synthetic databases also improves generalization to real databases, and synthetic pretraining produces strong starting models for continued training on real data. These empirical findings support synthetic database diversity as a promising way to scale relational-model training when public real-world databases are scarce.
summary.tldr: PluRel generates diverse connected databases, revealing empirical scaling laws and improved transfer from synthetic pretraining to real relational data.

title: PluRel: Synthetic Data unlocks Scaling Laws for Relational Foundation Models

abstract: A fundamental tension exists in the large-step inference of diffusion models via their deterministic probability flow ordinary differential equation (PF-ODE) trajectories, which we identify as the contractivity trap: efficient inference favors large step sizes, while aggressive steps and highly expressive denoisers can undermine contraction-based stability certificates for error suppression. To address this, we propose SteinDiff, a step-wise inference-time stabilization framework that employs Stein-derived corrections without requiring reference samples. Specifically, SteinDiff introduces a geometry-aware residual correction mechanism that regularizes large-step solver updates without retraining. To this end, we derive a closed-form Stein correction coefficient for step-wise solver adjustment, enabling reference-free adaptation to local data geometry. We further establish a score-controlled perturbation bound under distributional shifts and provide a complementary Stein perspective on EDM-style parameterizations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SteinDiff mitigates severe artifacts and improves generative quality across large-step inference settings.

paragraphs: Taking larger steps along a diffusion model's deterministic sampling trajectory can make generation more efficient. The paper identifies a tension: aggressive steps and highly expressive denoisers can undermine mathematical stability certificates based on contraction, which describe suppression of errors. The authors call this tension the contractivity trap.

SteinDiff adds a correction at each inference step to regularize large solver updates. The correction accounts for local data geometry, uses a closed-form coefficient derived through Stein methods, and requires neither retraining nor reference samples. Its purpose is to adapt the update itself so that large-step sampling is less vulnerable to severe errors.

Experiments report fewer severe artifacts and improved generative quality across large-step inference settings. Together, these contributions support step-wise stabilization as a way to mitigate the practical consequences of the identified tension, without claiming that every large-step trajectory becomes stable.
summary.tldr: SteinDiff applies reference-free, geometry-aware corrections to improve diffusion generation with large sampling steps.

title: Mitigating the Contractivity Trap in Diffusion ODEs via Stein Stabilization

abstract: Skeleton-based action recognition aims to understand human behaviors from body joint sequences and is especially challenging in the one-shot setting, where only a single labeled exemplar is available for each novel action. A key challenge is learning representations that capture the hierarchical and compositional structure of human motion while aligning effectively with high-level action semantics under extreme data scarcity. Existing approaches, largely based on Euclidean embeddings and low-level motion cues, struggle to model the tree-like organization of skeleton data, limiting cross-modal alignment and generalization to unseen action categories. We propose SkelHCC, a unified skeleton hyperbolic CLIP-driven cache adaptation framework for one-shot skeleton-based action recognition. SkelHCC introduces an Explicitly Hierarchical Hyperbolic CLIP (EH-HCLIP) module that embeds skeleton sequences and action language into a shared hyperbolic space. By leveraging the negative curvature and exponential volume growth of hyperbolic geometry, EH-HCLIP naturally encodes the joint–part–body hierarchy of human anatomy and yields structurally consistent cross-modal representations. To support efficient one-shot adaptation, SkelHCC further integrates a training-free LLM-guided Multi-granularity Voting Cache (LMV-Cache) for context-aware inference. Experiments on NTU RGB+D 60, NTU RGB+D 120, and PKU-MMD II demonstrate that SkelHCC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code will be available at https://github.com/lya19971103/SkelHCC

paragraphs: Recognizing an unfamiliar action from a single labeled example requires a useful representation of how body joints move together. Its motivation is that human movement has a hierarchy, from individual joints through body parts to the whole body, that ordinary Euclidean representations can struggle to capture.

The framework’s Explicitly Hierarchical Hyperbolic CLIP module places skeleton and language representations in a shared hyperbolic space. The geometry’s negative curvature and expanding volume support the tree-like organization of the joint–part–body hierarchy. A separate language-model-guided voting cache combines information at multiple levels of granularity, providing context-aware one-shot adaptation without additional training for that component.

Experiments on NTU RGB+D 60, NTU RGB+D 120, and PKU-MMD II show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These results support combining explicit anatomical hierarchy with language alignment when labeled examples of new actions are scarce. The training-free claim applies to the cache adaptation mechanism, within the broader learned representation framework.
summary.tldr: SkelHCC combines hierarchical hyperbolic skeleton-language representations with training-free cache adaptation to improve one-shot action recognition.

title: SkelHCC: A Hyperbolic CLIP-Driven Cache Adaptation Framework for Skeleton-based One-Shot Action Recognition

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning meaningful representations from unlabeled data. However, the standard protocol for evaluating these representations, linear probing, is computationally expensive, sensitive to hyperparameters, and provides limited insight into the geometric structure of the representation space. In this work, motivated by connections between neural network generalization and intrinsic dimension (ID) we propose IdEst, a method for estimating the ID of SSL representations via the Minimum Spanning Tree dimension estimator ($\mathrm{dim}_\mathrm{MST}$). Across diverse datasets, architectures, and SSL pretraining objectives, we show that IdEst strongly correlates with downstream linear probe performances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that IdEst enables efficient hyperparameter selection, significantly reducing the computational cost compared to supervised alternatives. Our results highlight intrinsic dimensionality as a principled geometric proxy for assessing SSL representations, complementing standard supervised probing protocols.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning produces representations from unlabeled data, but assessing their usefulness often requires training a supervised linear probe. That evaluation can be expensive and sensitive to hyperparameters. It also reveals relatively little about the geometry of the learned representation itself. IdEst explores whether a geometric measurement can provide a cheaper, informative assessment.

The method estimates intrinsic dimension using a minimum spanning tree dimension estimator. Intrinsic dimension describes the effective dimensional structure of the representations, giving a way to study how the learned data occupy their feature space. The paper motivates this choice through connections between intrinsic dimension and neural network generalization.

Across different datasets, architectures, and self-supervised objectives, IdEst strongly correlates with downstream linear-probe performance. The authors also demonstrate its use for hyperparameter selection, with substantially lower computational cost than supervised alternatives. These findings support intrinsic dimension as a useful proxy for representation quality. The proposed role is complementary to standard probing: it adds a geometric signal and a cheaper selection tool without claiming that correlation makes the two evaluations interchangeable.
summary.tldr: IdEst uses intrinsic dimension to assess self-supervised representations and select hyperparameters at lower cost than supervised probing.

title: IdEst: Assessing Self-Supervised Learning Representations via Intrinsic Dimension

abstract: Continuous diffusion for categorical data is a framework belonging to the diffusion family and aiming at generating discrete data. The scientific interest to such models has been constantly increasing these days because researchers try to achieve a challenging goal of finding reasonable alternatives to autoregressive large language models. In this paper, we study the properties of the structure of the latent space corresponding to discrete tokens expressed in terms of Kullback-Leibler divergence on diffusion path measures and accuracy of the correct token prediction by the optimally trained diffusion model. We find that FSQ tokenization scheme has the latent space structure with the properties that make it best suited for continuous diffusion for categorical data as verified through rigorous theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. To validate our findings in real-life scenario, we train several text-to-speech diffusion models having speech tokens as intermediate acoustic features, and show that the one based on FSQ tokens indeed performs the best, and, moreover, it outperforms its strong LLM-based counterpart, at the same time being significantly smaller and faster.

paragraphs: Continuous diffusion for categorical data generates discrete outputs through a continuous latent representation. This paper asks how the arrangement of discrete tokens in that latent space affects generation. The question matters because the token representation determines the structure on which the diffusion model operates, rather than serving only as a final output format.

The authors analyze latent-space structure using Kullback-Leibler divergence between diffusion path measures and correct-token prediction accuracy for an optimally trained diffusion model. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, they find that FSQ tokenization has properties making it best suited to continuous categorical diffusion under the criteria they study.

They then test the findings in text-to-speech systems that use speech tokens as intermediate acoustic features. Among the trained diffusion models, the FSQ-based system performs best. It also outperforms a strong language-model-based counterpart while being substantially smaller and faster. The application connects the theoretical importance of token geometry to observed differences in speech-generation performance and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: Theory and text-to-speech experiments identify FSQ token geometry as especially well suited to continuous diffusion over categorical data.

title: Optimality of FSQ Tokens for Continuous Diffusion for Categorical Data with Application to Text-to-Speech

abstract: We introduce Alterbute, a diffusion-based method for editing an object’s intrinsic attributes in an image. We allow changing color, texture, material, and even the shape of an object, while preserving its perceived identity and scene context. Existing approaches either rely on unsupervised priors that often fail to preserve identity or use overly restrictive supervision that prevents meaningful intrinsic variations. Our method relies on: (i) a relaxed training objective that allows the model to change both intrinsic and extrinsic attributes conditioned on an identity reference image, a textual prompt describing the target intrinsic attributes, and a background image and object mask defining the extrinsic context. At inference, we restrict extrinsic changes by reusing the original background and object mask, thereby ensuring that only the desired intrinsic attributes are altered; (ii) Visual Named Entities (VNEs) - fine-grained visual identity categories (e.g., "Porsche 911 Carrera") that group objects sharing identity-defining features while allowing variation in intrinsic attributes. We use a vision-language model to automatically extract VNE labels and intrinsic attribute descriptions from a large public image dataset, enabling scalable, identity-preserving supervision. Alterbute outperforms existing methods on identity-preserving object intrinsic attribute editing.

paragraphs: Alterbute edits an object’s color, texture, material, or shape while preserving its perceived identity and surrounding scene. The challenge is deciding which visual properties may change without making the object seem like something else. Existing methods can either lose identity through insufficient supervision or impose constraints so tight that meaningful attribute changes become difficult.

The method combines flexible training with tighter control at inference. During training, a diffusion model receives an identity reference, a text description of desired attributes, and a background image with an object mask. It may change both the object’s intrinsic attributes and its external context. At inference, reusing the original background and mask restricts changes to the intended object attributes.

Supervision comes from Visual Named Entities: fine-grained categories such as a particular car model that preserve identifying features while permitting attribute variation. A vision-language model extracts these categories and attribute descriptions from a large public image dataset. The reported improvements over existing methods support this combination of flexible identity categories and explicit scene control for identity-preserving editing.
summary.tldr: Alterbute combines flexible identity supervision with scene constraints to edit object attributes while preserving perceived identity.

title: Alterbute: Editing Intrinsic Attributes of Objects in Images

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) have emerged as a powerful foundation for long-range sequence modeling, with the HiPPO framework showing that continuous-time projection operators can be used to derive stable, memory-efficient dynamical systems that encode the past history of the input signal. However, existing projection-based SSMs often rely on polynomial bases with global temporal support, whose inductive biases are poorly matched to signals exhibiting localized or transient structure. In this work, we introduce WaveSSM, a collection of SSMs constructed over wavelet frames. Our key observation is that wavelet frames yield a localized support on the temporal dimension, useful for tasks requiring precise localization. Empirically, we show that on equal conditions, WaveSSM outperforms orthogonal counterparts as S4 on real-world datasets with transient dynamics, including physiological signals on the PTB-XL dataset and raw audio on Speech Commands.

paragraphs: State-space models can encode long histories of a signal using stable, memory-efficient dynamics. Projection-based approaches such as those derived through HiPPO often represent that history with polynomial bases that have global temporal support. The paper argues that this representation is poorly matched to signals containing localized events or short-lived changes.

WaveSSM introduces a family of state-space models built over wavelet frames. Their key property is localized support in time, which is useful when a task depends on precisely locating a transient feature. The architecture therefore changes the representation used to encode the signal's history so that temporal localization is built into the model's structure.

Under equal experimental conditions, WaveSSM outperforms orthogonal counterparts such as S4 on real-world datasets with transient dynamics. The reported evaluations include physiological signals from PTB-XL and raw audio from Speech Commands. These results support matching the model's projection structure to the temporal character of its inputs: localized wavelet representations help on the tested tasks where transient signal behavior matters.
summary.tldr: WaveSSM uses temporally localized wavelet frames to improve state-space modeling of physiological signals and audio with transient dynamics.

title: WaveSSM: Multiscale State-Space Models for Non-stationary Signal Attention

abstract: Training a family of large language models (LLMs), either from scratch or via iterative compression, is prohibitively expensive and inefficient, requiring separate training runs for each model in the family. In this paper, we introduce Star Elastic, a novel LLM post-training method that adds N nested submodels to a given parent reasoning model using the compute of one run (Nx savings) via a single post-training job. Beyond reducing training costs, Star Elastic also addresses a fundamental limitation in efficient reasoning: the rigidity of static architectures, which forces the allocation of constant resources regardless of token difficulty. By unlocking elastic budget control, Star Elastic enables a novel approach that uses different submodels for each reasoning phase (thinking and answering). Star Elastic supports (1) nesting along the SSM, embedding channel, MoE and FFN axes, (2) learning nested submodels via an end-to-end trainable router, and (3) curriculum-based knowledge distillation. We apply Star Elastic to the NVIDIA Nemotron Nano models; in particular, we demonstrate its effectiveness on hybrid MoE architectures with Nemotron Nano v3 (30B/3.6A), generating 23B (2.8A) and 12B (2.0A) variants with 160B training tokens. For Nemotron Nano v2 (12B), we produce 9B and 6B nested models using only 110B training tokens, achieving a 360x reduction versus training from scratch and a 7x reduction over state-of-the-art compression methods. All nested models match or outperform independently trained baselines of comparable size. Crucially, elastic budget control advances the accuracy–latency Pareto frontier, achieving up to 16% higher accuracy and 1.9x lower latency via dynamic per-phase model selection.

title: Star Elastic: Many-in-One Reasoning LLMs with Efficient Budget Control

abstract: Inferring the structure of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from data is a central challenge in causal discovery, particularly in modern high-dimensional settings where large-scale interventional data are increasingly available. While interventional data can improve identifiability, existing methods remain limited by soft acyclicity constraints, leading to optimization over invalid cyclic graphs, numerical instability, and reduced scalability. We introduce PACER (Perturbation-driven Acyclic Causal Edge Recovery), a scalable framework for causal discovery that guarantees acyclicity by construction. PACER parameterizes a distribution over DAGs through a joint model of variable permutations and edge probabilities, enabling direct optimization over valid causal structures without surrogate penalties. The framework supports a unified likelihood-based treatment of observational and interventional data, flexible conditional density models, and the incorporation of structural prior knowledge. For linear-Gaussian mechanisms, we derive closed-form expressions for the expected interventional log-likelihood and its gradients, yielding substantial computational gains. Empirically, PACER matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods on protein signaling and large-scale genetic perturbation benchmarks, while scaling efficiently to networks with thousands of variables and achieving up to two orders of magnitude speedups over penalty-based differentiable approaches. These results demonstrate that exact and scalable causal discovery from high-dimensional perturbation data is achievable through principled search space design.

paragraphs: Causal discovery often seeks a directed graph without cycles. Many optimization methods encourage this property with penalties while still exploring cyclic graphs, which can create numerical and scaling problems. PACER designs the search space so that every candidate structure is acyclic, using interventional as well as observational data.

The method represents a distribution over valid graphs through variable orderings and edge probabilities. It optimizes likelihood directly without surrogate acyclicity penalties, supports flexible conditional density models, and can incorporate prior structural knowledge. These results support constructing validity into the search space as a route to scalable causal discovery. Its exact acyclicity guarantee concerns valid graph structure; the reported recovery performance is established empirically.
summary.tldr: PACER searches only acyclic causal graphs, scaling to thousands of variables with reported speedups of up to two orders of magnitude.

title: PACER: Acyclic Causal Discovery from Large-scale Interventional Data

abstract: The scaling-law era has transformed artificial intelligence (AI) from research into a global industry, but its rapid growth also raises concerns over energy usage, carbon emissions, and environmental sustainability. Unlike traditional sectors, the AI industry still lacks systematic carbon accounting methods that support large-scale estimates without reproducing the original training process. This leaves open questions about how large the problem is today and how large it might be in the near future. Given its central role in hosting open-source AI models, the Hugging Face (HF) platform provides a large-scale and publicly accessible corpus for carbon accounting. We estimate aggregate training emissions of HF open-source models using available emissions, energy, compute, and model metadata. To address uneven disclosure quality, we introduce a tiered approach to handle incomplete metadata, supported by empirical regressions that assess estimation reliability. We further introduce AI training carbon intensity (ATCI, emissions per compute), a metric to assess the sustainability efficiency of model training. Our results show that training the most popular open-source models (with over 5,000 downloads) has already resulted in approximately 6.0$\times$10^4 metric tons of carbon emissions. Overall, this paper provides a scalable, empirically grounded framework for estimating training emissions from incomplete disclosures and informing future carbon reporting standards in the AI industry. Data and code are available at https://github.com/insait-institute/HuggingCarbon.

paragraphs: Estimating AI training emissions is difficult when developers disclose inconsistent amounts of energy, compute, and hardware information. It aims to quantify a broad collection of models despite incomplete records.

The contribution is scalable accounting under imperfect disclosure and a framework that could inform more consistent future reporting.
summary.tldr: Hugging Carbon estimates open-model training emissions from incomplete metadata and introduces emissions-per-compute accounting.

title: Hugging Carbon: Quantifying the Training Carbon Emissions of AI Models at Scale

abstract: In single-stream autoregressive interfaces, the same tokens both update the model state and constitute an irreversible public commitment. This coupling creates a silence tax: additional deliberation postpones the first task-relevant content, while naive early streaming risks premature commitments that bias subsequent generations. We introduce Side-by-Side (SxS) Interleaved Reasoning, which makes disclosure timing a controllable decision within standard autoregressive generation. SxS interleaves partial disclosures with continued private reasoning in the same context, but releases content only when it is supported by the reasoning so far. To learn such pacing without incentivizing filler, we construct entailment-aligned interleaved trajectories by matching answer prefixes to supporting reasoning prefixes, then train with SFT to acquire the dual-action semantics and RL to recover reasoning performance under the new format. Across two Qwen3 architectures/scales (MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B, dense Qwen3-4B) and both in-domain (AIME25) and out-of-domain (GPQA-Diamond) benchmarks, SxS improves accuracy–content-latency Pareto trade-offs under token-level proxies (e.g., inter-update waiting).

paragraphs: In a single-stream autoregressive interface, generated tokens both influence subsequent generation and become public commitments. Waiting to finish deliberation delays useful content, while speaking too early can commit the model to claims that bias later reasoning. This paper treats the timing of disclosure as something a model can learn to control.

Side-by-Side Interleaved Reasoning alternates partial public answers with continued private reasoning in the same context. Its training trajectories align answer prefixes with reasoning prefixes that support them, encouraging useful disclosures instead of filler. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the two action types, and reinforcement learning recovers reasoning performance under the interleaved format.

The authors evaluate two Qwen3 models, a mixture-of-experts model and a smaller dense model, on AIME25 and GPQA-Diamond. They report better tradeoffs between accuracy and content latency under token-level proxies such as waiting between updates. The evidence supports improved pacing of substantive content under those measures; it specifically concerns proxy-based latency rather than a stated wall-clock speed improvement.
summary.tldr: Side-by-Side trains models to disclose supported answer portions during continued reasoning, improving measured accuracy–content-latency tradeoffs.

title: When to Think, When to Speak: Learning Disclosure Policies for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Image-to-image relighting requires representations that separate illumination from scene properties while preserving dense geometry, material, and photometric cues. We use this task as a probe of visual priors: unlike recognition tasks that reward invariance, relighting tests whether visual features retain the information needed for light transfer. Through a controlled generative relighting framework, we find that strong semantic encoders can degrade relighting quality, exposing a semantic–photometric trade-off between abstraction and physical fidelity. We introduce Augmented Latent Intrinsics (ALI), which balances this trade-off by fusing dense, pixel-aligned visual features into a latent-intrinsic relighting model and refining it with self-supervision on unlabeled real image pairs. ALI improves relighting quality, especially on glossy, metallic, and transparent materials, and demonstrates that generative relighting is an effective tool for quantifying what visual encoders encode about the physical world.

paragraphs: Relighting an image requires changing illumination while retaining the scene’s geometry and material properties. The paper uses this task to investigate what visual representations preserve about the physical world. Recognition can reward features that ignore changes in lighting, whereas relighting needs access to the details that make those changes physically plausible.

Within a controlled generative framework, the authors find that strong semantic encoders can reduce relighting quality. This reveals a trade-off between abstract understanding and photometric fidelity. Augmented Latent Intrinsics addresses that trade-off by adding dense, pixel-aligned visual features to a latent-intrinsic relighting model and refining it through self-supervision on unlabeled pairs of real images.

ALI improves relighting quality, with particularly strong benefits for glossy, metallic, and transparent materials. These findings indicate that useful semantic features do not necessarily preserve all the information needed for light transfer. They also establish generative relighting as a practical probe for measuring which physical cues visual encoders retain.
summary.tldr: ALI improves relighting by preserving dense visual cues, revealing a trade-off between semantic abstraction and physical fidelity.

title: Relighting as a Probe of Visual Priors via Augmented Latent Intrinsics

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are evolving from conversational systems into strong reasoners for tasks such as Olympiad mathematics and competitive programming. While scaling parameters and test-time computation has driven progress, a key bottleneck is the lack of high-quality training problems: human-curated datasets are costly and limited, while existing synthetic corpora are often too easy or narrow. PromptCoT showed that injecting rationales into prompt synthesis increases problem difficulty. Building on this, we present PromptScale, a scalable framework that replaces hand-crafted heuristics with an expectation-maximization (EM) loop, where rationales are iteratively refined to guide prompt construction. This produces problems that are both harder and more diverse than prior corpora. The synthetic prompts support two post-training regimes: (1) Self-Play, where strong models improve autonomously via verifiable feedback without stronger teachers; and (2) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), where weaker models learn from teacher-distilled traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. In self-play, applying PromptScale to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 sets new state-of-the-art results at the 30B scale, with +4.4, +4.8, and +5.3 on AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25, +6.1 and +5.0 on LiveCodeBench v5/v6, and +35 Elo on Codeforces. In SFT, training Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct solely on synthetic prompts boosts accuracy to 73.1 (AIME 24), 65.6 (AIME 25), and 53.4 (LiveCodeBench v5), surpassing models trained on human or hybrid data. Analyses further confirm that PromptScale yields fundamentally harder and distributionally distinct problems. These results establish prompt synthesis as a new axis for scaling reasoning and position PromptScale as a scalable foundation for future open-source models. The implementation is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/PromptCoT.

paragraphs: Reasoning training depends on having sufficiently challenging and varied problems. Human-written collections are expensive and limited, while synthetic collections can be too easy or narrow. PromptScale builds on rationale-guided problem synthesis, replacing handcrafted heuristics with an expectation-maximization loop that repeatedly refines the rationales used to construct prompts.

The generated prompts support two training settings. Strong models use self-play with verifiable feedback and no stronger teacher. Weaker models use supervised fine-tuning with reasoning traces distilled from a teacher. This separates the production of challenging problems from the choice of how a model learns to solve them.

In self-play, the evaluated Qwen3 model achieves new state-of-the-art results at the 30B scale across the reported mathematics and programming evaluations. In supervised training, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct trained solely on synthetic prompts surpasses compared models trained on human or hybrid data. Further analysis finds that PromptScale's problems are harder and distributionally distinct. The findings support improving the training-problem supply as an additional route to scaling reasoning alongside model size and test-time computation.
summary.tldr: PromptScale iteratively refines rationale-guided problem synthesis to produce harder, more diverse training prompts for self-play and supervised reasoning.

title: Scaling Prompt Synthesis for Large Language Model Reasoning

abstract: This position paper argues that ICML should require a minimal drift-audit artifact for papers whose main claims materially rely on hosted LLM APIs. Hosted APIs can change behavior over time, undermining the scientific interpretability of results even when evaluation code and prompts are held fixed. While existing proposals address API contracts and change reporting, there is not yet a widely adopted, venue-aligned standard for attaching a minimal drift-audit artifact to results that rely on hosted endpoints. The paper proposes a lightweight artifact consisting of a small suite of invariant-checking probes (e.g., schema, tool-call, or refusal invariants), machine-readable provenance metadata, and a rerun script that can detect and characterize post-publication behavioral drift at bounded cost. It further argues that provider-side behavioral versioning and machine-readable changelogs are enabling infrastructure that would make drift-aware reporting more reliable and less burdensome. The paper concludes with concrete actions for conferences, providers, and tool builders, and with falsifiable predictions about improved replication stability and reduced time-to-diagnosis when results stop reproducing.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses a reproducibility problem in research that depends on hosted language-model APIs. An endpoint can change its behavior even when researchers preserve their prompts and evaluation code. That makes later differences in results harder to interpret because the externally supplied component may no longer behave as it did during the original study.

The authors propose that ICML require a small drift-audit artifact when a paper’s main claims materially depend on these APIs. The artifact would combine probes checking expected properties, machine-readable records of provenance, and a script for rerunning the checks. Suggested properties include response schemas, tool calls, and refusal behavior. The goal is to detect and characterize changes at bounded cost.

The paper also argues for provider-supported behavioral versions and machine-readable changelogs to make this reporting more reliable and manageable. It assigns actions to conferences, providers, and tool builders. Its anticipated benefits—more stable replication and faster diagnosis of failures to reproduce—are presented as falsifiable predictions, giving the proposal outcomes that could subsequently be tested.
summary.tldr: Research relying on hosted LLM APIs should include small, rerunnable artifacts that document and detect behavioral drift.

title: Position: ICML Should Treat Hosted LLM APIs as Versioned Dependencies and Require Drift-Audit Artifacts

abstract: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems have transformative potential across many domains, but also present profound new risks to child safety. AI is increasingly being misused to create AI-generated child sexual abuse material, facilitate child sexual exploitation, and reduce barriers to harm. In this position paper, we argue that protecting children from AI-facilitated abuse requires new approaches to AI safety. Existing safety techniques assume data accessibility, transparency, and evaluation practices that are incompatible with the ethical and legal constraints surrounding child sexual abuse material. We examine how these constraints create new technical challenges, such as limitations on dataset auditing, red teaming, and fine-tuning prevention. In turn, we outline 15 open problems in child safety across the AI development lifecycle—from dataset curation and model design to deployment and long-term maintenance. We propose targeted recommendations for researchers, developers, and policymakers to bridge the gap between theoretical AI safety and the realities of child protection. Our work aims to reframe child safety as a central, safety-critical dimension for AI research, motivating new work that translates responsible AI principles into concrete safeguards against the exploitation of children.

paragraphs: This paper argues that preventing AI-facilitated child sexual abuse requires safety approaches designed around child protection’s specific constraints. The authors describe risks involving generated child sexual abuse material and tools that facilitate exploitation. Their focus is on how AI research and development can produce concrete safeguards against those harms.

Conventional safety practices often assume researchers can access relevant data, inspect it transparently, and evaluate systems through established procedures. Ethical and legal restrictions surrounding abuse material make those assumptions incompatible with this setting. The paper examines resulting challenges for dataset auditing, red teaming, and preventing harmful fine-tuning.

The authors organize 15 open problems across the development lifecycle, from data curation and model design to deployment and ongoing maintenance. They also propose targeted recommendations for researchers, developers, and policymakers. This framing makes child safety a continuing technical and governance responsibility across a system’s lifespan. The intended contribution is to connect broad responsible-AI principles with the practical constraints that safeguards must respect to protect children.
summary.tldr: The paper outlines 15 open problems for child-protection safeguards that respect the distinctive legal and ethical constraints of this domain.

abstract: In this paper, we present a graphical model for protein secondary structure prediction. This model extends segmental semi-Markov models (SSMM) to exploit multiple sequence alignment profiles which contain information from evolutionarily related sequences. A novel parameterized model is proposed as the likelihood function for the SSMM to capture the segmental conformation. By incorporating the information from long range interactions in beta-sheets, this model is capable of carrying out inference on contact maps. The numerical results on benchmark data sets show that incorporating the profiles results in substantial improvements and the generalization performance is promising.

This model extends segmental semi-Markov models (SSMM) to exploit multiple sequence alignment profiles which contain information from evolutionarily related sequences. A novel parameterized model is proposed as the likelihood function for the SSMM to capture the segmental conformation. By incorporating the information from long range interactions in beta-sheets, this model is capable of carrying out inference on contact maps. The numerical results on benchmark data sets show that incorporating the profiles results in substantial improvements and the generalization performance is promising.

paragraphs: This paper develops a graphical model for predicting protein secondary structure. Its starting point is a segmental semi-Markov model, which represents structure in segments. The extension lets the model use multiple sequence alignment profiles, bringing information from evolutionarily related sequences into the prediction process rather than relying solely on the sequence being analyzed.

A new parameterized likelihood function describes segmental conformation within this framework. This gives the model a way to assess structural segments using the alignment information. The model also incorporates long-range interactions in beta-sheets, connecting structural information across separated parts of a sequence and enabling inference about contact maps.

Benchmark results show substantial improvements when alignment profiles are incorporated, and the authors describe the generalization results as promising. The stated evidence supports the usefulness of related-sequence information for this prediction task. The broader contribution is a modeling framework that accommodates both segment-level structure and long-range interactions, rather than treating these as unrelated sources of evidence.
summary.tldr: A segment-based graphical model improves protein secondary structure prediction by incorporating related-sequence profiles and beta-sheet interactions.

title: A graphical model for protein secondary structure prediction

abstract: We propose a multiclass (MC) classification approach to text categorization(TC). To fully take advantage of both positive and negative training examples,a maximal figure-of-merit (MFoM) learning algorithm is introduced to trainhigh performance MC classifiers. In contrast to conventional binaryclassification, the proposed MC scheme assigns a uniform score function toeach category for each given test sample, and thus the classical Bayesdecision rules can now be applied. Since all the MC MFoM classifiers aresimultaneously trained, we expect them to be more robust and work better thanthe binary MFoM classifiers, which are trained separately and are known togive the best TC performance. Experimental results on the Reuters-21578 TCtask indicate that the MC MFoM classifiers achieve a micro-averaging F1 valueof 0.377, which is significantly better than 0.138, obtained with the binaryMFoM classifiers, for the categories with less than 4 training samples. Furthermore, for all 90 categories, most with large training sizes, the MCMFoM classifiers give a micro-averaging F1 value of 0.888, better than 0.884,obtained with the binary MFoM classifiers.

paragraphs: The paper proposes training text-category classifiers together using a maximal figure-of-merit learning approach. The goal is to make full use of both positive and negative training examples. Instead of training each category as a separate binary problem, the multiclass scheme gives every category a score through a uniform scoring function.

This shared scoring setup allows classical Bayes decision rules to be applied across categories. Because the classifiers are trained simultaneously, the authors expect greater robustness than separately trained binary MFoM classifiers. That expectation motivates the design; the experiments then assess whether the joint approach improves classification, particularly where training examples are scarce.

On Reuters-21578 categories with fewer than four training samples, the multiclass approach achieves micro-averaged F1 of 0.377, compared with 0.138 for binary MFoM. Across all 90 categories, most with larger training sets, the scores are 0.888 and 0.884 respectively. These results show a much larger reported improvement for the sparsely represented categories than for the collection overall.
summary.tldr: Joint multiclass MFoM training improves text categorization, with especially large reported gains for categories containing very few training examples.

title: A MFoM learning approach to robust multiclass multi-label text categorization

abstract: The paper is concerned with learning to rank, which is to construct a model or a function for ranking objects. Learning to rank is useful for document retrieval, collaborative filtering, and many other applications. Several methods for learning to rank have been proposed, which take object pairs as ‘instances’ in learning. We refer to them as the pairwise approach in this paper. Although the pairwise approach offers advantages, it ignores the fact that ranking is a prediction task on list of objects. The paper postulates that learning to rank should adopt the listwise approach in which lists of objects are used as ‘instances’ in learning. The paper proposes a new probabilistic method for the approach. Specifically it introduces two probability models, respectively referred to as permutation probability and top k probability, to define a listwise loss function for learning. Neural Network and Gradient Descent are then employed as model and algorithm in the learning method. Experimental results on information retrieval show that the proposed listwise approach performs better than the pairwise approach.

paragraphs: Learning to rank builds a function that orders objects, such as documents returned by a retrieval system. Many approaches train on pairs of objects, learning which member of each pair should come first. This paper argues that training should also reflect the fact that the eventual prediction is an ordered list of objects.

The proposed listwise approach uses lists as training instances. It introduces two probability models, called permutation probability and top-k probability, to construct a loss function for learning from those lists. These probabilistic descriptions provide a way to evaluate ranking predictions at the list level. A neural network supplies the model, and gradient descent is used to train it.

Experiments on information retrieval show that the proposed listwise approach performs better than the pairwise approach in the reported evaluation. The finding supports the paper's argument for aligning the unit of training with the form of the prediction. The contribution includes both that change in perspective and a concrete probabilistic method for putting listwise learning into practice.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic listwise ranking method trains on lists and outperforms a pairwise approach in information-retrieval experiments.

title: Learning to rank: from pairwise approach to listwise approach

abstract: Deep networks have been successfully applied to unsupervised feature learning for single modalities (e.g., text, images or audio). In this work, we propose a novel application of deep networks to learn features over multiple modalities. We present a series of tasks for multimodal learning and show how to train deep networks that learn features to address these tasks. In particular, we demonstrate cross modality feature learning, where better features for one modality (e.g., video) can be learned if multiple modalities (e.g., audio and video) are present at feature learning time. Furthermore, we show how to learn a shared representation between modalities and evaluate it on a unique task, where the classifier is trained with audio-only data but tested with video-only data and vice-versa. Our methods are validated on the CUAVE and AVLetters datasets with an audio-visual speech classification task, demonstrating best published visual speech classification on AVLetters and effective shared representation learning.

In particular, we demonstrate cross modality feature learning, where better features for one modality (e.g., video) can be learned if multiple modalities (e.g., audio and video) are present at feature learning time. Furthermore, we show how to learn a shared representation between modalities and evaluate it on a unique task, where the classifier is trained with audio-only data but tested with video-only data and vice-versa. Our methods are validated on the CUAVE and AVLetters datasets with an audio-visual speech classification task, demonstrating best published visual speech classification on AVLetters and effective shared representation learning.

paragraphs: This paper extends deep unsupervised feature learning from individual data types to multiple modalities, particularly audio and video. It develops training approaches for several multimodal tasks. A key question is whether information from one modality can improve the features learned for another, even when the eventual representation is used for just one.

The authors demonstrate this kind of cross-modality feature learning: having audio and video available during feature learning can produce better video features. They also learn a shared representation connecting the modalities. To test that connection, they train a classifier on audio-only data and evaluate it on video-only data, and perform the reverse transfer as well.

Evaluation uses audio-visual speech classification on CUAVE and AVLetters. The paper reports the best published visual speech classification result on AVLetters and effective shared representation learning. These findings support two related benefits of multimodal training: improving features for an individual modality and learning a representation that supports classification transfer between different input modalities.
summary.tldr: Joint audio-video learning improves single-modality features and enables classifiers to transfer between audio-only and video-only data.

title: Multimodal Deep Learning

abstract: We present a novel approach for training kernel Support Vector Machines, establish learning runtime guarantees for our method that are better then those of any other known kernelized SVM optimization approach, and show that our method works well in practice compared to existing alternatives.
originalAbstract: We present a novel approach for training kernel Support Vector Machines, establish learning runtime guarantees for our method that are better then those of any other known kernelized SVM optimization approach, and show that our method works well in practice compared to existing alternatives.

paragraphs: Training a kernel support vector machine requires an optimization procedure, so the computational behavior of that procedure is part of making the learning method useful. This paper introduces a new training approach called the Kernelized Stochastic Batch Perceptron. Its central subject is the efficiency of learning kernel SVMs.

The authors establish learning-runtime guarantees that are better than those of any other kernelized SVM optimization approach known in the comparison they state. This is a theoretical claim about the proposed method's runtime guarantees. The significance is that the paper supports its efficiency argument through analysis of the learning procedure, giving a formal basis for comparing it with existing optimization approaches.

The paper also reports that the method works well in practice relative to existing alternatives. That practical finding complements the theoretical contribution without making an unrestricted claim that every training run will be faster. Taken together, the stated results present a new kernel SVM training method backed by stronger runtime guarantees and favorable practical comparisons.
summary.tldr: The Kernelized Stochastic Batch Perceptron trains kernel SVMs with stronger stated learning-runtime guarantees and favorable practical performance.

title: The Kernelized Stochastic Batch Perceptron

abstract: Convex regression is a promising area for bridging statistical estimation and deterministic convex optimization. We develop a new piecewise linear convex regression method that uses the Convex Adaptive Partitioning (CAP) estimator in an ensemble setting, Ensemble Convex Adaptive Partitioning (E-CAP). The ensembles alleviate some problems associated with convex piecewise linear estimators, such as instability when used to approximate constraints or objective functions for optimization, while maintaining desirable properties, such as consistency and O(n log(n)^2) computational complexity. We empirically demonstrate that E-CAP outperforms existing convex regression methods both when used for prediction and optimization. We then apply E-CAP to device modeling and constraint approximation for geometric programming based circuit design.
originalAbstract: Convex regression is a promising area for bridging statistical estimation and deterministic convex optimization. We develop a new piecewise linear convex regression method that uses the Convex Adaptive Partitioning (CAP) estimator in an ensemble setting, Ensemble Convex Adaptive Partitioning (E-CAP). The ensembles alleviate some problems associated with convex piecewise linear estimators, such as instability when used to approximate constraints or objective functions for optimization, while maintaining desirable properties, such as consistency and O(n log(n)^2) computational complexity. We empirically demonstrate that E-CAP outperforms existing convex regression methods both when used for prediction and optimization. We then apply E-CAP to device modeling and constraint approximation for geometric programming based circuit design.

paragraphs: Convex regression learns functions with a shape that is useful for convex optimization. This makes it relevant when a fitted model will become an objective or a constraint in a later decision problem. The paper addresses instability in piecewise linear convex estimators, an issue that can matter when those learned functions guide optimization.

The authors introduce Ensemble Convex Adaptive Partitioning, or E-CAP, by using the Convex Adaptive Partitioning estimator in an ensemble. Combining estimators alleviates some of the problems associated with individual piecewise linear fits. The method retains consistency and a computational complexity of O(n log(n)^2), preserving stated statistical and computational properties while improving stability.

Experiments report that E-CAP outperforms existing convex regression methods for both prediction and optimization. Evaluating both uses matters because a fitted function may be useful as a predictor and also serve as part of an optimization problem. The paper applies E-CAP to device modeling and approximating constraints for circuit design based on geometric programming.
summary.tldr: E-CAP combines convex regression estimators to reduce instability while retaining consistency and supporting prediction and circuit-design optimization.

title: Ensemble Methods for Convex Regression with Applications to Geometric Programming Based Circuit Design
